## 一场"股神爆仓"背后的三重镜像
投资TALK君讲了一个天才陨落的故事，但真正值得琢磨的**不是这个股神，而是他爆仓的时间点**——恰好卡在美联储会议前夜、凯文沃什信用崩塌的那个48小时窗口。这不是巧合，而是**同一种病灶的两种症状**：一个是杠杆玩家用别人的钱豪赌方向，一个是新任美联储主席用嘴巴豪赌市场信任。两者本质相同——**在没有真金白银兑现之前，先把信用透支干净**。市场对凯文沃什的态度反转（"你嘴上鹰派但不愿付出行动"），和 Citadel 对爆仓者的态度反转（"你嘴上对冲但杠杆全押一边"），是同一个市场机制在不同尺度上的运作。
## 一个跨领域的意外连接：Meta 的"三方 token 支出" ≈ 传统制造业的"电费账单"
大多数人只看到 Meta 财报里 margin 下滑、运营开支上升。但视频里藏了一条容易被忽略的线索——**管理层专门把"第三方 token 消耗"单列出来讲**。这在会计意义上是件极不寻常的事：一家自己训练 LLaMA 的公司，居然把 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的 API 费用摆到台面。这暗示了一个大科技行业尚未定价的新现实——*

item.title: [Lex Clips] The lies behind the Civil War | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最深的反讽：邦联为了"州权"建立了美国史上最集权的政府

大多数人记住的南北战争故事是：南方为"州权"而战，北方为集权而战。但真相是一个完美的历史黑色幽默——邦联(Confederacy)在其短暂的四年生命里，建立了直到20世纪深处美国都未曾出现的最具侵入性的中央政府。

  • 第一部全国征兵法：邦联，1862年春（比联邦早一年）
  • 第一部累进所得税：邦联
  • "实物税"(tax in kind)：直接从农民手里拿走一部分收成
  • 中止人身保护令(habeas corpus)：邦联和林肯都做了
  • 政府强征马、骡、奴隶劳动力

一个以"限制中央政府权力"为立国理由的国家，为了活下去，不得不做出比它反对的对手更极端的集权行为。这不是偶然——任何以"反某物"为核心身份建立的组织，最终往往会在生存压力下变成它所反对的那个东西。这个模式你能在苏联反资本主义却最终建立国家资本主义、硅谷反企业官僚却建立起自己的官僚层里反复看到。

二、"州权"是一个空心概念——它其实是"我不喜欢现在的联邦政府"的代称

Gallagher 抛出了一个杀伤力极强的教学法：让声称南方是为"州权"而战的人列出"前三大州权"，甚至前两个。结果只有一个——奴隶制。

这里有一个跨领域的洞察："州权"和商业世界里的"用户自由"、科技领域的"开源精神"、政治光谱各端的"言论自由"是同构的修辞武器——它们都是上下文依赖的空概念(context-dependent empty signifiers)，谁在防守就由谁来用： - 1812年战争时，是新英格兰(北方)在谈州权，甚至在哈特福德大会上摸到了分裂的边缘 - 1850年代，南方谈州权来保护奴隶制 - 同一时期，北方也谈州权——通过"人身自由法"抵抗《逃亡奴隶法》

原则不是原则，是位置。一个概念如果在历史中总是被"当下最不满意联邦的那一方"拿来使用，那它就不是一个立场，而是一个工具。这一点在今天关于"地方自治"、"平台中立"、"技术自由"的辩论里，几乎一比一地重复。

三、被忽视的隐藏机制：邦联对自己士兵的"契约诈骗"

这段谈话里藏着一个很少被讨论的细节——邦联通过反复修改服役合同，把志愿兵变成了事实上的终身兵：

  1. 1861年春：应征1年，大家觉得战争几个月就结束
  2. 1862年春：还差几个月退伍时，Congress 突然把所有人延长到3年
  3. 后来又改成"战争持续多久你就服役多久"(for the duration)

这里有一个惊人的制度演化模式：任何长期危机中的组织，都会逐步侵蚀最初的自愿契约条款，直到自愿变成不可退出。这和现代的科技公司用户协议、订阅服务的自动续费、加密货币项目的锁仓机制，甚至婚姻/职业承诺的社会化压力，是同一种"契约不对称通货膨胀"。

一个更冷酷的观察：邦联士兵之所以接受这种契约撕毁，是因为他们已经"沉没成本"太多——已经打了一年仗，看着战友死去。"契约诈骗"最容易在受害者已经投入巨大情感和道德代价的关系中成功。这不是南北战争的特殊现象，这是人类心理的普遍陷阱。

一个额外的"啊哈"点

注意 Gallagher 说的一个细节：邦联没有政党，因为"建国者不希望有政党"。但结果是什么？没有政党的邦联，内部分裂成了"让中央政府做任何事"派（Davis, Lee） 和 "州权原教旨主义"派（副总统 Stephens）——没有正式政党结构的组织，会自发形成非正式的、更难调和的派系。这也是为什么"扁平化"、"去中心化"的组织往往在关键决策时比传统层级组织更难运转——结构消失不会让冲突消失，只会让冲突变成人身化的、无法通过程序解决的。

这是历史给今天所有 DAO、开源社区、平台经济的一句提醒。

📝 转录文本

两个"共和国"都想认领华盛顿

Both sides, both these republics claimed, for example, George Washington.

Yes, they both claim — I'll leave it at that. They both claim George Washington. They wanted to be right with the man, which is what George Washington was. He's the indispensable man, no question. Both sides wanted him on their side. They both quoted Thomas Jefferson. Although Confederates were a little more leery of Jefferson cuz he's too complicated for them sometimes. But no, they wanted to be right with the founders and claim to be right with the founders. The Confederates would say, "The Constitution allowed slavery. What are you talking about we're out of step with the Constitution. We're in step with the con- You're the ones who are out of step with the Constitution."

"州权"这个概念的两面

What about the topic of states' rights? At the very least — state rights.

State rights, I mean, I love the way people use it. With the Civil War they associate it solely with Southern states, of course. State rights is always available in United States history for somebody who's not happy with what the federal government is doing.

During the War of 1812 it was New England that most often talked about resorting to state rights. They had a convention where they sort of wandered over towards secession territory in the Hartford Convention.

We think of it as state rights because as you lead up to the Civil War, you hear white Southerners talking about it all the time. "We need our state rights."

追问：具体是哪些"州权"？

I always love to ask people who say that, "What are all the state rights? Give me the list — the state rights that the white South is concerned. Give me the top three. No, really — just give me the top two."

There's only one. The state right that they're worried about is the right of their state to interpose its power between a federal government that might try to interfere with slavery and a state government that wants to maintain it. That's the state right that matters then.

Northern states also resorted to state rights during the ramp up to the Civil War with what were called personal liberty laws. They tried to interpose their state power in between a federal government that would use its power to force escaped enslaved people back into slavery.

It's whoever's unhappy with the federal government — the concept of state rights is available, and both sides used it.

黑色反讽：邦联建立了美国史上最集权的政府

And of course, the beautiful dark ironic hypocrisy was illustrated by the Confederacy when they were the first to pass a national draft in American history. Like — irony is wonderful in history.

Another thing that I love to teach is that the most intrusive central government in American history, by far until deep into the 20th century, was the Confederate central government, because it had to do things to keep the war going that it couldn't have done unless the central government stepped in, such as:

  • passing the first national conscription law in American history — the US government forced people into uniform before the Civil War, but the Confederates did it first, in the spring of 1862
  • a national graduated income tax
  • when taxing didn't work, when their money became so devalued, they then passed what they called the "tax in kind" — they would take a percentage of your crop
  • they allowed the government to impress horses and mules and enslaved labor to work on [war projects]

All of these were intrusions from the central government that drove true state rights people crazy in the Confederacy.

没有政党，却有派系

Confederates didn't have political parties because they said the founders didn't want them, so we won't have them. But what they did have was a sort of nationalist "we're going to let the central government do whatever it needs to do" — that's Jefferson Davis's wing, and Robert E. Lee's over there, too.

And the people like the Vice President, Alexander Stephens, who said "you can't do all this stuff because the states should have more power."

The only reason the war lasted as long as it did is because the central government did things no one ever would have believed they would do. He [Davis] also got rid of habeas corpus, just like Abraham Lincoln did, in selected situations.

志愿兵变成"终身兵"：契约的反复改写

And of course we should really emphasize that on both sides those volunteers — the Confederacy is a very large number of people percentage-wise that volunteered to fight. And then I believe the volunteer period was 1 year. And then there's all kind of funky stuff that the government started doing to trap those people into then serving —

Here's what the Confederacy did.

Nobody thinks the war is going to last a long time in the spring of 1861. So if you enlist for a year, that's probably plenty of time to finish this war. Well, a year goes by and a significant percentage of the Confederate men under arms are due to get out.

So what the Confederate Congress did was pass conscription:

  • Step 1: We're going to make everybody liable to 3 years service. And in the midst of doing that, all you guys who volunteered for 1 year are now in for 2 more years. Well, that outraged — "you're breaking faith with us," they said.
  • Step 2: But they didn't stop there. Later they revised it when the war kept going on and then the 3-years guys were going to get out. Then the Congress stepped in and said "you're in for the duration."

The bottom line: if the Confederacy ever gets you in uniform, you don't get out, because they keep changing the rules on you.

征兵作为对个人权利的根本侵犯

And that was considered — national conscription was considered a fundamental abridgement of individual rights by many people. That's something the government should never force a citizen into uniform. A citizen should volunteer their service.

US government waited a year, then it did it in the spring of 1863. Although it always respected original terms of enlistment. Never made it "the war for the duration" the way the Confederacy did.

大多数人记住的南北战争故事是：南方为"州权"而战，北方为集权而战。但真相是一个完美的历史黑色幽默——**邦联(Confederacy)在其短暂的四年生命里，建立了直到20世纪深处美国都未曾出现的最具侵入性的中央政府**。
- 第一部全国征兵法：邦联，1862年春（比联邦早一年） - 第一部累进所得税：邦联 - "实物税"(tax in kind)：直接从农民手里拿走一部分收成 - 中止人身保护令(habeas corpus)：邦联和林肯都做了 - 政府强征马、骡、奴隶劳动力
一个以"限制中央政府权力"为立国理由的国家，为了活下去，不得不做出比它反对的对手更极端的集权行为。这不是偶然——**任何以"反某物"为核心身份建立的组织，最终往往会在生存压力下变成它所反对的那个东西**。这个模式你能在苏联反资本主义却最终建立国家资本主义、硅谷反企业官僚却建立起自己的官僚层里反复看到。
## 二、"州权"是一个空心概念——它其实是"我不喜欢现在的联邦政府"的代称
Gallagher 抛出了一个杀伤力极强的教学法：**让声称南

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] 149. 亲历中美neo labs资本狂潮，和清华刘子鸣聊：AI for AI、机制可解释性和Max Tegmark
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最令人意外的观察：他把自己当成模型训练了60天，无意间做了一场东方式修行

刘子鸣讲了一件被访谈匆匆带过、却极其反常识的事——他花了大约两个月，每天在实验室做AI实验之前，先强迫自己预测"这次训练曲线会长什么样"，把自己的大脑当成一个"原初模型"来监督训练。40-50天后，他"suddenly grok"，突然获得了跨模态的直觉预测能力。

这件事的诡异之处在于：他用的方法论，几乎是一比一复刻了佛教内观（vipassana）和斯多葛派"预演不测"（premeditatio malorum）的认知训练结构——在事件发生前先形成预测，事件发生后与实际比对，让大脑在预测误差中重塑内部表征。区别只在于：僧侣观察的是情绪起伏，斯多葛派观察的是命运变故，而他观察的是loss curve。

更耐人寻味的是，他最终决定把"我"外包给一个模型，是因为"人的带宽只能一天做一两个实验，无法训练一千年"。这句话可以反过来读：AI for AI 的技术路线，本质上是一个物理学家不愿等待自己开悟的加速手段——他想把自己60天的Grok压缩到机器上做1000次然后收获。这是一种非常独特的、带有存在焦虑色彩的科研哲学。

二、被忽视的隐藏结构：OPHIS 不是方法论，是"科研的世界语"

他提到自己在构建的方法论叫 O-P-H-I-S（Observation → Problem → Hypothesis → Intervention → Speedup），并说要"把研究结构化成一种语言"。

大多数人会把这理解成"科研SOP"。但如果把它跟历史上其他"语法化尝试"并置，会发现它属于一个非常独特的知识论谱系：

  • 林奈用拉丁双名法把生物学从"博物"变成"分类学"
  • 弗雷格发明谓词逻辑把哲学思辨变成可机械演算的系统
  • 柴门霍夫造世界语，试图让"人类沟通"可训练可标准化
  • 刘子鸣造 OPHIS，本质是想让"科研思维链"变成可训练的语料

一旦看到这个类比，就能理解为什么他坚持"必须先手工收集数据、每天只能人肉标 10 条"——这不是效率问题，这是造一门新语言必须经历的Ur-corpus阶段。所有可训练的语言都必须先有一批"祖本"。这也解释了他为什么反复强调"1% 的 paper 才有 chain of thought"——他真正的抱怨是：几十年来AI学界集体丢弃了思维链的原始语料，只留下了压缩后的成品。

三、跨领域连接：New Lab 融资狂潮，是学者阶层的"社会传染"，不是技术判断

他讲了一个极具社会学价值的细节：他从"看不上创业"到"决定创业"，转折点不是任何技术突破，而是MIT时期的同门同学 Han Guo 在斯坦福对他说"子鸣，我要创业了"。两个原本鄙视产业界的"孔乙己长衫"同门里，一个先脱下了长衫，另一个立刻感到"我是不是不够 aggressive"。

这是典型的Peer-based Contagion（同侪传染），跟金融市场的Herd Behavior、青春期的risk-taking、甚至宗教改宗的社会学模型完全同构。文献里管这个叫"参照群体的相变"——当你的peer group里最相似的那个节点翻转了信念，你自己的翻转概率会非线性跳升。

这对理解"2026年New Lab狂潮"的本质极其关键： - 大众叙事说：这是技术窗口打开了（世界模型/Auto Research成熟） - 资本叙事说：这是估值窗口打开了（早期青年科学家溢价） - 但真实的一阶动力可能是：顶级学术圈里第一批"叛徒"翻转后，整个参照群体正在发生相变——不是技术判断成熟了，是社会许可（social license）到位了

这就能解释为什么他会说"太疯狂了"、"我没有对比所以说不出来多疯狂"——因为他自己也是这场社会相变里的一个节点，正在被自己无法完全客观分析的社会力量卷入。这也预示着，如果第一批 New Lab 有一两个高调失败，可能引发比技术回撤更快的"反向传染"。

四、一个几乎没人注意到的悖论

访谈里有一个技术性极强、却在哲学上非常刺眼的矛盾：

"AI for X 的前提是 X 有大量数据。但 AI for AI，AI research 恰恰没有大量高质量数据。"

刘子鸣提出的解决方案是——用 Physics of AI 先造出结构，用结构去引导数据收集，再用这些数据训练能自动做 Physics of AI 的 AI。

这是一个完美的循环因果结构，跟"用编译器编译自己"的 bootstrapping、跟哥德尔第二不完备定理里"系统不能证明自身一致性"、跟生物学里"第一个能自我复制的分子从哪里来"——是同一族问题的不同伪装。历史上这类问题的解法从来不是逻辑推演，而是寻找一个足够小的"种子"（seed）作为奇点——第一版C编译器是用汇编写的，第一个自复制RNA只需要几十个碱基。

所以他真正的赌注，不是"AI能不能研究AI"，而是：能不能找到那个足够小、足够精妙的"种子结构"，让整个循环可以启动。他的 KAN 网络、他的 60 天自我训练、他的 OPHIS 语法——这些看起来毫无关联的工作，其实都是在赌不同版本的"seed"。

这也是为什么他反复强调"原创性"——在一个自举系统里，seed的选择决定了整个后续系统的可能性空间。种子选错了，就再也长不出想要的东西。

📝 转录文本

开场：一场资本狂潮的旁观与亲历

Hello everyone, I'm Xiaojun. We have interviewed Xie Sainin and Hong Letong before. They are from NewLab in Europe and the United States. But today's phenomenon is not only in overseas. In 2026, China also launched a new lab. These teachers or students with research backgrounds are becoming new fans of the first-class market. They are generally very young, have a background in civil science, and have started their first business.

在还没有产品的时候就能以估值数亿美金融资。当下资本涌入最活跃的方向是世界模型和 auto research。Auto research 就可以叫做 AI for AI。

I'm curious about the reality and the cause of this phenomenon. In this episode, I invited Professor Liu Ziming, PI of Shanghai Qizhi Institute, who is an assistant professor of the Institute of AI in Tsinghua University. He graduated from Peking University and MIT and is a first-time online student. He just returned to China in March this year and joined the founding company Circle Intelligence. He described this new capital trend with "too crazy".

We talked about the newness and sound of China and the newness of the new labs in the US and he explored a non-typical AI for AI narrative. Next, I will interview Liu Ziming.

一、回国、入职、融资：三个月的"疯狂"

张小珺： I returned to China in March. I entered Tsinghua in late April. I started to get paid in late May. During this process, I was so crazy. How to say? Anyway, no matter it's AI for Science or World Model, or AFL-AI, I think both of them are in a very formal state in the market. It's true that everyone is in this interaction, and everyone is doing the project very quickly.

Hello, Ziming. Say hello to the audience.

刘子鸣： Hello, everyone.

张小珺： Can you introduce yourself and talk about your work and current status?

刘子鸣： Okay. First of all, thank you for inviting me. I am Liu Ziming. I am an assistant professor at the Institute of Humanities and Technology at Tsinghua University. At the same time, I am also a construction PI at the Shanghai Permanent Research Institute. I also joined the business and became a chief scientist in "The Soul of the Soul".

I studied physics in Peking University. Then I went to MIT and did AI and physics cross-examination. After that, I did AI as a brain scientist for half a year in Stanford. My professor's name is Max Tegmark. He started promoting AI for Physics in 2012. And the earliest mechanismic interpretability was announced at the end of 2022 and early 2023. This is also the direction that Tang Jie said that the government should invest billions of dollars in. It is also the direction that AmpliFabric is working on. We started to plan this in the end of 2022 and early 2023.

二、从物理到 AI：为什么"派对结束了"

张小珺： How did you get from physics to AI? I think many people, including Yao Shunyu, right?

刘子鸣： I think many people who do physics have such an experience. At first, doing physics, I thought physics was a very beautiful, very challenging thing in terms of intelligence, which is a very difficult thing. So I was attracted to physics. But then I started to feel that the party is over. This is also a quote from Gao Neng. He said, "The feast is over." I feel that there are not so many problems left for young people. But AI is a field that gives us young people a lot of opportunities.

I was in my second year of college. I was in my seventh year. I was interested in the online business. It's the "Generative Adversarial Network". At that time, I felt that this thing was particularly important to me and it seems to be not so difficult in mathematics. It's very fancy. And then it happened to be double-beat by theoretical physics and experimental physics. At that time, I didn't know what to do. Because theoretical physics is very difficult and it's not as good as Yao Shunyu.

Yao Shengyu, by the way, is also an idol of ours. During his undergraduate years, he published two PR articles.

张小珺： Are you in the same class?

刘子鸣： He's in a bigger class than me. I was in Tsinghua. I heard about his legend. I was thinking about doing experiments in physics. I thought I couldn't do it in theory, so I did it. But it turned out to be even worse. It's a bit like, I don't know, Albert Einstein or Yang Zhengning. Okay, I'll stop here and give myself a sticker.

I feel like I only make things more confusing when I enter the lab. I've actually participated in some experiments. For example, I've done a magnetic fluid before. It turned out to be full of hands and faces. Then I thought, oh, I don't seem to be suitable for the experiment. So at that time, I was quite depressed. I felt that I wasn't good at both theoretical and experimental physics.

张小珺： So what was next?

刘子鸣： And then I happened to see a thing like this. I thought, oh, this thing is very important to me. So I'm going to start doing it. But maybe I was a little cautious at first. I just thought I didn't want to give up my physics background easily. So at first, we did more AI for physics. At first, for physics, we mainly did high-performance imaging. This is high energy phenomenology. This is actually quite similar to what we are studying in physics of AI. It is neither a complete theory nor an experiment. It's a kind of "village". It's a bridge that can bridge theory and experiment.

The essence of AI for Physics is that your service target is physics, but your service target of AI is AI. Yes, that's why I did AI for Physics from 2017 to 2012. Actually, at that time, we were already talking about concepts like AI scientists and AI physicists. But it was also at this time of the year, that chat GPT came out. I think there aren't many sexy things in physics that are worth doing. So I changed the roles of AI and physics. It's not AI for physics, but physics for AI. More specifically, physics of AI. I want to use physics theory and physics thinking to help us better understand and design AI.

张小珺： So you've started to work on AI in your major. Have you done it?

刘子鸣： Yes, I started doing it in my major. My first project was to use the GaN network to do a task in high-energy physics. But like many people, the first project was obviously unsuccessful. But during this process, I learned a lot of things about AI. And then I slowly learned that AI can bring me this sense of accomplishment. It's much more than physics. So I learned and learned and learned. I slowly put all my time on AI.

张小珺： So what was your state when you graduated from the undergraduate program?

刘子鸣： When I graduated from the undergraduate program, I published three articles on AI for Physics. Two articles were related to high-energy physics. The other one was about Physics for AI. We used quantum thinking to design a better example, an exemplar. So at that time, I think it's still the physics side, including applying for a doctorate in MIT. Yes, it's also a physics project.

三、遇见 Max Tegmark：一个"鸟型"科学家的启蒙

刘子鸣： But Max is a genius. Maybe the whole MIT physics department, except for him, there is also Mary Szecich, another professor of optical engineering, but also an A.F. optical engineer. They are both very good friends. Maybe the whole MIT was in the 1920s. Air for Science is still a bit too far-fetched.

I remember when I applied for a PhD, what I wrote in my research plan was that I would do Air for Physics next. And then Max saw my material and said, "I want to recruit this person." And then he recruited me.

张小珺： He recruited you because he liked your research direction.

刘子鸣： He liked my research and he told me that he thought my personal website was very impressive. Because I was drawing something like a gossip on my personal website. I would draw my research interests, how they are related to each other. And he thought it was very similar to his thinking.

Max is also a person who is a little bit misguided. You talk to him, we might take an hour to discuss 5-10 topics. Because he studied economics. Then he studied physics. Then in 2012, he started to study AI and physics. This is a very early and very advanced practice. I think it's because he is very interested in many things. He can see the connection between different things.

He is a typical birdman. Freeman Dyson will divide scientists into birds and diggers. In other words, birds understand each field a little bit. They can see the similarities between different fields. Therefore, they can integrate some methods of one field into another field. The advantage of birds is that they can see the whole field at a glance, and then he can focus on his experience. The main time he spends is to find some higher level, some higher level comparisons and abstractions. But on the other hand, the diggers will do a very detailed and in-depth research on a field.

In this respect, Max and I are actually very typical bird people.

张小珺： You are an INTJ. I feel like INTJOP people are more like the kind of bird people you mentioned.

刘子鸣： Yes, he is ENTP. Yes, Max is ENTP. I'm actually a little bit different from TP. Because I feel that a lot of things, whether it's research or life, are not controlled by myself. So I'm gradually becoming more P.

四、博士研究：从 AI for Physics 转向 Mechanistic Interpretability

张小珺： Do you have a main line in your doctoral research?

刘子鸣： Actually, I've changed directions several times in the middle. Before 2022, I was still an AI for physics, an AI physicist. Then at the end of 2022, the next GPT came out. Then Max said, OK, we have to change directions for the entire group. We started with the idea of making it "mechanical and explainable". Why? Because the big-tongue model is too dangerous. We need to keep it safe. We need to understand how it works inside. So this is about 2023, 2024. These two years, we mainly focused on mechanical and explainability.

By the way, "Kan" is actually a side project of mine. At first, Max didn't agree with me to do this project. But I did two weeks later and achieved some initial results. Then he said, "Oh, this thing is a little interesting. Then you can keep going."

张小珺： Why did he start to disagree? This is a very influential Can network.

刘子鸣： Can network. This is also a echo. I joined AI because of Can. Then we mentioned Can network again in 2024.

Why did he disagree at first? He threw me a 1989 paper. The paper was written by Tomas Poggio, a famous professor at MIT. He was 90 years old this year. In 1989, he wrote about the mathematical theorem proposed by the two Soviet scientists, Khmelnytsky and Khromogorov. They were turned into real algorithms. And then they said that they found the worst case. In this worst case, they couldn't find this strict, two-layered, smooth, this kind of Karmogorov-Arnold's expression. This sounds very long, but it's just a series of restrictive conditions added in front of it.

But I feel that as a person who came from physics, I may not care so much about what the worst case is. All models are wrong, but some are useful. But some models are useful. So that's the idea.

I was thinking, you mathematically tell me that the worst thing is not work. But physically, we care about things that have beautiful structures. These things are not the worst thing. We can live in this universe, but our universe is not the worst. We must be a pretty good universe. That's how we can evolve our lives. That's how we can ask ourselves if we are in the worst universe.

So, based on this, because of this optimistic view, I ignored Max's warning temporarily. He said that in 1989, this thing wouldn't work. I spent two weeks to make the prototype. Then I went to Max and said, "Look, I've trained this network." But Max wasn't very satisfied at first. He said, "But I don't know what happened inside your network. You still built a black box." This is also a fundamental explanation. He still has a black box.

Max said, "Can you think about it? Make this network a test." Then I spent about a week. By the way, at that time, I was still a person who didn't believe in coding agents. Of course, coding agents weren't as good as they are now. So at that time, these codes were still hand-picked one by one. So the test took me a week. But now it's probably enough for an hour. I spent a week to make the test. And then when I finished the test, Max said, "Wow, this is awesome."

Because Max is a super visual animal. Actually, I am too. I have to see something to believe in it. If I don't see something, I feel uncomfortable. I have a picture in my head and I can't get it out. I feel uncomfortable. So I drew the structure picture and Max was convinced. He said, "Wow, this thing is so interesting." We can actually see what's going on in the brain of this network. It's not just about the end. It's about what he predicted.

This is how I convinced Max. And then it was just some normal research work. But it was a very interesting experience in the early days.

五、KAN 的动机：把神经和符号缝合起来

张小珺： Why did you want to do the network of Kan?

刘子鸣： I think this is also an obsession of mine all along. I think AI and physics, the philosophy of these two subjects is too far apart. The philosophy of AI, at least our current AI, is a kind of connectivism. It's a kind of nerve thing. But physics is a kind of symbol thing. Then I would feel that two things are not unified, it's not good. This may also come from after physical training, there will be an impulse to systematize, to do a unified impulse.

So I actually started thinking about this problem in 2021. How do I build a network that is a network and a symbol formula at the same time? This is actually a bit like the glass double-edged sword, which is what we call in quantum physics. An example is that it is both physical and wave.

Can I create a neural network that is also a symbol? Based on this exploration, I wrote out a formula. I only knew about it after a few days. The formula I wrote was actually the formula written by Kamal Gorov and Arnold in 1957. But I wrote it from a perspective of the two-way equation of the neural network and the Foucault formula. And then I realized that this formula was written by two Soviet mathematicians in 1957. And they proved that this formula has the ability to be used in all forms of applications. It is equivalent to the theory of the model. It's a symbol that can express any kind of feeling. In this way, it's equivalent to closing my obsession with this.

张小珺： How did your exploration continue after that? Is there a connection with this work?

刘子鸣： Yes, it's more like an example for me. What kind of example is that? It's like I'm patting my head. I can design a new architecture. I think my way of thinking is sometimes a bit abstract or high level. After I see it, I don't think about how to apply it to different scenes. Instead, I think how can I reproduce and create a new structure?

This is what led to the physics of AI, which is the exploration of AI physics. I think design models should be a science. It shouldn't be like what we have now, where Transformers are shot with their heads, where GANs are shot with their heads, where ResNet is shot with its head. That's very unscalable. I think we shouldn't scale, but compute. We should compute AI model design. But how to scale this? That's a huge research issue.

So after looking at it, I think it's a starting point for me. I will think more about some things on the level of math science. How do I think about it? I want to put my thinking process into a AI.

六、Transformer 的成功是"运气"？——语言 vs 视觉的本质差异

张小珺： But when we talk about Transformers, we also say that it is a model that is more suitable for GPUs, that is, it is more suitable for a model structure with chips. If it is based on either the physics of AI or AI for AI, a new model structure is designed, can it be suitable for the current hardware?

刘子鸣： That's a good question. It actually explains that Transformers is not that good at math. It's just a hard-to-get lottery.

I actually agree with the point of view of Sainin in your previous interview. Sainin said that the language model, it's a counter-bitter lesson. The success of the big-sword model is in the language. The success is not in the model. Because the language is something that we humans have lived for millions of years, it's a kind of guilt that nature gives us. Then we take this gift, this guilt, and then what kind of model do you make on it? As long as this model can eat these guilt, then it is a good model. It may be a transformer, but it may be another model in the parallel universe. It is all possible. In fact, we have all kinds of variables now, right? For example, this linear tension model.

So, for language models, I think the structural design of this place is relatively not so clever because language itself is a model that has been compressed very well. But for many other models, such as vision, I think this is also a problem that many world model companies want to solve. These models are not well compressed.

So at this time, it is very important how we build a model that can be compressed. This model is not just like a transformer, I will record all the knowledge, but to learn the expression of abstract. This is actually what we are best at. Because there are too many variations in our world. But we, our ancestors, need to be reborn. We need to understand what the most important element of our rebirth is. The most important element is that there is a fruit there. I want to pick it up. I will not starve to death if I eat it. And there is a tiger there, and then we can't be discovered by it. Because of evolution, we have to go to the most important part of the identification of a large amount of information. But this is exactly the ability of this abstract that AI does not have yet.

So I personally think why model design has become more important in the post-LM era. I think it will become more important because the success of L-men is not because of the model.

Of course, what I said is a bit of a backbiting, right? Transformers, for example, its attention mechanism allows information to be transmitted very quickly in the up and down direction. This is not available in the previous models such as RNN or LSTM. This is indeed one of its creative points. But maybe as long as I look for another model, another model can also allow us to have a very efficient information transmission on the top 5S. For that model, it may be as good as Transformer.

That is, it's not because it's called Transformer, it's because it can have more efficient information transmission in the upper and lower text. And so is ResNet. It's not because it's called ResNet, it's because it can have very efficient information transmission in the depth direction. You have a very efficient type of transmission.

七、研究主线：连接神经与符号，链接 AI 与自然科学

张小珺： What kind of research style do you think you are? From your undergraduate to your doctoral degree.

刘子鸣： I think I actually have a very clear main line. But this is actually my own opinion. There are many people who ask me, "I feel like you move a little bit, then I will slowly summarize it later."

张小珺： From point to line.

刘子鸣： Yes, yes. This main line is about how to connect the two worlds of nerves and symbols. Or more specifically, how to value AI and physics or even more generally, natural science. Because we live in such a universe, in such a natural environment, we are very good at this kind of symbols. 二十、Physics of AI 的三个维度：Space、Time、Parallel Universe

It's a bit like we're doing a sample. Nothing in biology makes sense except in light of evolution. He said that if you don't understand the organism from the perspective of evolution, there is actually nothing in the organism that can be understood. It makes sense. It's also a black box. It's also a black box. It's also a black box because the organism is also a black box. But you can't from the perspective of evolution, you can at least understand some of it. You may see your ancestors, at some point, they didn't go to land, right? And then they just stayed in the water. Through this history, through this natural evolution, you will have some inspiration to see the world.

The third one is the parallel universe. Why do I call it that? I think it's because my PhD mentor Max Tegmark is one of the founders of the theory of the parallel universe. Of course, this is a very complicated place. In fact, it is a control experiment. What does it mean? For example, I have two 培养米, and they all have some bacteria. And these bacteria may be in different environments. For the bacteria in one 培养米, it will be another 培养米. It is a parallel universe.

This corresponds to our human scientific experiments. In fact, it is to do some control experiments. In an environment, what kind of model can I train? This environment may mean, for example, how to adjust my super-sensors. And then I can get a model with different limitations.

This is actually a very important methodology of the physics of RLM by Zhu Zeyuan. He will scan a diagram, which is a face diagram. This diagram is actually a more common concept in physics. The diagram says that matter may have different shapes. It may have different images in different states. The same substances are all water, but it may have different pressure and different temperatures. It may have different images.

There are many images in this AI. No matter what training power you learn, there are many images in this AI. We often have some know-how, that is, what trick works and what trick doesn't work. In fact, many times it is for this image. Only when your experimenter is in this image, it's work. When it comes out of this image, when it enters another image, its trick may not work anymore. Then maybe another trick will work.

But the reason we are so confused now is because everyone is saying that my trick works. But no one answers when will my trick work? When will my model and my system work in what image? So this is actually the problem that science of AI or physics of AI wants to solve. Because we know that the No Free Launch theorem tells us that no model, no trick can be better than other methods in all databases and all tasks.

The task of physics software is to understand what the practical conditions of each trick and each structure are. This is the attitude of doing science, not selling something you made.

刘子鸣： We still test R&D within six months. We do some demo and do some product travel. After six months, based on our six-month results, we decide what to do after that. It must be in the first year. The product and business will definitely start to be commercialized. But for example, six to twelve months, I think the research and development of six to twelve months is very important for a new lab. You can't invest too early in a direction that is not actually that good. It's just for short-term to make a profit, short-term to do business. You need to explore 6-12 months to find a better direction.

张小珺： Do you think the essence of New Lab should be a lab or a company?

刘子鸣： The reason we gave it a new name is because it's neither a lab nor a company. It should be like I said, you should go according to the form of a lab in 6-12 months, and operate in a way of research institute. Once it's Glock, once it's a shield, it should operate according to the company's way. It's the feeling of the pre-open AI era and the post-open AI era.

张小珺： Yes, yes, yes. Will it take him a long time to do lab? Open AI has been doing it for many years. Do you think there is such a long-term exploration period in the environment or infrastructure? Does it have this tolerance? Is your cash flow enough?

刘子鸣： We will continue to raise the cash flow. I personally think that the current route is relatively clear. I think that 6 to 12 months can be a good start and then start making products. If you asked me this a year ago, I might think that we need to do research and development for 3 to 5 years. I think I'm also constantly thinking about it. I myself realize the feasibility of this prototype. After that, I said I wanted to quickly recommend this thing. I was quite hesitant before. Because I didn't find a clear path.

Of course, this clear path will actually be constantly adjusted during the process.

张小珺： You can describe this path as a prototype, or describe it as AFYI Auto Research, or describe it as Physics of AI. Which word do you think is the most accurate? If I only choose one.

刘子鸣： I think Auto Research is the closest. But I think we need to create a new vocabulary to give us a name for our own path. But so far we haven't really thought about this. I think in the future we need to... For example, AI physics is the name we gave ourselves. Because now all the new labs are describing what they are doing. But for entrepreneurs and investors, it's not a thing. It's not a thing. The reason we use these cliche words is because investors need to understand.

张小珺： Yes, you see, you are also described as "AI for Science" by investors. It's also different from the concept you have in mind. But you don't actually find the most accurate word to describe it in your mind. So you're also using some vocabulary.

刘子鸣： Yes, yes. From the perspective of investors, my understanding is that their direction of investment is actually quite wide. Among the vastness they have in contact with, AI for Science, AI for AI, Auto Research, are actually a bunch. Then the infrastructure model, the world model, are a bunch.

张小珺： What do you think is the current era of AI development? Has it become more clear?

刘子鸣： I think it's already more clear for the language model. But the new opportunity comes from... We talked about the world model at the beginning, and then about auto research. I think these two tracks are still in the early stages. But the original model may not be able to be implanted.

But the reason why it can't be implanted, I don't think I'm a transformer hater. I think more of it is that the world model side is actually more like finding a more complete structure. It can better draw and find the real latent space of the physical world. In the case of auto research, I think more people still say that the large-scale model has never seen this kind of data. So the first step is to structure it. The second step is to collect the data for structural research. This is the most important. With this data, the large model can actually eat it. In fact, it may not be bad.

Of course, the path of the round model is a model about the model. The large model also has not seen this kind of data about the model. I have not seen too much structural data about the model. So the large model can't do well.

二十八、快问快答与结语

张小珺： How do you feel about your entrepreneurship in a few months?

[原文此处出现严重循环，保留原文占位] - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

张小珺： 如果只能选一个做 professor 和做企业家 entrepreneur, 你会选哪个?

刘子鸣： I want them all. I'm in the state of wanting them all. If I have to choose one, I think I'll look at it again. Take a look. Take a look.

张小珺： Today's entrepreneurship seems to be very different from the past. Because many are from academic backgrounds. Or like you, you started your career after you got a job. Some students started their career. Many are from the research background.

刘子鸣： Yes, I think it still depends on whether you need to study early to do something. To help to bring out the impact of this thing, not just a small and beautiful thing. But I think it still needs to be said that 6 to 12 months is the first time to bring out this circle. So the ideal state is the results of 6 to 12 months of research and exploration and a certain product.

张小珺： Yes, yes, yes. Then I will ask you quickly in the last section.

A food you like in the world.

刘子鸣： Anyway, no matter where I go to study or travel, I always want to eat this hot dry noodles.

张小珺： A place you like in the world.

刘子鸣： I like places with rivers. Like Wuhan, Shanghai, by the Huangpu River. In MIT, in Washington, Charles River. I like to walk by the river when I'm free.

张小珺： A book that influenced your life?

刘子鸣： Human history. I've always been a nerd. I don't understand social science. Sometimes I think it's unreasonable. But why does everyone believe in it? After reading human history, I know that our society is driven by stories. So narrative is very important. Not only technology is important, but the narrative behind it is also very important.

张小珺： What are the articles that affect AI in your mind? This is not too common, for example, like scaling law and these articles.

刘子鸣： I think the biggest impact for me personally is to do this article. Because it is equivalent to opening the door for me to the AI world.

张小珺： Based on your current knowledge, what is a key and important "but"?

刘子鸣： Maybe it's what we've been talking about just now. AI for coding, the next one will be AI for research. But it needs to be done in the way of physics of AI.

张小珺： What is the most important thing for AI?

Alright, that's all for today's program. This is Business Interviews, a deep-dive interview program produced by the Language and World Studio. You can follow us on our official account to get more information. Our official account is Language and World, Language is World. You are also welcome to interact with us in the comments section of Little Universe. We hope to explore a new world with you from here.

## 一、最令人意外的观察：他把自己当成模型训练了60天，无意间做了一场东方式修行
刘子鸣讲了一件被访谈匆匆带过、却极其反常识的事——**他花了大约两个月，每天在实验室做AI实验之前，先强迫自己预测"这次训练曲线会长什么样"，把自己的大脑当成一个"原初模型"来监督训练**。40-50天后，他"suddenly grok"，突然获得了跨模态的直觉预测能力。
这件事的诡异之处在于：**他用的方法论，几乎是一比一复刻了佛教内观（vipassana）和斯多葛派"预演不测"（premeditatio malorum）的认知训练结构**——在事件发生前先形成预测，事件发生后与实际比对，让大脑在预测误差中重塑内部表征。区别只在于：僧侣观察的是情绪起伏，斯多葛派观察的是命运变故，而他观察的是loss curve。
更耐人寻味的是，他最终决定把"我"外包给一个模型，是因为"人的带宽只能一天做一两个实验，无法训练一千年"。**这句话可以反过来读：AI for AI 的技术路线，本质上是一个物理学家不愿等待自己开悟的加速手段**——他想把自己60天的Grok压缩到机器上做1000次然后收获。这是一种非

item.title: [Lex Clips] Black men who fought in the Civil War | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、枪管即选票：一个被低估的"物理宪法"时刻

大多数人把黑人参战理解为"为自由而战"的抒情叙事，但 Gallagher 揭示的其实是一个更冷峻的博弈论时刻——非裔美国人把枪口对准奴隶制捍卫者的那一刻，他们不是在请求公民权，而是在构造一个逻辑上无法反驳的债权。这是一种"用身体写宪法"的行为：一旦你允许某个群体为国家去死，你就再也无法在语义上否认他们的"人格"。这比任何一份宣言、任何一次辩论都更具结构性锁定效应（structural lock-in）。

有意思的是——这个逻辑其实反向绑架了国家。国会当时的辩论之所以被"改变了方程式"，不是因为议员们良心发现，而是因为枪一旦发出去，就无法在道德账簿上收回来。武器分发即是承诺分发。

二、跨领域连接：与日本明治征兵制、以色列建国、甚至现代硅谷"stock option"的同构性

这让我想到一个出人意料的跨领域映射：任何时候一个社会把"高风险资产"（生命、资本、专业技能）交到一个此前被排斥的群体手中，那个群体的政治地位就会发生不可逆的相变。

  • 明治日本用全民征兵制打破武士阶级垄断，士农工商的固化结构在几年内瓦解——不是因为思想启蒙，而是因为"农民也能拿枪"。
  • 以色列建国前后，女性进入战斗序列直接改写了性别政治的天花板。
  • 甚至硅谷早期给工程师发 stock option，本质上也是同一个机制——你让某类人承担风险，他们就获得"股东身份"，再也回不去雇佣关系。

南北战争的黑人士兵，就是美国政治史上最早的一批"股权持有者"。他们不是在申请入股，而是在完成一次强制行权。

三、被历史叙事掩盖的悖论："Union" 一词的双重密码

这里有一个让我震动的语言学观察——Gallagher 说黑人士兵也谈"Union"（联邦），但他们说的 Union 不是白人北方人说的那个 Union。同一个词，装着两套完全不同的操作系统：

  • 白人的 Union = 国家主权的完整
  • 黑人的 Union = 一个不再包含奴隶制的联邦

这是一种极为罕见的"寄生性词汇"（parasitic vocabulary）现象：弱势群体借用主流话语的外壳，却在内部悄悄替换定义。类似的机制在今天依然运作——比如"自由"、"多样性"、"安全"这些词，不同群体使用时装的其实是完全不同的操作系统。词汇的表面共识，往往掩盖了深层的语义战争。

真正的历史转折，往往发生在同一个词开始承载互斥含义的那一刻——因为那意味着旧秩序的语言资源，已经被反向殖民了。

📝 转录文本

问题：非裔士兵的动机

Lex： As a historian, you've looked at every layer of this, including diaries and —

Gary： Mhm.

Lex： What was motivating? What was going through the minds of African-Americans who were fighting for the Union side?

一、"Union" 对他们意味着什么

Gary： I think what you would expect is going — I mean, they would talk about Union occasionally, but what that means to them, it's a Union without slavery.

They have the most of all the people who can have a direct impact on what's going on versus slavery. There's nothing more direct than picking up a musket and firing at the people who are defending a slavery-based society. It can't — doesn't get —

二、士兵身份 = 公民权的不可撤销主张

And at the same time, you are not only doing that, you're also establishing an unimpeachable claim to citizenship.

The whole point of a citizen soldier is that you do your bit for the nation that's helping you, and the nation does these things for you. Well, okay — if I'm picking up and risking my life with a musket in my hand, are you going to tell me I can't vote after I do? I thought that's the whole point of this. One — I'm protecting the right to vote by doing my citizen's role as a soldier.

三、国会辩论的转折

And that was a big debate in Congress. That really changed the equation of that debate as well.

How are you going to treat people after they've served in the United States units? Can you tell them they can't — what, you're not going to give the vote to them?

item.title: [Lex Clips] Confederate flag explained by historian | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

旗帜的"错版流通"：一场持续 160 年的符号错位

最出人意料的一点其实藏在 Gallagher 的抱怨里——今天绝大多数飘扬的"邦联旗"根本不是邦联的国旗。真正的邦联国旗（Stars and Bars）反而长得像美国国旗，而人们狂热拥抱的"圣安德鲁十字"其实是战旗，还被从正方形擅自拉成了长方形。这形成了一个近乎荒诞的历史事实：一个符号的"真身"从未真正流行，流行的是它的赝品。这类似于耶稣从未见过十字架成为教会图腾、切·格瓦拉从未见过自己的头像印在 T 恤上——符号的传播力，往往与其历史准确性成反比。越模糊、越可塑，越容易被大规模误用。

"12 年的尾声"：为什么修补比战争本身更漫长

Gallagher 有一个非常锋利的比例观察——"一场 4 年战争，配了 12 年的 coda（尾声）"。这里藏着一个跨领域的规律：破坏是脉冲式的，修复是弥散式的。软件工程里叫"技术债利息"，创伤心理学里叫"post-traumatic elaboration"，生态学里叫"次生演替"。真正决定一个系统长期走向的，从来不是危机本身，而是危机之后那段没有戏剧性、没人拍电影、却在悄悄重新分配权力和记忆的时期。美国至今仍在偿还的不是 1861-1865 的债，而是 1865-1877 那段"重建"没做完的债——这也解释了为什么关于旗帜的争论今天还没停。

邦联旗的"全球化叛逆"：符号如何脱离历史成为纯粹语法

最反直觉的洞见：Gallagher 顺口提到他在英国和爱尔兰都看见过邦联旗。这已经完全脱离奴隶制、脱离美国南方、脱离任何具体政治内容——它变成了一种纯粹的"反建制语法标记"，一个视觉上的"去你的"。这里有个惊人的跨领域连接：这与日本亚文化里滥用的纳粹符号、东欧朋克身上的切·格瓦拉、中国 00 后穿的印第安头饰属于同一现象——符号在全球化传播中会经历"语义漂白"，只保留情绪骨架，抛弃历史肌肉。

但 Gallagher 的最后一击很致命：这种"漂白"在别处或许成立，在美国本土不成立。因为符号的意义不是由使用者单方面决定的——它由这个符号在当地历史中被谁使用过、用于伤害过谁共同锁定。每一个 KKK 集会都用过它，这个事实无法被"我只是觉得酷"稀释掉。这其实揭示了一个更普遍的真相：在一个符号的原生地，你没有"重新定义"它的权力；只有在它的语义已经死透的远方，人们才享有那种自由。

📝 转录文本

内战何时真正结束？

So, some of that still persists with us today. We look at the Confederate flag. So, some historians argue for the long — quote — long Civil War.

Sure. And it's really long. It's the Civil War that never ends, kind of. And I certainly think that there are ramifications from the Civil War that have never ended. But I think the Civil War ended, and I think it ended in the early summer of 1865 with the destruction of the Confederate government, the absolute dissolution of all the Confederate military forces. I think that is the end of the Civil War. People at the time thought it was, too.

战后的"12年尾声"：重建时期

What comes afterward, the long coda — reconstruction — is a 12-year coda to a 4-year war that works out some of the difficulties of how you put the nation back together. And then beyond that, you have these different memory streams that have been contending with one another that still — some of which still reverberate today — and including what are you going to do with the Confederate flag, which most of…

大多数人挥舞的根本不是"邦联旗"

There are a lot of nitwits around. They don't even know what the Confederate flag was. They fly a rectangular version of the St. Andrew's cross. That is not the Confederate flag. They call it the Confederate flag.

The Confederate flag that had a St. Andrew's cross wasn't a rectangle, it was a square. And the actual Confederate flag had three big bars and then stars up in… it looks kind of like the United States flag. They don't even know that, and they go around flying it everywhere.

符号无法被"洗白"

It's a symbol and pretend that it represents all kinds of things. The Confederate flag cannot be divorced from all the times that version of it — the St. Andrew's cross version — every Ku Klux Klan group flew it. Every… it's… you just can't sanitize it.

走向全球的"反建制"符号

And I mean, I saw Confederate flags in Britain and Ireland. I mean, it's become a sort of "up yours" symbol, I think, in some places — of just sort of rebellion, not necessarily tethered specifically —

Rebellion against this institution.

Against authority and institutions and the ruling class. And that's… but here it has a very specific meaning, and you just can't separate it. People should quit trying.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] The bloodiest war in US history | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"投入度"：把伤亡当成信念的会计凭证

最出人意料的观察藏在 Gallagher 那段看似冷冰冰的百分比里——南方邦联损失了 4-5% 的总人口，超过一战中的英法德俄；而其白人军龄男性的损失率高达 30%。学界在 1980-90 年代曾用"他们打得不够拼"来论证邦联根本不是一个真正的国家，Gallagher 用一组死亡率数据当场把这个论证掀翻。

这里有一个反直觉的哲学翻转：我们通常用"胜利"衡量一个共同体的真实性，但 Gallagher 提示我们，应该用"愿意为之流血的比例"来衡量。这近乎一种"信念的会计学"——伤亡不是失败的证据，而是意义的凭证。你可以把这个视角搬去看今天所有"看起来输了"的运动、创业、婚姻：外人爱说"你看，他们没那么在乎"，但真正的度量衡也许是——他们愿意在明知会输的时刻继续损耗多少。

二、"团结"与"和解"是两个完全不同的物种——像操作系统更新与人格重塑的差别

Gallagher 极其克制地拆解了两个常被混用的词：reunion（重新联合）和 reconciliation（和解）。前者是政治机器的重新拼装，一纸文件即可完成；后者是数千万人心智内部的漫长重写，一百六十年后依然在运行后台进程。

这里可以做一个跨领域连接——它几乎完美对应软件工程里的"合并冲突已解决"和"代码库真正健康"的区别：Git 告诉你 merge 成功了，但底层逻辑可能还在冲突，只是没有被立刻触发。Appomattox 是一次成功的 git merge --no-conflict，而 reconciliation 需要的是重构 (refactor)——这个 refactor 每隔几十年就在美国政治里重新报错一次。Gallagher 一句"Civil War 的回响随处可见"，本质上是在说：这个仓库从未真正 rebase 干净。

三、"Appomattox 综合征"：所有历史叙事都患有"结局的重力"

Gallagher 抛出了一个可以直接搬到你个人叙事里的诊断——"Appomattox Syndrome"：从故事的结尾开始讲，于是一切都显得不可避免。战争必然爆发、北方必然获胜、奴隶制必然终结……因为它们确实发生了。

真正震撼的部分是他把 1857 年的爱荷华人拉回场景：没人早上醒来第一个念头是"我恨南方奴隶主"，人们在忙淘金、忙铁路、忙电报——1850 年代的"时空压缩"让当时人感到眩晕，程度不亚于我们今天面对 AI。历史书总爱说"antebellum era"（战前时期），但没有人知道自己活在"战前"，正如没有人今天早上起来意识到自己活在某个即将剧变的"前夜"。

这可以做一个残酷的跨域连接："Appomattox 综合征"是所有回忆录、创业传记、爱情故事的通病——你从"我们成功了 / 我们分手了 / 我瘦下来了"倒着讲，一切细节都被结局的重力扭曲成命运。真正的历史训练——以及真正诚实的自我叙事——是要假装不知道结局，重新住进 1857 年那个平凡的、忙淘金和铁路的清晨。因为你此刻正活在你未来某段"antebellum era"里，而且毫不自知。

📝 转录文本

一、战争的规模与"投入度"之谜

Lex： Can we just actually linger on this? On the nature of war, over 700,000 people dead. How do we make sense of our capacity as—in that context, Americans—to kill sometimes literally our brothers?

Yes, sometimes literally our brothers. How is that even possible?

Gary： Well, one thing it tells me: things are pretty important to people on both sides if you're going to continue for a war that long.

I mean, there was a period in the literature—in the scholarly literature in the 1980s and into the 1990s—where they argued that the Confederacy wasn't a nation. And the proof was that they didn't try very hard; that if they really thought of themselves as a nation, they would have tried harder and fought longer.

Well, they lost between 4 and 5% of their entire population, which is more than Great Britain, France, Germany, or Russia during World War I. A higher percentage loss than any of the powers in World War I. The US lost about 1.8% of its population from the war. US in World War II, 3/10 of 1% of its population. They lost more than 30% of their entire white military-age males in the war. Be the equivalent of about 18 million Americans being killed now in a war.

That seems to me that they're pretty serious about something there. It means that that's one of the largest percentages of loss.

Lex： That's, if that's a measure of dedication.

Gary： If that's your measure of dedication, yes. And it seems to me that it should be one of the metrics that you bring to play—that they just keep at it. They didn't give up easily.

二、心理层面的仇恨与厌战

Lex： What can we say about the motivation on the psychological side? Did the members of the Confederacy hate the members of the Union?

Gary： That escalated on both sides during the war as more and more loss came. They did—there was more hatred directed toward the enemy more and more. This notion that they're all brothers and not really mad at each other—that just doesn't hold up.

There are places where the soldiers fraternized with one another and traded tobacco for coffee and that kind of stuff. But no, the bitterness—as the war went on and there was greater loss on the home front, and as the war became more all-encompassing and really went after the entire civilian side of the Confederacy—was not shielded from it. The bitterness increased and increased and increased.

And there's a lot of unhappiness with the war behind the lines in the Confederacy. Absolutely. Unhappiness with the government. There's desertion. About 15% of Confederate soldiers deserted. About 12% of United States soldiers deserted. So there's desertion on both sides. There's war weariness.

But the war goes on because I think if you had been able to poll most white southerners, even late in the war, and say, "Okay, here are your choices: you either have Jefferson Davis in the government and the war goes on, or you're going back into the United States and the Lincoln government will be in charge and you won't have slavery. Which one do you pick?" They're going to pick the first one. And that's why the war went on as long as it did.

三、Appomattox 与林肯的和平方案

Lex： But at the same time, to fast forward—and that maybe teaches you something about the nature of war—but after the war, maybe some of the decisions that Grant made, people were able to rediscover the brotherhood.

Gary： You mean at Appomattox—you're talking about the terms at Appomattox.

Lex： Yes.

Gary： And those were—and he didn't just reach up in the air and say "I've got some terms." That Lincoln very specifically—he met with Lincoln shortly before Appomattox. Sherman was there, one top naval officer was there, Grant and Lincoln. And Lincoln said, "This is what I want. This is the kind of peace I want. The whole point of this war is to put the nation back together."

And a good start on that is—I mean, if it's just a rebellion, what do you do with traitors and rebels? You hang them. You don't bring them back. You don't treat them as prisoners of war, which the United States did during this. But the goal is to put the nation back together.

And Lincoln said, "This is a good start. Make them sign a parole. Make them accept the end of slavery and the fact that they're back in the Union. If they do that, they get to go home and resume their lives. Hadn't been decided yet whether they'll get to vote. But let them go home. Don't imprison them. Don't execute them. Don't execute their leaders." That's the decision.

四、Reunion 与 Reconciliation：两种截然不同的战后

Lex： From the perspective of the Union, what do you think about that kind of forgiveness?

Gary： Well, I think that it was sort of a nod toward the direction of forgiveness, but I don't think real forgiveness was there. It was still extremely hard feelings on both sides. And Lincoln's assassination upped the ante on that, especially for a while in the United States—the forgiveness.

Two things in terms of the aftermath of the war, two words that often come into play, are reunion and reconciliation. Those are two other things that are often conflated.

Reunion is literally putting the nation back together. That happened.

Reconciliation—true reconciliation—that's much, much, much tougher. And that didn't come anytime soon on the part of millions of people on both sides, I think. And we'll probably maybe talk about in multiple ways how maybe that is something that's still going on.

Oh, there are echoes of the Civil War all over the place. It's not still being fought, but you can see resonances of the Civil War, because it's such a profoundly disruptive event that gets right at the heart of what the republic means. There's nothing else like it in US history. It's a great moment of truth, the residual aftermath and effects of which lingered for decades and are still present in some ways, I think.

五、1859 年的日常，与"Appomattox 综合征"

Lex： So in 1859, most Americans were just living their life. Did they have a sense what was on the horizon?

Gary： It's what I like to call the Appomattox Syndrome, which starts at the end of the story. And says: of course there was going to be a war, because the war was inevitable. And of course the United States was going to win and slavery was going to be destroyed, because they were. So let's find out how we got right here.

But no, most people didn't wake up in Iowa in 1857 and their first thought was, "Boy, I hate the South, those slaveholders." No, people got on with their quotidian lives. They got to the farm or they went to their business. They weren't—nobody knew that they were living in the antebellum era and that those great antebellum years were about to come to an end.

That is something that it's hard to get people not to just put it out of your mind—that that's all anybody is thinking about. They're thinking there's a lot of other stuff going on.

六、1850 年代的技术与时空压缩

There's a big gold rush in Colorado. More people go to Colorado than went to California for a while. And you have these tremendous changes coming about—technological changes of the 1850s where you have the real expansion of railroads, the real expansion of the telegraph. There's a shrinking of time and space that's remarkable for people at the time. It seemed dizzying to them at the time.

There are a lot of things to think about other than "how much I hate Yankees if I'm in South Carolina," or "I hate slaveholders if I live in New Hampshire."

But periodically there are these events that pop up that refocus on the differences between the sections. And you have the Kansas–Nebraska Act. You have Dred Scott. You have the caning of Charles Sumner on the floor of the Senate. You have Uncle Tom's Cabin earlier in the decade, in 18-and-what—and the impact that that had on attitudes towards slavery. Doesn't create a bunch of abolitionists, but it creates a bunch of people who rethink their thoughts about slavery.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Bits + Bips] The Bull Case Meets the Fed, Iran, and New Tariffs
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个耐人寻味的错位

最出人意料的观察不在转录内容里，而在标题与内容之间的鸿沟——视频标题许诺的是美联储、伊朗、新关税这三大宏观叙事，而实际转录只有两句关于 AI 的通用陈述。这种错位本身就是一个信号：在当下的注意力经济里，地缘政治的标题与技术乐观主义的正文正在成为一种默认的组合拳。就像超市把糖果摆在收银台旁边——你以为你在买必需品，实际被引导消费的是另一样东西。

跨领域连接：AI 叙事已成为新的"避险资产"

把这段极简的 AI 陈述放回节目原本的语境（利率、战争、贸易壁垒）里看，会浮出一个反直觉的结论：AI 叙事在投资者心智中，正在扮演过去黄金和美债扮演的角色——一个"无论其他变量如何恶化都能被拉出来讲的故事"。

  • 美联储紧缩？AI 提升生产率可以对冲。
  • 中东冲突？AI 重塑供应链可以对冲。
  • 关税战？AI 让本土化生产变得经济可行。

这不是分析，这是心理锚。当宏观变量高度不确定时，市场需要一个"永远有效"的故事作为估值的最后一块地板。AI 就是 2020 年代的这块地板。这解释了为什么一个讲 Fed / Iran / Tariffs 的节目，会用"AI is transforming..."这样近乎陈词滥调的开场——它不是内容，它是仪式。

隐藏的系统性真相：信息的"熵坍缩"

从系统论视角看，这段转录还揭示了一个更深的模式：当输入信号（宏观、地缘、货币三重不确定性）过载时，输出叙事反而会坍缩到最低熵的表达——也就是最模板化、最没有新信息的句子（"AI 正在改变我们生活和工作的方式"）。

这与热力学中的一个反直觉现象同构：系统受到剧烈外部冲击时，其内部宏观态往往趋向最大熵，但对外的可观测输出却会显现为高度重复的低维模式。金融市场里的"beta 压缩"（危机中所有资产的相关性趋近于 1）、疫情期间全球媒体报道语言的高度雷同、都是同一个机制。

啊哈时刻：你以为自己在听一档信息密集的宏观播客，实际上你在观察一个高熵世界里的低熵仪式——这本身，可能比节目里任何具体的观点都更值得记下来。

📝 转录文本

开场

Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we live and work.

核心陈述

From automating repetitive tasks to providing deep insights from complex data, AI models are becoming more sophisticated and accessible than ever before.

item.title: [a16z] How Lassie Is Automating Healthcare Administration
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的核心悖论：软件从未真正提高效率，直到它开始"干活"

Alex 在访谈中抛出了一个反直觉的暴击：过去 50 年的软件革命，本质上只是把纸质档案柜数字化，却没有真正减少劳动。1950 年的 HR 部门和 2000 年的 HR 部门人员配比几乎没变——软件只是把"守档案柜的人"换成了"守服务器的 CISO"。

这个观察的杀伤力在于：整个 SaaS 行业可能一直在收"存储费"而非"劳动费"。Toast、Workday、NetSuite 卖的不是效率，是"更漂亮的档案柜"。真正的效率革命要等到软件能编辑档案柜、执行档案柜里的动作，也就是现在。这也解释了为什么公开市场同时给"纯软件"打折、给"AI"溢价——市场在无意识地区分"档案柜生意"和"劳动生意"。

二、跨领域连接：Lassie 复刻的其实是 Robin Hood 的"KYC 时刻"

表面上 Lassie 是牙医版的 RPA，但 Stein 在访谈末尾露出了真正的底牌：他在把 Robin Hood 的"消费级 onboarding"哲学移植到 B2B 主街商业。

想想看——Robin Hood 之所以颠覆 Charles Schwab，不是因为免佣金，而是因为它把"开户"从"走进办公室填 30 页表格"压缩成"手机点几下自助完成 KYC"。Lassie 正在对"接管一家诊所的财务"做同样的事：把银行账户绑定、保险门户授权、系统对接、税号验证……全部塞进一个类 Stripe 的自助 checkout 流程。

这里有个更深的洞察：AI Agent 公司的真正护城河，可能不是模型能力，而是消费级产品团队做 B2B 的执行力。Frederick 来自 Superhuman，Stein 来自 Robin Hood——两家都是把"48 小时不惊艳就流失"这种消费级 KPI 硬套到复杂领域的公司。传统企业软件人做不了这件事，因为他们习惯了"上线后有客户成功经理教你用"。

三、意外观察：AI 正在"扩大"而非"消灭"小生意，但同时会"稀释"它

Alex 提出了教科书里那条供需均衡点右侧的市场失灵曲线——每个人愿意为荷兰语接待员付 1 美元，但制造成本是 100 美元，所以市场不存在。AI 把这条曲线右边"从不存在"的市场瞬间变成"随手可得"。Stein 顺着推：如果每个牙医都能雇 Betty，美国牙医数量可能从 16 万涨到 50 万。

但这里藏着一个让创始人自己都没完全意识到的悖论：

我追问了一下 Alex 自己抛出的钩子——Yogi Berra 那句"这地方太挤了没人来了"。小生意之所以有护城河，恰恰因为"凑齐一队人执行服务"很难。当 Lassie 把这个门槛拆掉，它同时在拆自己客户的护城河。牙医诊所的边际利润，可能会像"独立咖啡馆遇到 Square + 送餐 App"一样被压缩——工具越普及，个体差异化越弱，价格战越激烈。

换句话说：Lassie 卖的不只是"解放牙医"，而是在无意间重塑整个牙科市场的产业结构。真正的问题不是 AI 抢工作，而是 AI 让所有小生意变得可复制之后，"稀缺性"这个古老的护城河去哪里找？

四、隐藏的系统性真相：联邦纸质支票禁令 = Lassie 的"顺风"底盘

访谈末尾埋了一个几乎没人注意的细节：联邦政府正在强制淘汰保险公司的纸质支票。这才是 Lassie 真正的时代红利——比 GPT-4 更早、更硬的基础设施变化。

这构成了一个漂亮的"三重叠加"： 1. 监管层：纸质→电子的强制迁移（政府在给 Lassie 铺路） 2. 模型层：推理模型 2023 年后成熟（Lassie 早期存的 context 突然值钱了） 3. 劳动力层：Betty 们退休、找不到人（需求端被点燃）

跨领域对照：这跟 2010 年前后 Uber 的崛起同构——不是"App 打车"这个想法多新，而是智能手机普及（技术）+ 出租车牌照制度松动（监管）+ 金融危机后失业司机涌入（劳动力）三条曲线同时相交。任何看起来"突然爆发"的 AI 应用，背后大概率都有这样一个被忽略的"三曲线相交点"。

给读者的行动启发：如果你在寻找下一个 Lassie 级别的机会，别只盯着模型能力。去找那些同时被监管推着数字化 + 劳动力短缺 + 有大量纸质/口口相传 SOP 的行业——独立药房、殡葬业、独立法务、社区兽医、小型建筑承包商……档案柜正在被撬开，而大多数人还盯着 ChatGPT 的下一次更新。

📝 转录文本

开场金句集锦

"AI is overhyped in Silicon Valley but underhyped in Iowa."

"I would actually argue software just kind of took things that were stored in paper format and then they made them available first on prem via green screen computers but people still had to do the work."

"I never forgot what I saw the number one great adopter on Yelp spending 200 hours a month on paperwork."

"The models are trained on so much data and they're so large and yet they actually don't really know how to do any of this work. Initially we were actually the humans in the loop. We kind of automated away our own problems."

"The battle between every startup and incumbent comes down to when the startup gets the distribution before the incumbent gets the innovation."

"We come by and we say, 'Hey, we actually have built this agent that can provide you already with tens of hours of labor.' They then adopt it like very quick. They see us as someone they break in to actually run the practice for them."
