一、创业缘起：一次牙医预约改变的人生

主持人： So welcome and thank you for joining us.

Stein： Thank you for inviting us. Excited to be here.

主持人： Maybe we'll start with the basics. So, Stein, this whole company started with a conversation with you and your own dentist, Dr. Quan. What did he tell you that made you decide to quit your tech job at Robinhood and go process payments for him by hand?

Stein： Yeah, I did not know that my American dream would look like this. It was interesting — I was at Robinhood at the time, and I came to this country to start a company. So after 6 years I moved from Amsterdam to Silicon Valley. I was looking for a heart problem to solve.

And then my doctor, Dr. Quan — I was a patient there, so I saw him twice a year as you do with a dentist. He knew that I was looking for a heart problem and he said, "Do you want to see how I run my business?" And I said, "Absolutely."

He walked me to the back and I never forgot what I saw there. Just a small business owner that is the number one rated doctor on Yelp, spending 200 hours a month on paperwork and busy work — submitting claims by hand — and he had to stick around himself because he couldn't find people to help build up the patient side.

I'm like, "Wow, it's fascinating." This is a couple of years ago. I thought that this was a solved problem, because in the 70s my mom worked in a hospital and that's what she did — she brought bags of cash to the bank and then processed payments by hand. But it wasn't a solved problem here. So that's why this piqued my interest.

主持人： Though I have to ask — when he gave you this offer, were you like… was it that kind of reclined? Could he actually process your answer as yes versus no if your mouth was open and drills were in your mouth?

Stein： Well, up until now I don't have cavities, so knock on wood — it was just an examination. He took me aside after that. He knew I was looking for a heart problem. And then after that appointment he showed me what was going on.

I thought maybe it's him, right? But that didn't really make sense because he was very well rated and used all these modern technologies. So we started talking to other doctors — maybe Dr. Quan was just an anomaly. But then I also worked for a gastroenterologist in Scranton, Pennsylvania, and we saw the same there. I'm like, "Wait, you're doing this all by hand."

So then we figured out: there are hundreds of thousands of these small businesses that literally do this all by hand. That would be quite a fascinating problem to solve. We knew it was going to be hard, but we were kind of looking for that.

二、深入客户办公室：从"人肉Agent"起步

主持人： The Lassie story is so unique to me because you both spent months if not years before fully releasing the product, literally in the office of the customers. How did you convince them to let you in and to look through the heart of the business and get into the financials?

Stein： Yeah, it's a little weird, right? It's like, "Hello, I work at Robinhood on growth on the referral program. Can I get a job here? And by the way, Frederick worked at Superhuman on product — can we do the billing for you and take over the finances?"

I think that was the first sign that we were onto something big. Because to our surprise, all these doctors — when we first talked to all of them like Dr. Quan, because everybody likes to talk about their problems — when they started talking to us for hours, we knew: okay, this is a real problem they have. This is not some vitamin that maybe it's nice to solve. This is something that keeps them up at night. It makes them almost quit their job and say, "I got into this industry because of my passion and craft — because I want to take care of patients."

That was the first time these people were not saying, "No chance you can come work for me because you don't have any experience running finances." What about HIPAA and security reasons? They said yes. Dr. Quan said, "Just come and sit here, night five. You can do the job." Dr. Shah in Scranton, Pennsylvania sat us down behind the desk and said, "You can have access to anything you need — treat it like my son."

That was the first sign that this was very broken and not a solved problem. And then it triggered our intuition: okay, we might be onto something because this is a real pain people are desperately looking to solve.

三、技术演进：为等来的"智能层"提前铺好"上下文层"

主持人： From a technical perspective — Frederick, the business started in 2020, and so much was different then in terms of what was even possible to build. How has your product building process changed over time?

Frederick： I would say when we started the business, we were always obsessed with automating and putting the business on autopilot. So that hasn't really changed.

Back then the models weren't that good, though. Especially reasoning models didn't really exist in that form. But if you think about what it takes to automate any job, you're really looking at getting context on the work — which in the case of a doctor's office is basically access to all the historical data, the patient records, that sort of stuff. And then you need tools to do the work. This is true whether you're a human in the office or an agent.

So we started building the context layer and building the tools, and the intelligence layer wasn't that intelligent. But for the first job it wasn't that necessary — the most basic kind of automation didn't require that much reasoning.

Then as the models got really good, we had this huge tailwind — because we had all this context already built, all the tools already built, and we could just replace our intelligence as the models got better. The product would just get smarter over time. In that way we got a little lucky, but the core vision hasn't really changed at all. It was always about automating the work, not building tools they'd have to use.

四、Alex 的宏观论证：软件的"档案柜史"与劳动力时代

主持人： I feel like as the models have improved, we are more and more seeing software do the job of labor — which, Alex, I would say you were the first to famously argue would be the case. Curious how you think about that when you look at companies, and how it played into the thesis around Lassie.

Alex： Well, so I've given this whole presentation on the origin of software, which was basically: take a filing cabinet and put it into a database. I pick the t = 0 moment as Sabre Systems, because airlines would just keep reservations in filing cabinets. Sabre Systems was a joint project between IBM and American Airlines — that's why Sabre is spelled with two A's.

But then this took wind everywhere else. There are HR filing cabinets, and that became PeopleSoft. There are legal filing cabinets, and that became all of the LexisNexis products. There are accounting filing cabinets, and that became QuickBooks, and NetSuite. Every software was the origin of software. Software just took things stored in paper format and made them available first on-prem via green-screen computers — because that was more efficient to book an airline ticket and change it if you didn't have to use an eraser anymore.

But people still had to do the work. So I would actually argue the world didn't get much more efficient with software. Did PeopleSoft and then Workday make HR departments more efficient? I don't think so. The same number of people work in HR for the exact same size company in 1950 as probably in 2000. Instead of using filing cabinets guarded by Stein and Frederick, now you have an IT department and a CISO. So nothing really got more efficient. I'm exaggerating for effect, but…

从"哑存储"到"能执行"

What you can now do with software is: it can edit the filing cabinet. It's no longer just dumb storage — it's the smart implementation of changes against those things. If it's HR, let's do a background check. Let's do onboarding. Let's explain the benefits to this person. If it's accounting — I'm a dentist, I see I have overdue invoices, I look up QuickBooks. What do I do? Well, I might want to call and say, "Please pay me." That's what the filing cabinet should be doing, not just giving you information.

It just turns out that the work is orders of magnitude bigger than the storage of information the work is done on. That's really been the thesis, and you needed the technology to catch up so it can actually do it. In 2023, next-word prediction wasn't good enough to go run a practice or do background checks. But now things have gotten good enough, and that massively expands the market size.

与 Fintech 的类比：Toast 为什么在 1985 没被发明

If you think about fintech, fintech massively expanded the size of many non-financial markets, because now you could bundle in financial products with non-financial products. My favorite example is Toast. Toast could have existed in 1985. Everybody had an IBM PC. Microsoft DOS worked pretty well. Why wasn't there a restaurant software company in 1985?

Number one, it was too hard to use. Number two, you have this CAC issue — could you get a big restaurant that grosses $5 million a year to spend $100,000 on an MS-DOS software product for reservations, paying wait staff, showing the cook a little menu? Nobody would pay $100,000 for that.

But if you bundle in payment processing, you're effectively charging $100,000 for that, because maybe you get a 2% vig. So fintech made the market much bigger for software because of this bundling effect.

And that pales in comparison to now — software doing the job of labor. Fintech made it a little bigger, but now instead of being a dumb pipe or dumb storage, and instead of just charging incrementally more by bundling in financial processing, we can do work, and we can charge for work, at a way that is cheaper than humans, better than humans. But even both of those sell the opportunity short — because in many cases you can't even find a human.

五、Dr. Sloop 的故事：AI 不是"抢工作"，而是"找不到人"

Alex： Actually the best and funniest story of the Lassie announcement we did together with your amazing video — my first dentist, hopefully he's listening to this podcast, his name is Ronald Sloop. He was my parents' first friend when they moved to Florida. I'm from Florida.

主持人： Was he a Dutch guy? He sounds very Dutch.

Alex： No — Ashkenazi Jew from somewhere in Poland, Ukraine, whatever my family's from too. He's probably 75, 80 years old now. But part of why he retired was he lost his key woman who did the books and everything else. He said, "I can't deal with this anymore, I quit." And then he sold his practice to his junior practitioner and now he's out of the dentistry business.

He saw this announcement. He's like, "Oh my god, this is amazing." I'm not talking this up — my dad called me about this because he saw the prosperity. Dr. Sloop said that if this had been around, he wouldn't have retired. He's now doing nothing with his life, just playing golf in Southern California. He moved there from Florida.

Because it's just too hard to hire the person. So it's not like "oh AI is going to take the jobs." In many cases you can't find somebody. People don't realize this. Or you can't find somebody, but there's a — imagine there is something every human on earth would pay a dollar for, but the cost of manufacturing that thing is $100. You just have a market failure. I call this everything to the right of the supply-demand equilibrium point on an Econ 101 graph.

Why isn't there a Dutch receptionist at every dentist in America? Because there might be a guy who only speaks Dutch that shows up. Why not hire somebody who speaks Dutch? Because there's only a 1-in-a-hundred chance that a Stein who only speaks Dutch shows up. You'd have to pay that person 40,000 euro. It doesn't make sense. But if it were free or cost a dollar, every dental receptionist would have a Dutch counterpart.

So the market just expands massively once you throw in labor. You have this tiny market for software — which isn't that tiny, it's a trillion dollars. Concentrically around that, you have transactions, that's even bigger — that's why Visa has a very big market cap. And then the concentric circle around that is really orders of magnitude bigger.

六、Lassie 的实际市场画像

Stein： And we also see that. There are about 160,000 dental practices in the US alone, and they spend roughly $200,000 a year on administrative costs. And the interesting part is that — because we serve hundreds already — they can't find people.

Like what Alex shared, we come across every day: it is the doctor themselves, with their Harvard degree, that sits there till midnight. It makes them not like their job anymore. These small business owners just want to spend time on their patients. They don't want to spend time on administration, let alone working with Betty — or in this case, Wilder — because they can't find Betty.

A lot of people are surprised: isn't there a lot of skepticism? No, these people are in real pain and about to quit, or they hate this part of their job. So we come by and say, "Hey, we've built this agent that can already provide you with tens of hours of labor. Ask your friends or people in your study club if this is real." Or they Google it and see it's real. Then they adopt it very quick.

On the "why is this an interesting business" — this comes out of the P&L on the labor budget. We're already charging five figures for the first agent that only does 30 hours of labor a month, and there are 200 hours of labor to be done for Dr. Sloop. They see us as someone they bring in to actually run the practice for them.

Which is also complicated to do — because all of a sudden the requirement for software becomes: this is not a tool that I give Dr. Sloop and then Dr. Sloop is still on the line. In fact, one could argue a lot of AI companies are still like that — there is a human in the loop that ultimately decides what gets deployed. We can't do that. So we needed to build an agent — that's why it took us years — that errs on the side of correctness. Because if you take over a job reconciling all the insurance payments, interacting with the patient to bill, it needs to work. That was technically hard to do. Which also makes this super interesting from a technology perspective — you all of a sudden need to build autonomous systems that run on their own and don't have a human in the loop.

七、从"人在环内"到 98% 自动化

主持人： There was a great quote from Dr. Quan about you guys — that Lassie isn't replacing humans, but freeing them from wearing so many hats. Your launch video had a clip of him talking about how he can actually coach his kids' soccer teams now and go to their games. That's amazing.

There's a gap between wanting that and being willing to adopt AI — and actually having it run payments in a practice, and doing it so well that most of your growth is word of mouth, dentists recommending it to other dentists. How did you approach the technical build process for that? You guys are at 98% automation — walk us through that journey.

Frederick： I think a big part of it was us actually spending time in offices doing the work ourselves. I don't think we could have built a product that works as well as it does if we didn't know how to do the job.

Another part — we already talked about it — but a huge difference between SMBs and enterprises is that in SMBs there's nobody to use the tools. You can build a tool, but there's nobody there to use it. Dr. Sloop at night needs to go into the tool.

From the very beginning we focused on — initially, we were actually the humans in the loop. We took over all the work: "We'll just do this work for you." And we automated away our own problems. At some point, we got to a high enough level of automation that we felt comfortable handing it back over to the office.

Now, when we can't do something for some reason (which is pretty rare), we learn from what the staff tells us. We think about it as: we want to get to a sufficient level of automation across any product before we sell it. For us that's like 95% plus — not necessarily 100. I don't think we're going to wait until we get to 100 with one product and then do the next one.

We really think about the business as a whole — how much of the business can we automate, how much of the labor can we do with software. As soon as we can take over a job, we take it over and then move to the next one. Over time we'll learn the long tail of cases.

Stein： For a business it also doesn't matter that much. Let's make Dr. Sloop famous in this podcast…

Alex： He's going to learn.

Stein： If Dr. Sloop said he can become a customer — maybe we should talk about someone else that's still active.

主持人： We could reactivate him.

Stein： He might come out — that's how he sounded. That's the Series B story — we got Dr. Sloop out of retirement. We had a dental shortage, and now we don't. 100 million more people in the States get good dental care.

It's fine for a business owner if there is a tiny sliver of claims that need to be touched every week. They live in a nightmare world where you have to update 200 ledgers a week — that's how many patients they see — go to an insurance portal, update a system of record, check against the bank account 200 times a week. If you instead need to do that a handful of times, it saves 10, 20 hours.

I often compare it with how we are served as tech companies. It's the third company I'm building, and it is a lot easier and with a much smaller team than we used to do 10–15 years ago — because there are great tools we can use. Are all these tools completely running our finances autonomously yet, or our payroll, or HR? No. But they do save a tremendous amount of time.

That's how we approached this build as well. We didn't want a human in the loop because we want software that scales and can be implemented quick. But it's fine if it does — in this case, for the first agent — 98% of the work and there's a sliver left. And then the interesting thing: we have thousands of staffers basically giving us input on how to make that appeal that the agent currently cannot do.

We come from the consumer world. Frederick worked at Superhuman. I worked at Robinhood. So we have a very high bar for shipping. We don't release it before it's like, "Okay, this is good, it can be hands-off and it works." And then these staffers help us get it to an even higher percentage.

八、护城河讨论：初创 vs. 现存者，AI 时代的新规则

主持人： From an implementation and onboarding perspective, you guys integrate with existing practice management systems for the most part, versus making them switch a bunch of software to adopt Lassie. And Alex, you have written and talked a lot about startups getting distribution before an incumbent can innovate. Curious your thoughts on that in the AI era — and would also love to hear how you thought about which path to take there.

Alex： I had this epiphany when I was building my company. I call this the TiVo problem — TiVo and ReplayTV both invented the digital video recorder so you could pause online television, which is an amazing innovation but a terrible company. You have very few good outcomes:

  • Option one: You end up selling to one of the big guys like Comcast or Time Warner Cable — but they're not going to pay much, partially because if Comcast bought you, all the competitors would say, "We're not going to allow this to work." So you have what I call a control discount versus a control premium.
  • Option two: They copy what you've done many years later, much crappier (if that's a word), because they have all the customers.
  • Option three: You do a licensing deal with them, and they take all the economics because they have all the customers.

Hence my recognition was: what a lot of startups should do is the boring thing — build the raw pipes, own the customer, and then you get to build the fun feature on top. I still stand by this. Four years into TrialPay, I realized what I should build is this thing called Stripe. This is not revisionist history — Stripe had five people. "We should do boring payment processing, which is a commodity business, because if we do that we own the customer, chronologically we get them first. Then we had this other thing" — which in my case was offers-based payments — "which was very lucrative, but you can only do that if you control the pipe." Just the same way you can only build the digital video recorder if you have digital video to record.

AI 如何重写规则

How does this change with AI? In many cases these are non-categories — there is no incumbent.

Imagine I say I have a great idea: I'm going to do background checks for new employees as part of onboarding, and integrate with Workday, the biggest HR information system. That's a great idea. But it's such an obviously great idea that this thing called Workday might copy it — and they own all the customers. The battle between startup and incumbent — the incumbent might win because of their ability to add things. And that is actually magnified in the AI era.

Why are big companies not good at replicating small companies? One reason: they hire very bad engineers and have lots of process. But now AI kind of makes a bad engineer into a pretty good engineer. So that excuse kind of goes away a little bit.

But this is the cool thing about a lot of AI software companies — the AI that does the work. Who is the giant-ass incumbent of dental software? You and I know the answer, but it's not the same thing as "here's Workday, it's a tech company, they already have software and they can add something."

I remember a company I think called X1. Microsoft Outlook had really bad search, and this company funded by Idealab and all these VCs did search for your Outlook email — it was so good. But it's like, "You know who I think is going to do this eventually? Microsoft." That company unfortunately went to zero — Yahoo bought it a long time ago.

The battle between every startup and incumbent comes down to whether the startup gets the distribution before the incumbent gets the innovation. But one change is: the incumbent can get the innovation much more quickly.

The other is: there are a lot of categories where there never was an incumbent software company because the only job to be done was actual human labor. That's really exciting — you don't have to worry about "these guys are going to come in and eat my lunch." There are a lot of industries that just don't have an incumbent software solution.

For the industries that do — the risk is very high that they'll release AI features. If you look at the public markets, they're saying: "Oh, you're a software company — software is dead, software sucks, software is zero." "Oh, you're an AI." It's the opposite of what VCs are saying. But AI is software. Software is AI. The two are the same. I don't think everybody's come to that realization yet.

Stein： And we see exactly that — there isn't an incumbent that can do this job quickly.

Alex： Well, the incumbent was named Betty and she quit two weeks ago. That's the incumbent.

Stein： Yeah — or a billing agency.

Alex： It's Dr. Sloop's old assistant. That's the incumbent.

Stein： Or a version of that that's somewhere overseas or in the States. That's exactly what you're competing with. That's what intrigued us so much about these small businesses — there is no major player there. If you show up with software they have never seen before — which is now possible — they will adopt it, and you can grow.

Which is very defensible. The schlep you have to do to actually do the labor and talk to all these systems — you need to build an ontology to make sure everybody in this ecosystem is on the same page about an insurance claim and the patient payment, because all these systems have a slightly different definition. That makes it harder to build because there's no incumbent, but makes it extra defensible.

What we had to do was: first figure out all these read-and-write integrations between all these systems that Betty — the AI version — needs access to. Then figure out the data model that can be used across all these systems. Then on top of that, build agents. You can't really build agents without actually doing the work. There's years of work you need to do to get that going.

分发问题：小企业主是最难触达的客户

The go-to-market side as well. You need to knock on millions of doors. The interesting thing — we just talked about it — is not that they're skeptical about AI. Dr. Sloop is like, "Oh, I wish this was there." How do you get hold of Dr. Sloop? Because Dr. Sloop is not done at 7pm. There's an emergency patient that calls, then he goes back to the office to treat that patient. Dinner with the kids, then opens the computer — and "oops, the supplies need to be ordered because Betty left, so I need to do this myself right now."

For any company selling to SMBs, the interesting puzzle here — that's why this is super interesting go-to-market work — is: how do you adopt and spread AI in small businesses? Super interesting puzzle to solve. The crux: how do you get busy, non-technical owners to that adoption?

九、Onboarding：把 Robinhood 的 KYC 哲学搬到牙医诊所

主持人： I imagine the other part of the question — this is not like you download the AI app from the app store and then you're all done. How do you actually do the onboarding? And how much of that can you automate? That's part of what makes a business selling these things work or not work. Because if you have to send your own Betty to every single office in the country…

Stein： It would be amazing if it's just like download the Lassie app. These systems and processes are very manual.

Alex： I kind of think AI is overhyped in Silicon Valley but underhyped in Iowa. There are a lot of people in Iowa — how do you solve that last-mile distribution problem for Lassie?

Stein： It's a super interesting problem. Assume you can knock on all these doors and get them to try it. Then how do you get this adopted? Because the same argument still stands — they're very busy, they are not technical. Good luck setting up AI in their business.

That's also why our consumer backgrounds come in handy. At Robinhood or Superhuman, the time window is 48 hours. If the thing doesn't work and you don't provide core product value, you're out. These doctors are very much the same. Because not only are they hard to reach and hard to work with, if it doesn't work in a couple of months, you're out the door. It really needs to be plugged in and then do the job.

A lot of the work went into not only building this agent, but how do you set people up on that agent such that almost all the friction is gone. That was a lot of work, and it's already to a point that it's self-serve almost. There are a few more things left, but literally: the doctor in Iowa — let's not use Sloop again — says, "Yes, I want this." They go to almost a Stripe-like checkout or a Replit-like onboarding flow, where they hook up the bank account of the practice, they link the system of record, they link all the insurance portals that claims come in from. It confirms business information — are these the doctors that actually work in your practice? Under the hood, it configures things.

There are one or two pieces left, but we're months out until you basically have an agent you can almost set up self-serve. That was a big part — or is a big part — of bringing this technology to people in Iowa: can you build an almost-consumer-like onboarding flow where a lot of the complexity is abstracted away and happens under the hood?

I think I'm very impressed by Robinhood — I'm a little biased because I worked there. But in order to set up an account for a user without a human in the loop (which is what Robinhood pioneered — back in the days there was Charles Schwab, and "Hello, I want to open an account" meant going into the office), Robinhood pioneered that you can self-serve your way onto an account — KYC is getting done, your bank is getting linked. A lot of product work went under the hood there.

We ran into similar situations. How do you connect all these insurance portals and kick off the process such that the digital claims are coming in reliably? How do you reliably link a bank account, all these systems of record? A big part of this was figuring that piece out.

十、The Master Plan：从牙医到全世界小生意

主持人： To that point, there's more you can build and are building for dental practices — then there's all these other types of healthcare practices that could use Lassie, and then the broader universe of small businesses. How are you prioritizing what you build, who you sell to? Is there a world where Lassie for dentists makes Lassie for physical therapists better?

Stein： The master plan.

主持人： Yes.

Stein： Are we at that part of the episode?

主持人： Yes.

Stein： Three steps. The end goal here is that every small business should run itself, and the busy work is done by agents. We want to build an agent for the business that then will interface with the personal agent of a consumer — highly likely — that will interface with an agent at the insurance company or other parties the business needs to interact with.

Step one: to Alex's point, there are 160,000 dental practices in the US alone, $200,000 in labor that Dr. Sloop and others can't find. Serving that market first, you're looking at $1 billion in recurring revenue as a market. That's step one.

Step two: we will likely pick another doctor office type that is not well served and has a big TAM and needs consumer-like product — because, as discussed, a big part of this is: you get the AI to work 95% accurate-ish, it needs to really work, and the onboarding needs to be as simple as onboarding on Coinbase or Stripe.

Step three: we've then trained AI agents to run the small business. All small businesses at an abstract level have a system of record they need to read and write into. They all have customers — in doctor offices they happen to be patients — and interacting and transacting around payments, booking appointments. So the end goal is: if we serve all the doctor offices, we help all the small businesses across the world, because we're just the best at building AI agents that salt-of-the-earth people — people in Iowa and Paducah, Kentucky, and hopefully in Amsterdam down the line where I'm from, and Germany, Hamburg where Frederick is from — can start using as well.

That's the end goal. But similar to Superhuman and Robinhood, we work with laser focus on getting one thing really, really right, and then scale from there.

主持人： But the end goal is to help them all.

Stein： Amazing. I love that as a master plan.

主持人： It's a good one. A big one.

十一、新老经验：什么该带走，什么该忘掉

主持人： You both have been part of scaling many important companies in the past — Robinhood, Coinbase, Superhuman among others. And building a company in 2026 is a whole brave new world, so different than ever before. What are the biggest things you've carried over? And then what have you had to unlearn, or what do you think is new to being founders right now?

Frederick： There's a bunch of stuff we're applying now that I learned at Superhuman. For one, focusing on the right ICP and being really strict about who you onboard, to basically guarantee they're going to have a great experience.

In our case it's particularly important, because if we onboard the wrong practice — say we can't actually automate that much of their work — now we're kind of stuck with this customer. We claimed we're going to automate a bunch of labor for them, we can't do it. Are we going to do it? Are we going to offboard them? It's particularly painful, maybe more painful than in a kind of old-world product.

We've also obsessed about getting to the core product value really quickly. Our onboarding is like a story or a playbook or a movie — we have set points and checkpoints we want to reach in certain time frames, and we make sure it happens every time. And we measure that.

One thing that's really different about product building from back then to now: in the past, I think it was much more about functionality — the ability for the user to do something. Now, we think really only about what kind of labor can we automate, what work can we do, where can we save time.

If you're thinking about patient billing — previously you would have built the ability to send a statement and the ability to receive a patient payment. But if you look at where does the actual work of patient billing go today, it's figuring out: is the statement we're going to send the correct amount? And once the statement is sent, the patient calls and asks, "Why do I owe this amount? Do I really have to pay this? I thought this would be covered." So if you're looking at where the time goes, it actually goes into customer communication or some fuzzier part of the work.

When we're shipping a product like that, we're really thinking: once we deliver patient billing, the office should not have to spend any more time on patient billing. Which is super different to giving them a tool that they then need to use — which doesn't really save them a lot of time.

主持人： And neither of you were dental experts before you started the company — that's safe to say?

Stein： You go twice a year — that's pretty good.

主持人： You're supposed to, right? I'm just doing my civic duty.

招聘哲学：AI-native mindset 是新维度

主持人： How big is the team now? When you're hiring, are you looking for expertise in dental? What are the characteristics of team members you want to hire?

Stein： This is now mainly on our mind, because we found really great product-market fit in a large market where you can go after the labor that they can't find.

We have two takes on that. One — not much has changed, contrarian maybe take. You still need people with steep slope, ambitious and driven, with skills that are top-five-percentile either in engineering or in selling. Getting hold of Dr. Sloop is the same exercise as before — you can do it in a more AI-native way, but the skills are the same.

Maybe the only new thing is the AI-pilledness of a person. We see a pretty clear division across the board: do you believe that the way you code will change completely as a result of building a company in this era? Building out a finance department — do you think that's going to be completely different than before?

We interview specifically for that, because we want to build a 2026 version of a big organization — where we ship twice as much as others, we move four times as fast. Because we should not only have AI adopted in these businesses; the big puzzle for us is how do you build a team that also incorporates AI in all these functions.

So yeah — on one hand nothing has changed, because the bar is still the bar. I used to be a track-and-field runner, almost became a professional track-and-field runner but took a different path in life. My friends went on to the Olympics. Olympic running is still the same — you need to train twice a day, push it to the edge. That's not given to everyone, mentally and physically. That has not changed in company building.

What has changed is what you can do and the output you can generate — just four or five times more. That's the big experiment we're doing together. How quick can we get to all the dentists in America and build a really good product such that 200 hours are gone? How quick can we bring it to another vertical and help all small businesses? That's the big interesting experiment we're going to do over the coming years.

十二、AI 时代的悖论：更容易开公司，但也更难开公司

Alex： It's so much easier — if everybody can hire Betty, right? Just materialize a Betty. How does that change? It could actually work out where for small businesses, it's much easier to start one and run one — but then actually paradoxically it's much harder to be one.

If you think about moats in the AI era in general — we often talk about it with respect to software companies. It's so easy to go replicate XYZ software. "I did it on Replit, or on Lovable, or on Claude." You hear this left and right all the time. Much harder to say, "I'm going to go replicate Dr. Sloop's practice."

But one of the things that makes a small business somewhat defensible is that it is an accumulation of people that are required to deliver the end product. If you know who Yogi Berra is — famous Yankees baseball player that said all these things that make no sense but are quoted often — one of my favorite ones: "It's so crowded, nobody goes here anymore." It doesn't make sense.

But I guess my question is: how do you think small business changes if it's easier to run one? Because theoretically that could erode the margins of a small business — such that it's so crowded, nobody goes here anymore. This one moat that exists of just materializing people to deliver a product — it's now so much easier, but therefore it's actually harder.

Stein： Our current take on that: this assumes there's a cap on demand. If you just look at the dental practice — the same applies to trying to find a good plumber — there's just twice as much demand as can currently be supplied. This is a great opportunity for everybody to have great dental care and go twice a year.

The same can be said about primary care doctors. I grew up in the Netherlands. I had a very different primary care experience than most people in America. Because it's really hard to find the good primary care doctor that is in your community, knows you, your family, and takes care of you.

We see this as an opportunity to create — now there are 160,000 dentists, or hundreds of thousands of dentists. What if America has half a million dentists, or can see twice as many patients, maybe with the same amount of dentists? Plumbing is the same. A lot of these small businesses — they wish they could bake more pies, but they're constrained on labor.

What this unlocks: people have twice as much time for the craft. And that is an exciting future. All of a sudden you're going to see a better world. That's currently our view, which is super exciting about this technology.

That's also to your point — when we launched and finally told the world what we've been up to, a lot of people talked about how it's an optimistic example of how this new technology can be used. Because there's a lot of "what's going to happen to the world." But nobody can really be against cleaning up busy work for small business owners that should be baking pies, or polishing nails, or cleaning teeth, or drilling — depending on who you are, of course.

十三、剩下的技术难题：模型知道很多，却不知道"怎么干活"

主持人： So you started the business in 2020 — pre-AI, or pre what we think of as the generative AI revolution — the BC/AD divide of November 2022 when ChatGPT launched. What are the remaining hard problems? Now you have reasoning models — what cannot be done right now? What do you feel we still need more technical advance for? Sometimes it's a 90/10 thing where the last 10% is really really hard, but you can't be a feature-complete solution until you've done that. From a technical lens — where does work still need to be done? And what does the curve of that look like? It's not a question of AGI for small business, but you know — where are we on that curve?

Frederick： One thing that's interesting: the models are trained on so much data and they're so large, and yet they actually don't really know how to do any of this work. They don't have the workflows encoded in any way.

For example, we're working on a product now where we have to collect all these SOPs and documents about "how are you supposed to bill insurance claims to certain payers." To some extent humans would do the same — but there's a big amount of human knowledge encoded in these office managers, and they just know how to do this work. That's weirdly not that accessible on the internet.

We have a big advantage there because we have all this historical data out of their ERPs that we can look at and infer some of these workflows from. But that's something we notice a lot. When we started using some of the later reasoning models, we kind of assumed, "Oh, they probably just know how to do this work — like, why would they not, they're trained on all of this data." But it turns out they don't know all the intricacies of most of these workflows.

Less specific to Lassie, but I'm personally excited about smaller models that learn faster and can learn on less data. That'll be really cool. Over time we'll have intelligence disseminated everywhere. To the point where — like the Pixar lamp has its own personality — why not? I want my intelligence to be everywhere. It feels like we're super far from that.

I don't know if it'll benefit us necessarily that much. But there is something about the models not being able to learn very fast. As it relates to us — we put a lot of product work into how do you actually get input from people about their preferences and how they've done the work, in a way we can then use to actually make our agents smarter. From a product-UX perspective there's a bunch of interesting stuff to solve there.

十四、当"抗辩成本"归零：保险行业的下一次重塑

Alex： Maybe one final question between technical and non-technical. I've been thinking about this a lot: how the world changes when the marginal cost of arguing goes to zero.

I was thinking about this because Cigna, who I have for my health insurance, will only send paper checks. I was like, "Oh, I must have missed the online enrollment." Nope. They don't have one. Why? Well, they're kind of hoping you might lose the check, you might not deposit it. It's this intentional delay.

It's the same for a lot of insurance — "deny, deny, deny." They want to deny. And on the other side — "pretend that when my house burned down, I had a Picasso in there." Both parties are trying to cheat each other. This is not new to the insurance industry.

But now that everybody has this superpowered thing that costs effectively nothing to argue in perpetuity — "I can argue with you and then you can argue with me" — how does that change the business dynamic of things like insurance payments and collections? Because in many cases the counterparty the dentist is dealing with is the insurance carrier. A big part of accounts receivables comes from insurance companies.

Stein： It's quite interesting because it's pretty well regulated. If a dentist does a crown and you provide them with the correct narrative — Frederick was already talking about it — there is a document at Cigna that specifies: if you give me this X-ray and this narrative, we will cover that.

For a human it's quite hard to follow those rules. Take dentistry — there are 50, 60, maybe 100 common billing codes. It's a lot to remember for Mildred or Betty the staffer. In this case, our agent has all the documentation, has access to the X-ray that is the relevant one, knows how to build a treatment plan, and will submit that with the insurance company. The insurance company just needs to follow the rules. Then they will pay it out.

保险公司的隐藏激励

The other thing — because we're very deep in this industry — is an interesting dynamic. It took me a while to understand: Cigna also has an incentive to have good doctors in-network that are happy with them. Because every year they need to go to Andre and say, "Do you want to renew your dental plan with us?" And the reason is: he's going to look at, "Are there good dentists in the area that are covered, that Alex and Olivia can go to?" If the answer is no, because there's competition in this market, they will go to another insurance company.

There is actually an incentive to keep Dr. Sloop and Dr. Quan in-network, because otherwise they will not renew the plan with their employers. It is a lot more — for us it's quite interesting — why I also think these agents are so well equipped to do this work: there's very clear documentation, to Frederick's point.

数字化档案柜：另一个被忽略的战场

We can talk about this for hours another time, but we are also literally digitizing the file cabinet. It's really interesting — it's really hard to find these files, they're there. Once we have them we know how to do this.

All these payments you talked about — a lot of doctors across America still get paid on paper too. They get $100,000 in checks deposited on their desk. I did this — for Dr. Quan, I literally knock knock knock, open the door, sit on my bar stool. There's the mailman that gives me a stack. And I kid you not, I open all these envelopes, deposit $100,000 in cash — well, in checks — in the bank account of the doctor. Then I have to go to work on all these itemized invoices attached to the checks.

The interesting thing: even if we had the models, you couldn't really do this up until a couple of years ago because that was the status quo. The file cabinet was literally the file cabinet. In the file cabinet were the checks and the itemized invoices you need to do part of the job to keep the doctor office running.

Then the federal government stepped in and said this has to stop. You cannot do paper checks anymore for much longer. So they mandated this industry to switch to direct deposits — offer that as an option to a doctor. If a doctor says, "I want to flip the switch," you need to do that. Same as these itemized invoices — you need to create a digital file format for that. And we are also writing that tailwind. You will see that a lot of these small businesses — I think the stats are 70% are still paid on paper — are going through this massive digitization revolution right now, because of a federal inflection point that's regulatory.

Combined with these models being so good, this makes it super interesting. Because even if you had the models 5 years ago — yeah, the payments are still on paper. And we are digitizing that in the meantime. Which is also what we talked about earlier — it is not one-click and kaboom, because otherwise the whole country would be on digital payments. Why would Dr. Sloop not do this? Well, Dr. Sloop needs to also spend 50 hours figuring out with Cigna and Delta and all the other insurance companies, "How do I flip the switch?" It then comes into the bank account. Do you want the staffer to have access to that bank account? Likely not, because the rent payments are there — data you don't want your staff to see. That's why the status quo is the way it is.

We built this massive engine that basically says: "Hey, give us the business info, the tax ID number, and some other nonsense. We will do that conversion to digital payments." Which is also a hard product problem to solve — but we have productized that.

Super interesting to think about what other industries still have that. That's an even more interesting moat: okay, you can apply these models, bring them to Main Street — super hard. In addition to that, how do you convert data that's currently living in a file cabinet to a digital file format such that you can actually automate the work?

Frederick： To your earlier point about digital file cabinets not being that much more efficient — part of the reason all these payments are still on paper is that the staff basically prefers doing the work by hand on paper. If you just digitize everything, now you have a PDF instead of paper in front of you. You actually need tools to use that PDF, and it's preferable to just work off of a sheet. There wasn't much of an incentive to digitize. Now that's obviously different.

十五、Go-to-Market：面向"美国主街"的全新剧本

主持人： Obviously there are a lot of dental practices that want or even desperately need products like Lassie, but they are distributed and all over the country and there are a lot of them to reach. How do you think about reaching them? How do you bring agents to these mainstream American businesses?

Stein： This is a very different playbook than where currently the cutting edge is. It's like you have these models good enough, apply them in enterprises, do a few steak dinners, sign a contract, and then you have 10 million in ARR booked.

We literally need to go find thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of small businesses. It's a super interesting problem to solve. We've built this agent that's really good. What we're doing right now is literally mapping out: where are all these dentists, in this case? Then, after the next small business type in the country — who's the owner? What systems are they on? Are there any intent signals we can find? Like, they're looking for a job because they say it on Indeed. Then get in touch with these people with a message that resonates with them, that cuts through the noise.

This is especially — our customer type is very different. If you were to sell to me, you'd find me in Clay, enrich with some Apollo data, look me up on LinkedIn — "Okay, this is the guy that's going to buy my HR system." We can't really do that, because Dr. Sloop is not in that database. He's often not on LinkedIn.

This is a completely different playbook that we're developing here. That's another very compelling thing we're figuring out: what is the go-to-market playbook to adopt AI at many, many businesses? That's an exciting opportunity and untapped.

尾声

主持人： Thank you both so much for coming to chat with us today. This was awesome. We are very excited for the future of Lassie. Anyone who's listening who might be interested in working with the Lassie team to build something generational here — check it out at lassie.ai. And you guys are very actively hiring, from what I understand.

Stein： Oh, yeah.

主持人： Amazing. Great. Well, thank you guys again.

Stein & Frederick： Thank you so much. Thanks for hosting us.

[music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、被忽略的核心悖论：软件从未真正提高效率，直到它开始"干活"
Alex 在访谈中抛出了一个反直觉的暴击：**过去 50 年的软件革命，本质上只是把纸质档案柜数字化，却没有真正减少劳动**。1950 年的 HR 部门和 2000 年的 HR 部门人员配比几乎没变——软件只是把"守档案柜的人"换成了"守服务器的 CISO"。
这个观察的杀伤力在于：**整个 SaaS 行业可能一直在收"存储费"而非"劳动费"**。Toast、Workday、NetSuite 卖的不是效率，是"更漂亮的档案柜"。真正的效率革命要等到软件能编辑档案柜、执行档案柜里的动作，也就是现在。这也解释了为什么公开市场同时给"纯软件"打折、给"AI"溢价——市场在无意识地区分"档案柜生意"和"劳动生意"。
## 二、跨领域连接：Lassie 复刻的其实是 Robin Hood 的"KYC 时刻"
表面上 Lassie 是牙医版的 RPA，但 Stein 在访谈末尾露出了真正的底牌：**他在把 Robin Hood 的"消费级 onboarding"哲学移植到 B2B 主街商业**。
想想看——Robin

item.title: [Lex Clips] The controversial reason slavery was abolished | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被刻意"去诗化"的解放宣言：一份看似枯燥的提单

最令人意外的是，这份人类历史上最具道德重量的文件之一，被林肯故意写得像一张海运提单（bill of lading）。他并不是不会写雄辩的文字——葛底斯堡演说证明他能。他是主动放弃修辞，因为任何一句诗意的表达都会暴露它的真实性质：一场对私有财产的战时征用。

这背后藏着一个反直觉的政治工程学：当你要推行一项极端激进的变革时，最有效的伪装是把它写得极端无聊。 这一模式在跨领域中反复出现——重大立法常常藏在拨款法案的附录里；改变互联网走向的往往不是宣言，而是 RFC 文档；商业帝国的转型经常包装成"重构"或"合规更新"。林肯发现了这一规律的南北战争版本：修辞越低，穿透力越强。

二、权力的量子悖论：只能在无权之处行使权力

真正让人拍案的是那个几乎荒诞的法律结构——林肯只能在他没有实际控制权的地方解放奴隶，而在他有控制权的地方却无权解放。 签署宣言的那一刻，它在字面上没有解放任何一个人。

这不是漏洞，这是宣言的基本几何形态。它的效力与美国陆军的推进速度精确耦合：自由不是从纸面向下传导的，而是沿着军靴的行进线一米一米地物理扩散。这一点对我们理解"权利"这个概念有颠覆性意义——我们习惯把自由想成一种抽象的道德原则，但 1863 年 1 月 1 日之后，自由被证明是一种物流现象。

跨领域连接：这与今天的"数字权利"惊人相似。你在某个平台上的言论自由，边界取决于该平台服务器所在的司法管辖区、海底光缆的走向、以及某国的防火墙延伸到哪里。权利的地理学从未消失，它只是换了一层皮。

三、道德进步的"特洛伊木马"结构

第三个隐藏的洞见是关于如何让一个社会接受它还没准备好接受的东西。民主党人愿意为"联邦"流血，但拒绝为"解放一个黑人"流血。林肯的解法不是说服他们改变价值观，而是重新包装同一个行动：这不是解放，这是削弱敌人的战争工具。

这揭示了一个几乎普适的社会变革模式——深层的道德革新几乎从不以自身的名义完成，它总是搭乘一辆实用主义的马车进城。

  • 全民医保常常以"降低企业成本"进入议程
  • 环境保护法规常常穿着"国家能源安全"的外衣
  • 女性进入职场的历史转折点是二战的劳动力短缺，不是女权论证

林肯最深的政治智慧或许不是他反对奴隶制，而是他清楚地知道：在一个社会里，正确的事情往往必须先伪装成有用的事情才能被允许发生。 这既是历史的悲哀，也是变革者不得不掌握的语法。

而《第二没收法案》与《解放宣言》之间那个微妙差别——林肯故意去掉了"联邦派例外"条款，让宣言比国会立法更宽——是一个被忽略的细节：在这份被刻意写得像账单的文件里，林肯偷偷把范围扩大了。 无聊的外壳下藏着他真正的意图。

📝 转录文本

一、解放宣言作为战争策略

Lex： So, uh the Emancipation Proclamation was in part a military strategy.

Gary Gallagher： Abraham Lincoln based it entirely on his war-making power as commander-in-chief in a time of open rebellion. His inclination, there's no— He's often been criticized for not including so the soaring language he was capable of in the Emancipation Proclamation. One historian likened it to a bill of lading. It had all the soaring language of a bill of lading.

He did that on purpose. He did it because he he he doesn't have the power to strike at slavery in the absence of a war, the president doesn't, and he did it because he knows that he can't win the war with only Republicans in the army. He needs to keep Democrats on board with the war as well. They're not in favor of emancipation. The one way that they might accept it is as a tool to help achieve union, and to do that we've got to strike at the rebels way— strike at slavery. That will hurt their war effort, and it will also punish the people who brought on the war, and that would make—

二、面向忠诚州的政治考量

So, Lincoln hoped that by basing it strictly on his war power, it might be more widely accepted across all parts of the loyal states, uh and not as controversial as it was. It was still intensely controversial.

It alienated many Democrats when he issued it, who said, "You're changing what this war is about. We're willing to to shed our blood and maybe risk our lives to restore the union of the founders. I'm not going to risk my life to free a black person." That's a very very common attitude among Democrats.

三、宣言的真实适用范围

Lex： So, what did the the Emancipation Proclamation actually do? It emphasized the freeing of slaves in the South.

Gary Gallagher： It's even more complicated than that. The only place that Lincoln said he had the power as the war leader to strike at slavery is where the rebels were actually still in rebellion and in control. So, any place where the US Army was in control, any place— he said that is is in essence United States territory. Now, I can't free them there because I don't have the power. I can only free them where we don't have the power.

So, he exempted parts of states and areas in the South that it didn't apply to as of the moment he signed it. Going forward, any place that the United States Army went where it hadn't been on January 1st 1863 the Emancipation Proclamation applied and enslaved people would be freed by it.

At the literally at the time he signed it, it didn't free anybody because he's only saying I can free them where we're not in control. We have to be in control for this to have effect— for this to have power.

四、军队作为自由的边界

Lex： So, in part this is why the army was the boundary which the freeing was happening.

Gary Gallagher： It's absolutely the boundary. And Congress had already passed what was called the Second Confiscation Act. It passed this in in July of 1862. It announced that all enslaved people belonging to rebels were free. It— it didn't apply to people who could prove they were unionists living in the South and on states. Lincoln didn't make that distinction in the Emancipation Proclamation. His proclamation is broader than the Second Confiscation Act was.

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Shreyas Narla and Kadambari Shah on the 'The 1991 Project' | Ideas of India
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最令人震撼的观察：这个项目在无意识地"重演"1991改革本身

听完全部内容，最让我意外的不是印度改革的细节，而是这个"1991 Project"团队正在以一种近乎神秘的方式，复刻他们所研究的那场改革的每一个组织学特征：

  • 改革靠的是 少数互相信任的人 + 冷邮件式的横向连接（Rangarajan 从来不认识 Y.V. Reddy，凭一份公务员名单发掘他）——这个项目也是靠三个人 + 给部长发冷邮件、在机场"劫持"Chidambaram 起家的；
  • 改革之所以停摆是因为"没人培养下一代技术官僚"——项目团队因此把培育 stage-level 的年轻政策人才（1991 Fellowship）当成核心答案；
  • 改革在 M Document 里坚持 general equilibrium（六件事必须一起做）——项目也拒绝了"只做口述"或"只做档案"的单一路径，而是把口述史 + 专家委员会报告 + 传记 + 视频 + 会议 打包成一个整体才起作用。

换言之，他们不是在"研究"改革者的方法论——他们是在无意识地"是"那个方法论。 这是一个极罕见的"研究者—研究对象同构"现象。

二、跨领域连接：印度的"知识考古学"是一种不同于西方的认识论

Niranjan Rajadhyaksha 有一句轻描淡写却颠覆性的话被反复引用："印度经济思想史不在大学、不在期刊里——它埋在专家委员会报告里。"

这在跨领域上意味着什么？

  • 西方的知识传承走的是 university → journal → citation 的学术资本主义路径；
  • 而印度独立后 45 年里，连财政部首席经济顾问的姓名与任期都没有一块木牌记录——这不是"落后"，而是一种 完全不同的知识拓扑结构：印度的政策思想是通过 委员会 (committee) 这一临时性合议体 来沉淀、协商与传递的；
  • 类比：这更接近 中世纪伊斯兰世界的 majlis 传统，或 中国明清幕府/幕僚制度——知识不是被"发表"的，而是被"参与"的。

这就解释了一个诡异现象：为什么印度改革者的智识路径必须靠"triangulation"（三角验证），而不能靠单一权威文本——因为根本不存在那样的文本。这个项目本质上是在为印度发明一种它从未拥有过的知识基础设施。

三、被忽视的深层洞见：Manmohan Singh 的真正遗产不是改革，而是"人才管道"

这是整场对话中最反直觉的一个转折。所有讣告都在谈 Manmohan Singh 作为总理的核电协议、NREGA——只有这个团队看到了他真正的"元贡献"：

"改革之所以在 1991 之后能持续 15 年，然后戛然而止——是因为 Manmohan Singh 这一代人培养下一代的机制断裂了。"

这里有一个隐藏的系统性真相：制度变革的半衰期取决于制度设计者的 mentorship 半衰期。

  • 一个改革者如果只输出 policy，他的遗产会在 10-15 年内衰减；
  • 一个改革者如果输出 具备复制能力的年轻人（Rakesh Mohan、Montek、Shankar Acharya、Y.V. Reddy 都是他"扫描"出来的），遗产可以延续两三代；
  • 但当mentorship 的"复利"停止再投资时，整个改革共识会在一个隐蔽的临界点崩塌——外界看不到，因为它是渐进的。

这个洞见把政治经济学、组织行为学、复杂系统理论 (compound institutional capital) 串在了一起。而且它给现在的中国、越南、任何处于改革中段的国家提出了一个致命问题：你们的改革者今天在培养谁？

四、一个"啊哈时刻"：口述史的悖论——最专业的档案工作，反而必须从"业余的直觉"开始

Nona 告诉他们："别管方法论，先跟着直觉去做"——而最后产出的却是研究人员可以严谨引用的一级史料。这里的悖论是：方法论上的过度前置反而会杀死可用性，因为你会为了"正确"而错过所有那些愿意接你冷邮件、活着的、快 90 岁的当事人。这与创业中的 "ship first, iterate later" 是同一个认知结构——在窗口稍纵即逝的领域，'足够好的行动'胜过'完美的准备'。这或许是这个项目留给未来所有 institutional history 项目最重要的一课。

📝 转录文本

Ideas of India · The 1991 Project 五周年对谈

主持人： Shruti Rajagopalan
嘉宾： Kadambari Shah、Shreyas Narla
主题： 1991 改革 35 周年 & The 1991 Project 5 周年

一、开场：这不像访谈，更像团队例会

Hi, welcome to Ideas of India. दो इट फील्स लाइक आई एम इन वन ऑफ आवर टीम मीटिंग्स, बिकॉज़ टुडे माई गेस आर माय वंडरफुल कोलीग्स कादंबरी शाह एंड श्रेयस नारला — हु बीन ऑन द पॉडकास्ट बिफोर, एंड हूम ऑल ऑफ यू नो एस माय लिसनर्स।

टुडे वी आर गोना टॉक अबाउट द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स एंड द 1991 प्रोजेक्ट। दिस वीक एंड मंथ इज़ द 35th एनिवर्सरी ऑफ द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स — इट्स ऑलमोस्ट हार्ड फॉर मी टू बिलीव — एंड आल्सो द फिफ्थ एनिवर्सरी ऑफ़ द प्रोजेक्ट। वी किक्ड इट ऑफ इन द 30थ ईयर ऑफ़ द रिफॉर्म्स। सो इट इज़ सच अ प्लेज़र टू हैव बोथ ऑफ़ यू हियर।

"Glad to be back. नो, वी प्रीटी मच बीन हियर द होल टाइम। थैंक यू फॉर हैविंग अस, श्रुति।"

二、项目的缘起：一场 COVID 期间的意外发现

सो द वे इट स्टार्टेड — वी वर टॉकिंग अबाउट द रिफॉर्म्स। वान ऑफ़ आवर कॉलीग्स एंड गुड फ्रेंड प्रखर मिश्रा वाज़ ऑन द टीम बिफोर ही वेंट ऑफ़ टू डू हिज़ डॉक्टरल स्टडीज। सो श्रेयस, प्रखर एंड आय यूज़्ड टू वर्क विथ ईच अदर।

इट वाज़ कोविड, एंड वी वर टॉकिंग अबाउट द रिफॉर्म्स, एंड आय रियलाइज़ दैट दे डिडन्ट नो टू मच अबाउट इट — व्हिच इज़ रियली वियर्ड नाउ, बिकॉज़ दे आर अबाउट एस नर्डी एस इट गेट्स व्हेन इट कम्स टू द पॉलिसी वर्क स्पेस।

एंड आई वास लाइक: इफ दे डोंट नो एक्ज़ैक्टली व्हाई द 1991 रिफॉर्म्स हैपन ओर हाउ दे हैपन, देन नो वन विल नो। बिकॉज़, एस आई ऑलवेज से — 70% प्लस ऑफ़ इंडिया वाज़ बोर्न आफ्टर '91। व्हिच मीन्स ऑलमोस्ट टू-थर्ड्स ऑफ़ इंडियंस वर बोर्न आफ्टर द रिफॉर्म्स, एंड दे रियली डोंट हैव एनी लिव्ड एक्सपीरियंस ऑफ सोशलिज्म एंड लाइसेंस-परमिट राज।

Shreyas 的自我怀疑

"आय ऍम अ लॉयर बाय ट्रेनिंग, व्हिच मीन्स दैट आई एम गोइंग टू ओनली लुक एट द लॉ एंड नेवर रियली आस्क द क्वेश्चन — 'व्हेयर डिड दिस कम फ्रॉम, हाउ डिड दिस कम अबाउट, व्हाट्स द कॉन्टेक्स्ट?'
सो व्हेन आई लुक एट अ लेबर लॉ, व्हेन आई लुक एट इंडस्ट्रियल डिस्प्यूट्स एक्ट, व्हेन आई लुक एट द MRTP — फ़र्स्ट, यू नो, दैट वाज़ द एक्स्टेंट ऑफ़ माय एक्सपोज़र टू हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ पॉलिसी।"

एंड दिस इज़ एग्ज़ैक्टली व्हाट द कन्वर्सेशन वाज़ फाइव इयर्स एगो। आय हैड अ हेडलाइन अंडरस्टैंडिंग ऑफ व्हाट द रिफॉर्म्स वर — यू हियर द ऐब्रिविएशन "LPG" एंड दैट्स अबाउट इट। आय काइंड ऑफ़ गेट अ सेंस ऑफ़ हु नरसिम्हा राव वाज़ एंड हु मनमोहन सिंह वाज़। विनय हैड रिटन The Half-Lion; संजय बरू ने Accidental Prime Minister लिखी।

बट अगेन — आई एम अ पोस्ट-'91 चाइल्ड। आय बेसिकली ग्रू अप विथ हैविंग कंज़्यूमर गुड्स एट होम। सो आय डोंट हैव लिव्ड एक्सपीरियंस।

三、危机的本质：付不起两周的进口账单

टु आन्सर योर क्वेश्चन, श्रुति — आर इनिशियल एफ़र्ट्स वर एक्चुअली जस्ट टू टेल पीपल व्हाट हैड हैपन।

राइट नाउ वी हैव अ वेस्ट-एशियन क्राइसिस — वी हैड अ सिमिलर वेस्ट-एशियन क्राइसिस एंड वॉर, ऑइल प्राइसेस वेंट अप, ऑल दीज़ थिंग्स हैपन। एक्सेप्ट इंडिया हैड सच फ्यू रिज़र्व्स दैट इट केम टू अ पॉइंट वेयर इंडिया डिड नॉट हैव इनफ मनी टू पे फॉर मोर देन टू वीक्स वर्थ ऑफ इम्पोर्ट्स।

एंड इन अ कंट्री एस लार्ज एस इंडिया, देयर आर मेनी साइलेंट क्राइसिस — पीपल नॉट गेटिंग जॉब्स, पीपल स्टिल सो पुअर, हार्ड टू स्टार्ट अ बिज़नेस। बट द क्राइसिस व्हिच बर्थ द रिफॉर्म्स वाज़ जस्ट अबाउट नॉट बीइंग एबल टू पे योर बिल्स — व्हिच वाज़ एन इनॉर्मस एम्बरैसमेंट। टु एक्चुअली हैव टु शिप द गोल्ड आउट ऑफ़ द कंट्री, बिकॉज़ नो वन ट्रस्टेड योर इकोनॉमिक एबिलिटी टू पे समथिंग बैक।

सो द इनिशियल पार्ट ऑफ़ द प्रोजेक्ट वाज़: लेट्स टेल पीपल व्हाट हैप्पेंड। इन व्हॉट ऑर्डर इट हैप्पेंड, व्हाट वाज़ द पॉलिटिकल इनस्टेबिलिटी (थ्री प्राइम मिनिस्टर्स इन क्विक सक्सेशन), व्हाट वाज़ द इकोनॉमिक इनस्टेबिलिटी (गल्फ वॉर, राइज़िंग ऑइल प्राइसेस, इनॉर्मस डेफ़िसिट्स, अ करेंसी विद अ ह्यूज ब्लैक मार्केट)।

इट वाज़ सपोज़्ड टू बी अ रियली सिंपल प्रोजेक्ट, आदम। वी स्टार्टेड आइडिएटिंग अराउंड मार्च, एंड इट वाज़ सपोज़्ड टू एंड बाय एंड ऑफ़ जुलाई। एंड देन ऑफ़ कोर्स — एस श्रेयस सेज़ — नथिंग इज़ एवर डन व्हेन वी टच इट।

四、Shreyas 加入 & 传记撰写的起点

आय वाज़ कॉल्ड ऑन टू वर्क ऑन राइटिंग द बायोग्राफ़ीज़ ऑफ द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। बिकॉज़ ऑफ़ माय जनरल इंटरेस्ट इन पॉलिसी हिस्ट्री, यू सेड: "हे, व्हाई डोंट यू डॉक्युमेंट हु दीज़ रिफ़ॉर्मर्स वर, एंड एग्ज़ैक्टली व्हाट देयर पॉइंट्स ऑफ इंटरवेंशन वर?"

बट श्रेयस वाज़ लाइक: "आय ऍम नॉट एन इकोनॉमिस्ट एंड आय हैव नो आइडिया व्हाट आय एम टॉकिंग ऑन।" आय थिंक ही गॉट स्केयर्ड बाय द MRTP एक्ट — एवरीवन वाज़ स्केयर्ड ऑफ़ द MRTP एक्ट।

आय स्टार्टेड सॉर्ट ऑफ़ डॉक्युमेंटिंग दीज़ प्रोफ़ाइल्स — फ़ैसिनेटिंग टु सी हाउ देयर बैकग्राउंड्स वर, हाउ दीज़ प्लेयर्स इंटरैक्टेड विद ईच अदर। डॉ. रंगराजन एस डिप्टी गवर्नर, देन कम्स बैक एस गवर्नर। मॉन्टेक सिंह अहलूवालिया, वर्ल्ड बैंक → इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र → कॉमर्स सेक्रेटरी '91 → फ़ाइनैंस सेक्रेटरी।

सम ऑफ़ देम हैड रिटन देयर मेमॉयर्स। सम हैड रिटन एस्सेज़ ऑर बुक चैप्टर्स। बट वी हैड ऑल द बिग नेम्स — मनमोहन सिंह, नरसिम्हा राव, मॉन्टेक। एंड देयर वर सम जर्नल पेपर्स दैट डॉक्युमेंटेड सम नेम्स — बट यू नो, दीज़ आर लॉन्ग-फ़ॉरगॉटन, 25–30 इयर्स ओल्ड।

五、口述历史的诞生：从 K.P. Krishnan 的一次会面开始

आय रिमेम्बर गोइंग टु मीट K.P. Krishnan विद प्रखर, एंड ही स्टार्टेड ड्रॉपिंग द नेम्स ऑफ़ डिफ़रेंट सेक्रेटरीज़ / जॉइंट सेक्रेटरीज़ हु वर इन द मिनिस्ट्री एट दैट पॉइंट। आय हैड नॉट हर्ड ऑफ़ जयंता रॉय — बट ही वाज़ द कॉमर्स मिनिस्ट्री इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र। एन.के. सिंह हैड जस्ट रिटन हिज़ मेमॉयर — ही केम अप इन कन्वर्सेशन।

एंड देन दे सेड: "यू विल हैव टु टॉक टु द एक्चुअल रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। बट दे आर आल्सो ओल्ड — व्हिच मीन्स दैट वी डोंट हैव द लक्ज़री ऑफ़ टाइम।"

देयर वर सेवरल ऑफ़ आर रिफ़ॉर्मर्स हु वर नॉट मेडिकली इन अ पोज़िशन टु टॉक टु अस — एंड दैट वाज़ ऑलरेडी फ़ाइव इयर्स एगो। सो देयर वाज़ अ सेंस ऑफ़ अर्जेंसी।

"Chinese Whispers" 问题

फॉर इन्स्टन्स, अजय शाह एंड निरंजन राजाध्यक्ष — दे हैव हर्ड द स्टोरीज़ फ़र्स्ट-हैंड फ़्रॉम विजय केलकर ओर रंगराजन। नाउ वी आर हिअरिंग अ सेकेंड वर्ज़न ऑफ़ इट। यू डोंट वांट दिस टु बी अ 'Chinese whispers' काइंड ऑफ़ थिंग — देयर दे हिअर इट फ़्रॉम अ सोर्स, एंड देन वी हिअर इट फ़्रॉम देम।

印度制度记忆的缺失

आय रियलाइज़्ड वी डोंट हैव गुड इंस्टिट्यूशनल हिस्ट्री एंड मेमोरी। सो मच ऑफ़ दिस वाज़ डन बाय टेक्नोक्रैट्स। वी डोंट हैव अ सिस्टम वेयर व्हेन अ ब्यूरोक्रैट लीव्स एन ऑफ़िस, दे डु एन एग्ज़िट इंटरव्यू ओर एनी काइंड ऑफ़ हैंडऑफ़।

वी कैन्ट ईवन फ़ाइंड इन इंडिया द स्टार्टिंग एंड एंडिंग डेट्स — एंड व्हेन आय से डेट्स, आय डोंट मीन the exact date, आय मीन the year — व्हेन समवन स्टार्टेड एंड एंडेड इन अ पर्टिकुलर डिपार्टमेंट।

Shankar Acharya 的木板轶事

दिस रिमाइंड्स मी ऑफ़ अन एनेकडोट डॉ. आचार्य मेंशंड। व्हेन ही बिकेम चीफ़ इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़र, देयर वाज़ नो बोर्ड — लाइक अ वुडन प्लैक इन द ऑफ़िस ऑफ़ द CEA — दैट लिस्टेड ऑल प्रीवियस CEA'ज़ विद डेट ऑफ़ अपॉइंटमेंट टु डेट ऑफ़ रिटर्न। नाइन पीपल हैड ऑलरेडी हेल्ड दैट पोस्ट। ही फ़ाइनली गॉट इट डॉक्युमेंटेड — बट ईवन देन, फ़ॉर सम ऑफ़ द अर्ली वन्स, दे डिडन्ट हैव द एग्ज़ैक्ट डेट, ओनली अ रफ़ मन्थ।

45–50 इयर्स ऑफ़ इंडिपेंडेंस, एंड वन ऑफ़ द सीनियरमोस्ट टेक्नो पोज़िशन्स — इन द फ़ाइनैंस मिनिस्ट्री, ऑफ़ ऑल मिनिस्ट्रीज़ — डिडन्ट हैव अ क्लीन रेकॉर्ड।

"印度的第二次独立"

आय थिंक दिस इज़ इंडिया'ज़ सेकंड फ़्रीडम। द रिफ़ॉर्म्स आर एस इम्पॉर्टेंट एस गेटिंग यूनिवर्सल एडल्ट फ़्रैंचाइज़, बिकॉज़ पार्टिसिपेटिंग इन द मार्केटप्लेस इज़ एस इम्पॉर्टेंट एस पार्टिसिपेटिंग इन द पॉलिटिकल स्पेस। एंड नॉट एवरीवन वाज़ अलाउड टु पार्टिसिपेट इन द मार्केटप्लेस — विदर एस अ कंज़्यूमर ओर एस अ प्रोड्यूसर।

六、方法论：如何做一次严肃的口述史

बट ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ — यू कैन गो टॉक टु देम, यू मस्ट मेक देम फ़ील कम्फ़र्टेबल, दे विल स्टार्ट स्पीकिंग, दे विल रिकलेक्ट, दे विल शेयर। ऑफ़्न दे गो: यू प्रेस द रेकॉर्ड बटन एंड यू जस्ट रन विद इट।

एट दैट पॉइंट, द 1947 Partition Project वाज़ डूइंग अ लॉट ऑफ़ द राउंड्स इन इंडिया। दिल्ली वाज़ राइफ़ विद दीज़ सेशन्स। सो यू काइंड ऑफ़ हैड अ सेंस ऑफ़ हाउ ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ वर बीइंग डन।

बट वी कुड नॉट डु दैट फ़ॉर समथिंग लाइक दिस। पार्टिशन इज़ अबाउट पर्सनल मेमोरीज़ ऑफ़ ट्रॉमैटिक इवेंट्स — वी'र नॉट ट्राइंग टु गेट द टेक्स्चर ऑफ़ समथिंग, वी'र एक्चुअली ट्राइंग टु गेट द टेक्निकल डिटेल्स।

借鉴：世界银行 + Stanford + Nona Storr

वर्ल्ड बैंक हैड डन एन इंस्टिट्यूशनल मेमोरी प्रोजेक्ट, बट इट फ़ेल्ट लाइक अ बिट ऑफ़ "इन-ग्रुप स्पीक"। दे ट्रांसक्रिप्ट्स रेड लाइक एन ऑनगोइंग कन्वर्सेशन, आय वाज़ ईव्ज़ड्रॉपिंग विदआउट मच कॉन्टेक्स्ट।

देन प्रखर टैप्ड इनटु हिज़ नेटवर्क्स। यू'ड मेड द कनेक्शन विद Nona Storr एट GMU — शी हैड डन ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़ इंटर्नली एट Mercatus। शी सेड इट्स फ़ाइन टु सेंड देम क्वेश्चन्स इन अडवांस, बट यू कैन्ट बी टू स्पेसिफ़िक — यू'ल ऑल्टर देयर मेमोरी बिकॉज़ यू आर प्रॉम्प्टिंग देम। बट यू ऑल्सो कैन्ट बी लूज़ी-गूज़ी। यू'ल हैव टु फ़ाइंड दैट राइट बैलेंस।

वी स्पोक टु Ryan Perkins एट Stanford, हु वाज़ द क्यूरेटर फ़ॉर द साउथ एशियन एंड इस्लामिक स्टडीज़। Stanford हैज़ अ रिच डिटेल्ड वर्क ऑन ऑरल हिस्ट्री प्रोजेक्ट्स — लव्ली "10 tips to remember", टेम्पलेट्स फ़ॉर कॉन्ट्रैक्ट्स, हाउ यू हैंडल पोस्ट-प्रोडक्शन।

七、给 Rangarajan 发的第一封冷邮件

द फ़र्स्ट पर्सन हु रेकॉर्डेड विद अस वाज़ अ कोल्ड ईमेल टु डॉ. रंगराजन। एंड आय हैव लिव्ड इन अ टाइम व्हेन डॉ. रंगराजन'ज़ सिग्नेचर वाज़ ऑन द ₹100 नोट। ही वाज़ RBI गवर्नर — अ रियली बिग डील।

आय हैड नो अंडरस्टैंडिंग दैट इफ़ वी कोल्ड-ईमेल्ड हिम, ही विल राइट बैक। नॉट ओनली डिड ही राइट बैक — ही रोट बैक इन 24 आवर्स। ही डिडन्ट आस्क अस हु वी वर, ही डिडन्ट आस्क फ़ॉर एनी क्रेडेंशियल्स। ही जस्ट सेड: "दिस इज़ फ़ैंटास्टिक, यू गाइज़ आर डूइंग समथिंग अमेज़िंग। हाउ कैन आय हेल्प?"

एंड दैट वाज़ इट। वी वर ऑफ़ टु द रेसेज़। दिस वाज़ पीक कोविड, जस्ट बिफ़ोर द डेल्टा वेव। श्रेयस, प्रखर एंड आय मैनेज्ड टु गो टु मद्रास स्कूल ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक्स एंड रेकॉर्ड द फ़र्स्ट टू सेशन्स इन-पर्सन।

ही आस्क्ड फ़ॉर 3–4 वीक्स बिफ़ोर, प्रेप्ड, लुक्ड ऐट द क्वेश्चन्स, मेड नोट्स। वी वर लाइक: "ओह! नाउ वी डु दिस विद एवरीवन एल्स।" ही टोल्ड अस ही नीड्स ब्रेक्स। सो वी वर लाइक: "ओह! वी शुड डु दिस विद ऑल ऑफ़ देम, बिकॉज़ पीपल गेट एग्ज़ॉस्टेड, देन दे स्टार्ट मिसरिमेम्बरिंग डिटेल्स।"

आय ऑलवेज जोक: व्हेन वी ग्रो अप, वी वांट टु बी लाइक रंगराजन।

八、机场"劫持" Chidambaram

आय वाज़ इन दिल्ली, वॉकिंग एट टर्मिनल थ्री। आय कुड सी — Mr. Chidambaram — ही इज़ सो डिस्टिंक्टिव, द व्हाइट वेष्टी। नो बिग गार्ड्स, नोबडी, जस्ट हिम।

आय हैड दिस 10-सेकंड डिलेमा: "शुड आय, ओर शुड आय नॉट?" आय सेड — वेल, यू नो, दिस इज़ नाउ ओर नेवर, आय डोंट नो व्हिच अदर वे टु रीच हिम। सो आय जस्ट सेड, "श्रुति सैद-कोस्ट हिम" — आय गॉट हिज़ अटेंशन।

आय सेड: "मि. चिदंबरम, फ़्रॉम... वी डु द 1991 Project।" आय गेव द क्विक 10-सेकंड स्पीएल। "वी आर डूइंग दीज़ ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, टॉकिंग टु द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स।" अंटिल देन ही वाज़ जस्ट स्टेयरिंग एट मी।

देन आय सेड: "वी रेकॉर्डेड फ़र्स्ट विद डॉ. रंगराजन, एंड वी फ़िनिश्ड अबाउट फ़ोर आवर्स विद हिम।" — एंड हिज़ फ़ेस चेंज्ड कम्प्लीट्ली।

द क्रेडिबिलिटी एंड रेप्युटेशन दैट रंगराजन हैज़ — इट पास्ड ऑन टु अस, हेल्प्ड बिल्ड आर गुडविल सो मच दैट द मोमेंट आय ड्रॉप्ड हिज़ नेम, मि. चिदंबरम सेड: "जस्ट ईमेल मी, लेट्स सेट इट अप।"

九、Kadambari 加入 & 第一次录音的紧张

Kadambari जॉइन्ड लिटरली अ मन्थ आफ़्टर वी फ़िनिश्ड विद डॉ. रंगराजन इन डिसेंबर। स्टार्टेड विद अस इन जन। द फ़र्स्ट वन शी वाज़ ऑन वाज़ मॉन्टेक सिंह अहलूवालिया, फ़ॉलोड बाय डॉ. शंकर आचार्य।

"आय रिमेम्बर हाउ नर्वस आय वाज़ इन दैट वेरी फ़र्स्ट वन। आय थिंक आय बेयरली सेड थ्री वर्ड्स इन दैट एंटायर रेकॉर्डिंग। बट आय वाज़ जस्ट सो टेकन बाय सच अ सेंस ऑफ़ कॉलेजिएलिटी बिटवीन द डिफ़रेंट रिफ़ॉर्मर्स। ईवन व्हेन दे आर डिसअग्रीइंग विद ईच अदर, देयर इज़ अ सेंस ऑफ़ रेस्पेक्ट — व्हिच इज़ वेरी रेयर टु सी टुडे।"

आफ़्टर दैट फ़ॉलोड डॉ. अशोक देसाई, मि. नारायण मूर्ति। "आय फ़ील लाइक सो मच आय कुड लर्न, नॉट जस्ट फ़्रॉम देयर स्टोरीज़, बट द वे दैट दे कंडक्टेड देम्सेल्व्स।"

一个"啊哈"瞬间

व्हेन मॉन्टेक स्टार्टेड, अ फ़्यू मिनट्स इन, डॉ. राकेश मोहन कॉल्ड हिम — इट वाज़ अराउंड द टाइम ऑफ़ द बजट। दीज़ पीपल आर आउट ऑफ़ ऑफ़िस, यट स्टिल इंटरेस्टेड। द मोमेंट काड सेड "वुड यू प्लीज़ मेक एन इंट्रोडक्शन फ़ॉर अस टु राकेश मोहन?" — वेल, द होल थिंग इज़ हिस्ट्री। नाउ वी हैव डॉ. राकेश मोहन ऑन रेकॉर्ड।

"यू आर नॉट द ओनली हस्लर, श्रेयस। यू कोस्ट पीपल एट एयरपोर्ट्स — आय कोस्ट देम ऑन Zoom।"

十、专家委员会报告：印度经济思想的隐藏档案

"द हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ इंडियन इकोनॉमिक थॉट इज़ नॉट फ़ाउंड एट यूनिवर्सिटीज़ एंड जर्नल आर्टिकल्स — इट इज़ रियली बरीड इन एक्सपर्ट कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स।"
— निरंजन (राजाध्यक्ष)

दिस वन सेंटेंस निरंजन हैज़ ऑलवेज टोल्ड मी, बट इट रियली डिड नॉट लीव मी। वी डिडन्ट हैव अ डीप यूनिवर्सिटी कल्चर, वेरी फ़्यू जर्नल्स, अ लॉट ऑफ़ पीपल इन गवर्नमेंट वर नॉट राइटिंग फ़ॉर इकोनॉमिक जर्नल्स।

सो हाउ डु यू गेट ऑल दिस मैटेरियल? इट्स रियली थ्रू कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स।

挖掘过程：从图书馆到复印店

आय यूज्ड टु गो टु नेहरू लाइब्रेरी बैक इन द डे एंड गेट द फ़िज़िकल कॉपीज़ एंड स्कैन देम। ऑफ़्नटाइम्स दे ऑल वुड रेफ़र टु द P.C. Alexander Committee Report — ओह माय गॉड। पार्लियामेंट लाइब्रेरी हैड इट। वी वर एबल टु गेट एक्सेस, गेट अ कॉपी, स्कैन इट, कीप इट।

एज़ इट हैप्पेन्स — डॉ. पनगारिया वंस राँग टु आस्क: "डु यू, बाय चांस, हैप्पन टु हैव द Alexander Committee Report?" वेल, वी हैड इट! एंड ही टोल्ड अस, "यू आर द ओनली पीपल हु हैव इट।"

कैन यू इमैजिन? दिस इज़ समवन हुज़ बीन द वाइस चेयर ऑफ़ द नीति आयोग। ऑल दिस कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स यूज्ड टु लिव ऑन द प्लानिंग कमीशन वेबसाइट, बट व्हेन इट गॉट रीवैम्प्ड इनटु द नीति आयोग वेबसाइट, अ लॉट ऑफ़ दिस स्टफ़ गॉट मिस्ड।

Abid Hussain, P.C. Alexander, Sukhamoy Chakravarty, एंड Arjun Sengupta — दीज़ आर लाइक फ़ोर कमिटी रिपोर्ट्स दैट केम अप ओवर एंड ओवर एंड ओवर एगेन। दे वर द वेरी अर्ली वन्स। एंड नोबडी हैड कॉपीज़ ऑफ़ देम।

दिस इज़ अ लेबर ऑफ़ लव — स्टैंडिंग इन लाइन एट अ फ़ोटोकॉपी शॉप, गेटिंग इट डिजिटाइज्ड, मेकिंग श्योर द ऑरिजिनल कॉपी वाज़ सेंट बैक। अ लॉट ऑफ़ ब्लड, स्वेट एंड टियर्स हैज़ गॉन इनटु दिस।

十一、网站的演化：从一页滚动到"思想与影响"时间轴

द फ़र्स्ट पार्ट ऑफ़ व्हाट वी डिड — इट वाज़ जस्ट अ वेरी सिंपल वन-पेज स्क्रोल। एज़ द प्रोजेक्ट ग्रू, वी रियलाइज़्ड वी नीडेड टु शो अ लॉट मोर।

现在的四大板块

गोइंग टु द वेबसाइट, यू विल सी फ़ोर बकेट्स:

  4. Conversations & Video Series — India's Reform Journey Revisited, Conversations on Deregulation, Talking Trade, Book Spotlight

"Ideas and Influences" 板块

व्हाइल डूइंग द ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, वी नोटिस्ड अनदर स्टोरी इमर्जिंग — द इंटलेक्चुअल रूट्स ऑफ़ रिफ़ॉर्म थिंकिंग।

फ़ॉर एग्ज़ैम्पल: Bhagwati & Desai (1968) India: Planning for Industrialization — क्रिटिक्ड प्रोटेक्शनिज़्म, अडवोकेटेड मार्केट रिफ़ॉर्म, फ़ोरशैडोइंग द इकोनॉमिक रिफ़ॉर्म्स। सम लेस-वेल-नोन वर्क्स लाइक Sudarshan on how post-1991 policies impacted poverty and progress।

नाउ ऑन द वेबसाइट देयर इज़ अ टाइमलाइन फ़्रॉम 1920 टु टुडे — ऑन द डिबेट्स, इवेंट्स, पीपल दैट कंट्रिब्युटेड टु दिस इंटलेक्चुअल स्टोरी बिहाइंड द रिफ़ॉर्म्स।

Rabbit-hole 方法论

वी आर प्रोज़ ऐट फ़ॉलिंग इनटु रैबिट होल्स। श्रेयस'ज़ रैबिट-होल टेंडेंसी रियली केम आउट इन द ऑरल हिस्ट्री प्रेप। कादंबरी'ज़ रियली केम आउट इन द वेबसाइट।

फ़ॉर इंस्टेंस — मोस्ट ऑफ़ द रिफ़ॉर्मर्स कॉल देम्सेल्व्स Fabian Socialists। सो देन यू'र लाइक: "OK, हु आर दीज़ Fabian Socialists?" — Sidney & Beatrice Webb, Harold Laski। यू हैव टु फ़ाइंड द बुक, फ़ाइंड अ क्लीन कॉपी, चेक इफ़ इट्स कॉपीराइट-एक्सपायर्ड।

द बिगेस्ट थिंग, कादंबरी, दैट यू मैनेज्ड टु डु — यू प्रोवाइडेड कॉन्टेक्स्ट। नॉट अ लॉन्ड्री लिस्ट ऑफ़ बुक्स — यू कॉन्टेक्स्चुअलाइज़्ड दीज़ वर्क्स।

十二、Doug Irwin 的邮件 & Manmohan Singh 的遗产

डग अर्विनne acknowledge किया अस in one of his major papers — एंड फिर एक ईमेल भेजी: "Shruti, this is such a fantastic repository. It made my life easy."

द डे वी गॉट दैट ईमेल, श्रेयस वाज़ एक्चुअली फ़्लोटिंग। ही वाज़ लेविटेटिंग इन हिज़ चेयर। हिज़ फ़ीट वर नॉट ऑन द ग्राउंड।

Vikrant Pandey - 概念验证

Vikrant Pandey — दैट डॉक्टरल स्टूडेंट एट यूनिवर्सिटी ऑफ़ मुंबई (नाउ प्रोफ़ेसर देयर) — अगेन, अ कोल्ड ईमेल। यूज्ड अ बिग चंक ऑफ़ द रिपॉज़िटरी फ़ॉर हिज़ डिज़र्टेशन। दैट रियली पुल्ड इट टुगेदर फ़ॉर मी। दैट कैरीड मी ऑन फ़ॉर टू इयर्स।

Manmohan Singh 的讣告

वी हैड आस्क्ड डॉ. मनमोहन सिंह फ़ॉर ऑरल हिस्ट्रीज़, ही हैड अग्रीड। बट ड्यूरिंग कोविड ही वाज़ रियली इल। लेटर ही सेड: "आय वरी दैट माय मेमोरी विल बी फ़िक्शन। आय डोंट कम्प्लीट्ली ट्रस्ट दैट आय रिमेम्बर एवरी डिटेल। व्हाट यू'व डन इज़ अमेज़िंग — कैरी ऑन।" वी नेवर रेकॉर्डेड विद हिम।

व्हेन ही पास्ड अवे (24 डिसेंबर), एवरीबडी रोट अबाउट द रिफ़ॉर्म्स। मेजर न्यूज़पेपर्स कॉपी-पेस्टेड आर मैटेरियल एंड पुट इट ऑन देयर फ़्रंट पेज। वी बिकेम द प्राइमरी रिपॉज़िटरी फ़ॉर एवरीवन राइटिंग ऑन मनमोहन सिंह।

星探 Manmohan Singh

ओनली अस टॉक्स अबाउट हिम एज़ अ फ़ैंटास्टिक टैलेंट स्काउट। माय फ़ेवरेट स्टोरी इज़ Y.V. Reddy — मनमोहन सिंह अपेरेंटली यूज्ड टु लुक ऐट द लिस्ट ऑफ़ IAS ऑफ़िसर्स हु वर रियली गुड ऐट इकोनॉमिक्स, हु गॉट अ गुड रैंक। ही सेड: "या, ही शुडन्ट बी अ डिस्ट्रिक्ट कलेक्टर समवेयर फ़ार अवे — ही शुड बी ब्रॉट इनटु द इकोनॉमिक अडवाइज़री एंड टेक्नोक्रेसी।"

एंड सो मच ऑफ़ व्हाई द रिफ़ॉर्म्स कंटिन्यूड फ़ॉर सो लॉन्ग आफ़्टर 1991, एंड स्टॉप्ड आफ़्टर 15–20 इयर्स — इज़ बिकॉज़ ऑल दिस पीपल हैड मूव्ड अप, एंड नो वन हैड बॉदर्ड टु कल्टिवेट दैट नेक्स्ट जनरेशन।

十三、会议、视频、"Yes-And"文化

रिफ़ॉर्म्स आर वेरी पॉलिटिकली रिस्की एंड रेप्युटेशनली कॉस्टली। यू कैन्ट टेक अ रैंडम आइडिया ऑफ़ द स्ट्रीट — इट नीड्स टु बी एन आइडिया दैट हैज़ मेड इट्स इनरोड्स विद अ लॉट ऑफ़ क्रेडिबिलिटी एंड ट्रस्ट विदइन गवर्नमेंट।

हाउ डु यू डु दैट? थ्रू एक्सपर्ट कमिटीज़। एंड टु ईवन गेट कमिटीज़ सेट अप — यू नीड टु हैव दिस पीपल नो ईच अदर।

सो वी स्टार्टेड डूइंग: - रिसेप्शन्स एंड मिक्सर्स फ़ॉर ओल्डर एंड यंगर जनरेशन्स - इंडिया आइडियाज़ कॉन्फ़्रेंस (2022 Goa on Political Economy → 2023 Chennai on Digital Transformation → Deregulation in Indian States) - IMF मीटिंग्स के दौरान DC में मिक्सर — केम आउट ऑफ़ मनमोहन सिंह ऑब्च्युअरी सोर्स

Yes-And Culture

पीपल एट Mercatus जस्ट डोंट हैव बैगेज। इन इंडिया देयर वर सो मेनी नेसे-सेयर्स: "नो वन विल कोऑपरेट। इट विल बी सो एक्सपेंसिव। नो वन विल टॉक टु यंग पीपल।" Mercatus वाज़ जस्ट लाइक: "रन विद इट।" दे वर लाइक: "या, Stanford हैज़ द बेस्ट मेथडोलॉजी, यूज़ इट।"

Mercatus हैज़ दैट कल्चर ऑफ़ 'Yes-And' — दैट इम्प्रूव-ऑफ़-कॉमेडी कल्चर।

Mercatus 的思想史根基

आय ऍम सराउंडेड बाय हिस्टोरियन्स ऑफ़ थॉट। Peter Boettke, Tyler, Mario — ऑल फ़ैंटास्टिक हिस्टोरियन्स ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक थॉट। स्टडीइंग द हिस्ट्री ऑफ़ इकोनॉमिक थॉट ऐट Mercatus — इट्स जस्ट समथिंग यू डु। GMU माइट बी द लास्ट प्लेस दैट स्टिल डज़ इट ऐट द PhD लेवल।

十四、政策论文系列

द नेक्स्ट सेट ऑफ़ रिफ़ॉर्म्स — व्हाट डज़ इंडिया नीड टुडे? वी हैव अल्रेडी पब्लिश्ड:

  • Shreyas — India's Competition Law and the risks of being anti-big or anti-scale
  • Arvind Panagariya — India's trade policy and the case for returning to a more liberal trade regime
  • Amartya Lahiri & Devashish Mitra — creating productive jobs through labor-intensive manufacturing
  • Sarthak Pradhan & Pranay Kotasthane — India's climb up the innovation ladder
  • Praveen Krishna — India's trade agreements
  • Shruti & Shreyas — how India's labor laws prevent firms from scaling
  • Ankita Dinkar & Samriddhi Surana — electricity challenges faced by Indian manufacturers

वी स्टार्टेड दिस टू इयर्स एगो, एंड लुक हाउ रेलिवेंट एवरीथिंग बिकेम — फ़्रॉम द ट्रेड वॉर टु सेमीकंडक्टर्स। वी कुड सी दिस कमिंग।

十五、1991 Fellowship — 州级人才管道

अ लॉट ऑफ़ द मैक्रो-स्टैबिलिटी, करेंसी, मॉनेटरी, फ़िस्कल साइड ऑफ़ द रिफ़ॉर्म्स वर ऑल डन ऐट द यूनियन लेवल। द वर्स्ट हैज़ बीन क्रॉस्ड — दिस ईयर वी हैड अनदर बैलेंस-ऑफ़-पेमेंट स्ट्रेस, बट इट डिडन्ट टर्न इनटु अ क्राइसिस।

नाउ व्हाट रिमेन्स इज़ ऑलमोस्ट ऑल स्टेट-लेवल सब्जेक्ट्स — लैंड, एग्रीकल्चर, एनर्जी।

टू प्रॉब्लम्स: 1. मोस्ट पीपल डोंट थिंक ऑफ़ स्टेट-लेवल रिफ़ॉर्म्स एज़ द "कूल थिंग"। 2. एनी टाइम यू टॉक टु थिंक टैंक्स — "व्हेयर इज़ द टैलेंट?" — आय हैव हर्ड दिस लैमेंट फ़ॉर 20 इयर्स।

解决方案

Mercatus हैज़ हंड्रेड्स ऑफ़ फ़ेलोज़ — हाइ-स्कूल, अंडरग्रैड, PhDs, पोस्ट-डॉक्स, प्रोफ़ेसर्स, इमरजेंट वेंचर फ़ेलोज़, पॉलिसी फ़ेलोज़। 6–800 फ़ेलोज़ एवरी ईयर।

सो: The 1991 Fellowship — यंग पीपल वर्किंग ऑन 1–2 पॉलिसी एरियाज़ ऐट द स्टेट लेवल। 3 years of incubation।

  • हैच्ड द आइडिया लास्ट अक्टूबर
  • लॉन्च्ड जनवरी
  • अनाउंस्ड फ़ेलोज़ लास्ट मंथ
  • 12 फ़ैंटास्टिक यंग फ़ेलोज़, 10 डिफ़रेंट स्टेट्स — कवरिंग अबाउट हाफ़ ऑफ़ इंडिया

Ankita Dinkar इज़ द प्रोग्राम मैनेजर, रनिंग द ऑरिएंटेशन इन न्यू दिल्ली राइट नाउ।

आय डोंट वांट अनदर 20 इयर्स टु पास फ़ॉर द सेम लैमेंट। आय हैव टेकन इट अपॉन माइसेल्फ़ दैट वी विल सॉल्व दिस प्रॉब्लम।

十六、致谢

Oral History Team:
K.P. Krishnan, Ajay Shah, Niranjan Rajadhyaksha, Nona Storr, Ryan Perkins, Prakhar Mishra, Gaurav Chintamani (और उनके students Anshul Jain, Prakhar Yadav), Saurabh Mishra, Varun (Chennai), Ashish Krishnamurthy (audio), Berri Han (transcripts), Akrit Harikumar (scrubbing)।

Legal Team: Raksha Deka, Pradyumn Kasta।

Reformers who spoke to us: Dr. Rangarajan, Dr. Vijay Kelkar, Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Dr. Shankar Acharya, Dr. Rakesh Mohan, P. Chidambaram, Dr. Ashok Desai, Jairam Ramesh, Martin Wolf (recorded by Shreyas), N. R. Narayana Murthy, Tarun Das।

Website: Sameshan and Arvind (EV winners); Mercatus IT team, Jeff Holmes।

Essayists: Dinyar Patel, Anupam Manur, Anirudh Burman, Uday Bhatia, Renuka Sane, Ovee Karwa, Sahil Deo, Shambhavi Joshi, Aditi Bhomick, Samriddhi, Bhargavi Zaveri, Jaidev Joshi, Shahid Mohammad Lone, Harini Subramanyam, Zerick Dastur।

Video Series Guests (partial): Naushad Forbes, Amit Varma, Manish Sabharwal, Karthik Muralidharan, Rajeev Mantri, Vinay Sitapati, Arvind Subramanian, R. Sharan, M. R. Sharan, Nitin Pai, Doug Irwin, Larry White।

Board of Advisors (informal): Montek Singh Ahluwalia, Dr. Rakesh Mohan — मेंटर्स जो हमें call the "Library of Congress of the 1991 Reforms"।

Institutional Support: Daniel Rothschild, Ben Klutsey, Tyler Cowen, Peter Boettke, Kinshuk Dang (newsletter to econ clubs), Kilan (ऑपरेशन्स), Harry David (publications, Boettke's former student), Ashleigh Sheller (events), Nilekani Philanthropies & Dr. Janhavi Nilekani (conference partners)।

十七、结语

"पीपल हु आर विलिंग टु डु द वर्क — दैट्स व्हाट इज़ स्केयर्स।"

"आय एम ग्यान इज़ मुफ़्त। नाउ आय हैव टु गिव द ग्यान एंड द आइडियाज़ — समवन हैज़ टु डु द वर्क, व्हिच इज़ ऑलवेज द हार्ड पार्ट।"

"थैंक यू फ़ॉर हैविंग अस ऑन द पॉडकास्ट, एंड फ़ॉर द मेंटरशिप। आय हैव द मेंटरशिप एज़ ऑलवेज।"

"सी यू गाइज़ सून इन द ऑफ़िस।"
