item.description:
## 一、最令人震撼的观察：这个项目在无意识地"重演"1991改革本身
听完全部内容，最让我意外的不是印度改革的细节，而是**这个"1991 Project"团队正在以一种近乎神秘的方式，复刻他们所研究的那场改革的每一个组织学特征**：
- 改革靠的是 **少数互相信任的人** + **冷邮件式的横向连接**（Rangarajan 从来不认识 Y.V. Reddy，凭一份公务员名单发掘他）——这个项目也是靠三个人 + 给部长发冷邮件、在机场"劫持"Chidambaram 起家的； - 改革之所以停摆是因为"没人培养下一代技术官僚"——项目团队因此把**培育 stage-level 的年轻政策人才**（1991 Fellowship）当成核心答案； - 改革在 M Document 里坚持 **general equilibrium**（六件事必须一起做）——项目也拒绝了"只做口述"或"只做档案"的单一路径，而是把口述史 + 专家委员会报告 + 传记 + 视频 + 会议 **打包成一个整体**才起作用。
**换言之，他们不是在"研究"改革者的方法论——他们是在无意识地"是"那个方法

item.title: [Lex Clips] How the Confederacy almost won the Civil War - historian debunks myth | Gary Gallagher
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的"胜负条件不对称"——这是一场被误读的战争

大多数人被数字迷惑：2200万 vs 900万，工业压倒农业，看起来北方赢定了。但 Gallagher 抛出了一个反直觉的框架——联邦方的"胜利门槛"比北方低一个数量级。北方必须"征服"，南方只需"让北方厌倦"。这不是军事问题，而是博弈论中的"不对称目标函数"：一方追求 max，另一方只需让对方的 cost function 超过 tolerance 阈值。

这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：这正是越战、阿富汗战争、乃至今天所有游击战与反恐战争的底层结构。Gallagher 自己就点了越南这个例子——美军没有输在战场上，输在了本土客厅的电视机前。换句话说，南方邦联是"游击叙事"的祖师爷之一，只不过它披着正规军的外衣。这也解释了为什么"1864年夏天"这个时间点如此关键——那是林肯连任选举前夕，一场政治溃败几乎就要发生。内战不是在战场上决定的，而是在选票箱前差点被翻盘。

二、令人意外的观察：南方最大的敌人不是北方，而是"只有一个李将军"

Gallagher 说了一句极其精准但很少被强调的话："The Confederacy only ever found one [good army commander]. And that's Lee. And they had more than one army."

这句话的含义是灾难性的——南方的战略架构是"单点故障"（single point of failure）系统。这在工程学里是最忌讳的设计。你有多条战线，但只有一个能打的将军，那么你的战略就必然退化为"李在的地方赢，李不在的地方输"。田纳西、密西西比、维克斯堡的连续崩盘，本质上不是运气不好，而是组织架构的必然产物。

跨领域连接：这和现代创业公司"过度依赖创始人"、大型组织"关键人物风险"、甚至 AI 系统"单一模型依赖"是同构的问题。南方邦联死于"人才板凳深度不足"——一个比奴隶制、比工业差距更精细也更现代的死因。

三、被忽视的"感知战争"：真正的分裂发生在开战之前

访谈末尾那段最容易被读者略过，但它可能是整段对话里最有当代意义的洞见：南北双方在开战前就已经在互相"脸谱化"了——南方人是懒惰、暴力、习惯于用棍棒解决问题的野蛮人；北方人是没有家庭观念、只知道追逐金钱的物质主义者。"It doesn't even matter whether any of that is true."

这句话是整个访谈的隐藏钥匙。内战的本质是一场"感知战争"，不是资源战争、不是制度战争。真正的战争在人脑子里已经打完了，战场只是"结算界面"。

出人意料的跨领域连接：这与社交媒体时代的"信息茧房 → 极化 → 部落化"路径完全同构。19世纪的报纸、小册子、教堂布道，就是当年的算法推荐系统——它们把"另一方"渲染成异类，直到不打一场无法收场。Gallagher 提到"新教教会因奴隶制分裂"——这是极其惊人的信号：当一个社会连"共同的上帝"都无法共享时，共同的国家也就不远了。

更令人不安的推论：南北的共同点其实远远多于分歧——共同语言、共同宗教、共同的建国文献。但人类有一种令人费解的能力：在共同点如此之多的情况下，仍然能精准地找到差异并将其放大到不可调和。这个机制没有随内战消失。它只是在等待下一次被激活。

一个额外的、你可能没想到的角度：南方军官的"宗教性"远高于北方——Lee、Jackson、Stuart 都是虔诚的教徒，Grant、Sherman、Sheridan 相对世俗。这不是巧合。当你在为一个"必败"的事业而战时，宗教是唯一能给"坚持下去"提供合法性的叙事。这也解释了为什么"迷失的事业（Lost Cause）"神话在战后能长期存活——它本质上是一种宗教结构，不是历史叙事。

📝 转录文本

一、开战之初：那个"胜利必然属于北方"的迷思

Let's uh at the start — first shots fired at Fort Sumter, as you mentioned. And this thing starts brewing and escalating towards a full-on war. What are the different advantages of each side from a military perspective?

Here is one of the great misconceptions about the Civil War. Among the people who know anything about it — which in the US is a very small percentage — but if they know anything, they know United States victory was inevitable, because the United States had 22 million people, the Confederacy had 5 and 1/2 million white people, and 3 and 1/2 million enslaved people. The United States economy was infinitely more powerful than the Confederate economy. The United States had the United States Army. The United States had the United States Navy.

Really? Who's going to win this war? The US. It's inevitable. Next question.

It's not true at all. The US did not have those advantages — but the Confederacy had compensating advantages.

二、南方的"低门槛"胜利条件

And one of those advantages was: it had a much lower bar to cross for success. It didn't have to invade the United States, didn't have to capture Washington, it didn't have to project its military power into New England. All it had to do was convince a majority of the civilian population of the loyal states that it wasn't worth the cost to make these rebel states come back into the Union.

These are two democratic republics at war, and in the end the civilian sector decides. Somebody my age — we have the perfect example: Vietnam. The United States was not defeated militarily in Vietnam, and it didn't matter. Cuz when the people said "we're not going to support this war anymore," the war's going to come to an end.

The smart people in the Confederacy understood this. They understood it at the time. Lee understood it. Jefferson Davis understood it. You had key people saying: there's no way that a nation as large as ours, and a population as large as ours, has ever been subjected in a war like this. A tie is as good as a win for the Confederacy. And they came very close to that in the summer of 1864.

三、地理、后勤与"防守方"优势

The other thing is the sheer size of the Confederacy is a huge advantage to them. It's huge. With a very poor transportation and communication infrastructure in many ways — and to move a large army deep into the Confederacy is a huge logistical problem. The same thing had happened to the British both during the American Revolution and the War of 1812. They confront this — the Confederacy is as big as all of Western Europe. That's a problem.

It's also a problem that the Confederates are literally fighting to defend their homes. That's almost always a stronger factor than trying to impose your will on somebody else. All of these factors help the Confederacy.

The US did have an army. The army had 15,000 men in it in 1860. 15,000. The Navy had fewer than 50 vessels — most of them on overseas stations. There were exactly three vessels available to blockade the Confederacy at the beginning of the war. A Confederate coastline is 3,600 mi long. Probably not going to be able to shut down a lot there.

So the point is: there are factors that help both sides. To me, the conditions for victory are the most important factor that favors the Confederacy. We just have to make it painful enough to the United States that they're going to say: "let them go. We never liked South Carolina anyway. Just let them go. It's not worth it. It's killing too many of our boys. It's costing too much money. And we don't have to worry about slavery in the territories if they're gone — cuz they'll be gone and our territories will be free of slavery."

So again, the union is the invading force. Geography comes into play, as you mentioned — land. And so in some sense it's a miracle that the war lasted as long as it did, and then there was as much motivation.

Yes, that they stuck to it. Because again, victory for the Confederacy was: stop the war.

四、将领对决：西点军校出身的同门相残

Neither side has an advantage in terms of its leadership. The generals all come — you often used to read frequently "Confederates had better generals" — but this is the first war where West Pointers are in charge. They were subalterns in Mexico. West Point is the United States Military — where the professional officer corps gets its training. It was established under Jefferson. It's the premier engineering school in the United States, and West Point-trained engineers are very very prominent. When they get out of the army — and even when they're in the army.

But by the time of the Civil War, it is West Pointers who were lieutenants and captains in the war with Mexico who are now going to be the people in charge. Almost every army commander, almost every corps commander — which is the next level — are West Point graduates. They took the same classes from the same professors, read the same textbooks, served under either Winfield Scott or Zachary Taylor in Mexico. They bring the same background and body of doctrine and training to the table. It would have been weird if one side or the other had an inherent advantage in leadership.

The one place where the US ends up with an advantage is that, over the course of the war, it found — in my view — four men who could command armies effectively: Grant, Sherman, Philip Henry Sheridan, and George H. Thomas. The Confederacy only ever found one. And that's Lee. And they had more than one army, so that's a problem. If you have more than one army but only one really good army commander, that puts you at a disadvantage.

五、军事平衡：技术、组织与士兵体验

In what ways would the two sides balance militarily?

Both brought the same notions of how to fight a war to the table, because the officer corps on both sides had been trained in the same way. Neither side has a real advantage in terms of technology. Both sides used the railroad. Both sides used the telegraph. The United States could have used repeating weapons, but decided not to. The Confederacy didn't have the industrial capacity to produce them.

So the war is fought by infantrymen for the most part, carrying muzzle-loading single-shot muskets — rifle muskets. That's the weapon that inflicts 85% of the casualties in the Civil War, and they both have exactly the same thing. And they have the same kinds of artillery pieces. The United States Navy is much bigger — and the Navy is important — but armies really decide the war. And the armies are organized exactly the same way. They get officers the same way. They're very similar.

So what was the actual fighting like? Like you mentioned, most of it was with muskets. What was the experience of it like?

It's linear formations — shoulder-to-shoulder kinds of formations that would allow you to maintain unit integrity on a battlefield, which is one reason casualties were high. They line up and fight each other.

As the war went on, they resorted more and more — one of the developments was that field entrenchments became very common by 1864. Both armies, if they would stop for the night, they would entrench. They'd throw up field works, which gave the defenders a much greater power vis-à-vis the attacking force. They came to decide that you needed about a three-to-one advantage in numbers to have a successful attack once field entrenchments were in place.

But it's an infantryman's war overwhelmingly. And the infantryman's experience on both sides — the United States side was a little better supplied. Union soldiers ate a little better. For the most part, they got regular issues of clothing a little more regularly than the Confederates did. Their uniforms all kind of looked the same. The Confederates would have had a more motley look. But the Confederates didn't lose any battles because they didn't have enough shoes, and they didn't lose any battles cuz they didn't have enough powder. They never had a problem with that.

So it's a war where each side looks like the other side. In terms of what the armies actually — if we had wandered through the armies and watched them in battle, they would have looked the same to us.

六、疾病：比子弹更致命的敌人

But it wasn't just about bullets. There's also dysentery and disease.

Two out of every three soldiers who died, died of disease. It depends on what unit you're in. If you're in the Irish Brigade — ah, God love them. You know, just point us towards something and let us indulge in self-immolation for God's sake. The Irish Brigade had the reverse: they had two men who died from battle wounds for every man who died from disease. But overall, it's one man died from battle wounds and two died from disease.

Overall casualties — killed, wounded, prisoners of war — about a million and a half casualties in the Civil War.

七、移民、族裔与偏见

There's this idea that a big part of the American spirit is the Scots-Irish spirit — the fighting spirit. Do you think there's some truth to that?

Well, the songs are Irish songs that both sides sing with different words. There are a lot of Irish soldiers in the Union Army. But in the entire military-age white population of the loyal states in 1860, just about a third were born somewhere other than the United States. And they made up about a quarter of all the soldiers. So they're actually underrepresented in the United States Army. Far lower percentage of foreign-born soldiers in the Confederate Army, but there they're a little bit overrepresented.

So there are lots of foreign-born soldiers in the army. The largest group are not Irish. They're the second largest group. The largest group are Germans on the US side. The Irish are second, and then you'd go way down the line for yet others.

We talked pretty thoroughly about slavery. Can we talk about immigration? What was the view at the time of immigrants?

Well, I think you know the answer to that: "We need to have all that stuff done, but we don't especially like the people doing it." That's basically it.

Oh, America.

The anti-Irish — a lot of it is bound up with anti-Catholic sentiment. Cuz Irish are changing the nature of the country. The country's a Protestant British country, and here come all these Irishmen — especially in the '40s and '50s (my Gallaghers came in the late '50s). They are changing the nature and they take over. "Look at them. They don't know their place. Pretty soon they're taking over cities, and they all cheat when they vote. We know that. You can buy an Irish vote for one drink."

This all sounds familiar, right?

The cartoons were brutal on depicting African-American characters, but they also depicted the Irish as sort of simian characters, often with a jug of whiskey in one hand. There's profound prejudice. And prejudice against the Germans, whom they called "the Dutch" — that was what the soldiers would call the German regiments, "Dutch regiments." Yeah, there's a lot of ethnic prejudice.

八、宗教与战争的正当化

So both sides were primarily Protestant Christians.

Overwhelmingly.

At that time it's a very religious country. So the religious sentiment was pretty strong.

Units had chaplains, and there were Catholic priests with Catholic units. Yes, very big presence.

Was Christianity used to justify —

Of course it was. Both sides used it. Yes. I don't mean to jump on your question, but yes, they did.

How was it used to justify fighting for a nation?

Yeah, there's a lot of fighting in the Bible. A lot of people killing other people — but as long as you're doing it for the right reasons, you can. And you could use it different ways. You can deal with setbacks by saying, "Well, God tests us. We're being tested. What do you do when God tests you? You don't give up when God tests you. You try harder when God tests you."

The very top leaders — this is interesting. The top leaders on the Confederate side — the most famous ones, Lee, Stonewall Jackson, Jeb Stuart — they were much more overtly religious than people like Grant, Sherman, Philip Sheridan. Much, much more. Lee is an Episcopalian. Jackson was a Presbyterian. Their official reports, their correspondence, it's filled with allusions to religion — much more than Grant's or Sherman's.

九、非裔美国人参军：象征与现实

What about African Americans in the army?

There were about 200,000 black men who served in what were called United States Colored Troops units (USCT).

Those are on the Union side.

Yes. Okay — let's just dispense with the hallucination that there were a lot of black men in the Confederate Army. That is such total ridiculous nonsense, utterly unsupported by any evidence that anyone would consider credible. This whole notion — it's just preposterous. And I'm really managing my language right here. I'm not saying what I really think it is.

I've seen estimates of as high as 100,000 black men in the Confederate army. Really? No, no. Were there black men with the Confederate armies? Yes — enslaved black men who are doing all kinds of non-military things in the army, to free more white men to shoulder muskets and shoot at Yankees. That's what's going on in the Confederate army.

There are a lot of black men around Union armies before they became soldiers as well. But these 200,000 black men join the military service during the war. They're in the navy and in the army. They'd always been in the navy — the US navy — and they're not segregated in the navy in the way that they can be in the army. You have integrated crews on naval vessels, although they're separated in some ways. There've always been black sailors in the navy.

The army — no, that was a big thing. It's a big thing to put black men in uniform. And for a Confederate, it's bad enough if you announce emancipation, but then you start arming black men — that, to Confederates, is urging a widespread slave rebellion, basically.

Black regiments on the Union side was enraging the Confederate side.

Yes. And they have white officers, for the overwhelmingly. There are few black officers, but overwhelmingly the USCT units have white officers leading them.

But symbolically that is really a powerful thing, right?

It's hard for modern Americans to understand just how jarring that would be to a Confederate. That not only would you have enslaved people no longer enslaved — but you would have the men in uniforms carrying muskets.

十、黑人士兵的动机：公民权的自我确认

So you as a historian — you've looked at every layer of this, including diaries. What was motivating? What was going through the minds of African-Americans who were fighting for the Union side?

I think what you would expect. They would talk about Union occasionally, but what that means to them is a union without slavery. They have — of all the people who can have a direct impact on what's going on versus slavery, there's nothing more direct than picking up a musket and firing at the people who are defending a slavery-based society. It doesn't get more direct than that.

And at the same time, you are not only doing that — you're also establishing an unimpeachable claim to citizenship. The whole point of a citizen soldier is that you do your bit for the nation that's helping you, and the nation does these things for you. Well — okay, if I'm picking up and risking my life with a musket in my hand, are you going to tell me I can't vote after I do? I thought that's the whole point of this. I'm protecting the right to vote by doing my citizen's role as a soldier.

And that was a big debate in Congress. That really changed the equation of that debate as well. How are you going to treat people after they've served in the United States units? Can you tell them they can't — that you're not going to give the vote to them?

十一、平等权利：终结奴隶制只是起点

How many people in the black regiments — but also, you know, folks like Frederick Douglass — saw that black Americans and white Americans should have equal rights?

Well, Douglass saw that, of course. But even within their context, their notion of equal rights doesn't mean that black women are going to vote. Just like for white people, it didn't mean white women would vote. But in terms of the context of the time, yes — equal rights should come out of this. Abolishing slavery is the first step of this. It's not the end game. The end game is equal rights for everybody.

Did many people see that?

No, a tiny percentage of people saw that. There's a notion that's very common that somehow the white north turned its back on black people after the war, and it should have tried harder during reconstruction to force the white south to convey full equal rights to black people. The assumption there is simply flawed. Most white people in the north didn't believe that. They believed: first save the union, and yes, we'll need to kill slavery as well. Those are the two things on the list. Check, check — we've done those. Full equal rights for black people is not on their list. And they were not willing to do the things that would have taken to do that — including the white soldiers in uniforms who wanted out of the army after the Confederates surrendered.

Said, "Well, now we need the army to make the white south do the right thing vis-à-vis black people." They would have said, "What are you talking about? I signed on to do this. We did it. Send us home right now."

I think that's one of the lessons you learn from human history across the different places where slavery was abolished: abolishing slavery is not the end of a journey. It's the beginning of a journey.

And then sometimes — quite often — takes at least 100 years to go from that to something you would identify as equal rights. And then maybe even beyond that, there's a complicated story about even outside of rights, just how society sees the different people.

Cuz there's a difference between passing — I mean, the Great Society passed most of the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, the Fair Housing Act. You got all of this legislation that does a lot of the legal stuff. But it's what's in people's heads that takes longer — and is a more frustrating process.

十二、分裂的余温：永远等待被点燃的燃料

Remains — as has appeared in human history — potential fuel for the division to rise up again.

Of course. And people can exploit that. It's waiting to be exploited, and people exploit it.

This is something we do as humans. We like to otherize certain groups.

Good to have an enemy.

And the Civil War for our country is a story of this. So understanding the Civil War is in part extremely important for understanding the division — maybe the dormant division — that's there.

Yes. And even before the war, there were notions about the other side. For a lot of people in the free states looking south, they said: white southerners are lazy, they're violent, they don't want to talk out of a problem — they'll do what Preston Brooks did to Charles Sumner: they'll beat him over the head with a cane. And they're used to this, because they have slavery, and they're used to brutalizing black people. That's just how they approach things.

And the white south would look north and say: they don't care anything about family, they're all just lusting after money, all they care about is material things, they don't have any sense of kinship or family. That's what Yankees are.

It doesn't even matter whether any of that is true, of course. Perceptions are more important than reality with human beings. And the perceptions on the eve of the Civil War were that the other side was different in a lot of ways.

They also had profoundly profound commonalities: they had a common language, a common religion, a common history, these founding documents — all of that would pull people together. But they found ways to see differences. And it divided some of the churches. Protestant churches divided over slavery.

And many of these themes continue to today.

item.description:
## 一、真正的"胜负条件不对称"——这是一场被误读的战争
大多数人被数字迷惑：2200万 vs 900万，工业压倒农业，看起来北方赢定了。但 Gallagher 抛出了一个反直觉的框架——**联邦方的"胜利门槛"比北方低一个数量级**。北方必须"征服"，南方只需"让北方厌倦"。这不是军事问题，而是**博弈论中的"不对称目标函数"**：一方追求 max，另一方只需让对方的 cost function 超过 tolerance 阈值。
这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：**这正是越战、阿富汗战争、乃至今天所有游击战与反恐战争的底层结构**。Gallagher 自己就点了越南这个例子——美军没有输在战场上，输在了本土客厅的电视机前。换句话说，**南方邦联是"游击叙事"的祖师爷之一**，只不过它披着正规军的外衣。这也解释了为什么"1864年夏天"这个时间点如此关键——那是林肯连任选举前夕，一场政治溃败几乎就要发生。**内战不是在战场上决定的，而是在选票箱前差点被翻盘。**
## 二、令人意外的观察：南方最大的敌人不是北方，而是"只有一个李将军"
Gallagher 说了一句极其精准但很少被强

item.title: [Lex Clips] The greatest president in America's history | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

华盛顿的超能力，是"减法"而非"加法"

大多数人分析伟大领袖时，习惯罗列他们做了什么——征服、建国、改革。但 Gallagher 在这里揭示的核心悖论是：华盛顿的政治天才恰恰在于他两次主动"消失"。放下军装，放下总统。他的历史地位不是靠"多做"建立的，而是靠在权力巅峰选择做减法建立的。

这是一个反直觉的系统性洞察：在一个奖赏"影响力最大化"的世界里，最高等级的影响力反而来自可信的自我限制。经济学里叫 credible commitment，博弈论里叫 tying one's hands，禅宗里叫"止"。华盛顿等于是把这三样东西同时演绎给了一个还没有先例可循的新国家看。

跨领域的意外连接：硅谷的"创始人-CEO 过渡困境"（Founder-to-CEO transition problem）本质上就是华盛顿问题的现代翻版。乔布斯、马斯克、扎克伯格没有一个人能做到华盛顿式的两届而退。18 世纪那个"骑马回农场"的弗吉尼亚种植园主，其实完成了一件当今世界市值最高的公司创始人们都做不到的事——把身份认同与位置解耦。

Grant 的"看不见就不管"，是被低估的认知超能力

Sherman 那段自白极其惊人，而且很少有人从认知科学角度读它：Grant "不在乎视线之外敌人在做什么"——这不是懒惰，也不是无知，而是一种主动抑制默认模式网络（Default Mode Network）的能力。人脑的默认工作方式就是不停模拟别人的意图、担忧看不见的威胁。绝大多数聪明人（包括 Sherman 自己）被这种模拟消耗掉了。

Grant 的稀有之处在于他能关掉这个模拟器，把认知带宽全部投给"我的下一步"。这解释了一个通常令历史学家困惑的现象：为什么 Grant 战后作为总统显得平庸——因为政治正是一个"必须持续模拟看不见的敌人"的领域，把 Grant 的战场超能力放进政治，反而变成了盲点。

更深一层：这里藏着一个组织学定律——上级承担"外部不确定性"的能力，直接决定了下级能不能发挥天才。Sherman 说得清清楚楚："Grant liberated Sherman to become a great general." 华盛顿之于汉密尔顿、麦迪逊、杰斐逊那群"比他聪明"的人，是同一种关系。领袖的智商上限不重要，领袖吸收焦虑的能力才是团队天才浓度的乘数。

"我们也需要地下室"——一个偷偷埋下的反脆弱宣言

对话最后那句被笑声掩盖的话："we need the basement too... you never know when you might need a new sub-basement"——是整段访谈里最容易被跳过的哲学炸弹。

它在说：一个真正有韧性的政治系统，不能只有华盛顿、林肯、FDR 这种"顶楼"。它需要平庸的、糟糕的、甚至灾难性的总统作为对比样本和抗体接种。这是 Nassim Taleb 讲的反脆弱性在宪政领域的翻译：系统必须偶尔经历坏领导，才能进化出对坏领导的免疫力。

出人意料的推论：按这个逻辑，一个只出圣君的国家其实是脆弱的——因为它从未测试过自己的护栏。美国宪政制度之所以在 250 年间反复受冲击而不垮，恰恰是因为它定期"接种"了地下室级别的总统。华盛顿的伟大不能孤立地被欣赏，它必须放在"我们也熬过了 X 和 Y"的对照组里，才成立。

这解释了一个奇怪的现象：为什么美国人一边不断哀嚎"这是最坏的时代"，一边这个国家在 250 年里从来没真正解体过。因为哀嚎本身，就是免疫系统在工作。

📝 转录文本

谁是美国历史上最伟大的总统？

Lex： Who is the greatest president in the history of the United States?

Gallagher： Yeah. In my view, it's neck and neck with Washington and Lincoln. Without Washington, there's no United States. So, it's sort of hard to go against him. He set all kinds of precedents that were really important.

Lex： Just giving away power.

两次交出权力——一个欧洲人无法理解的举动

Gallagher： Twice. He did it twice. The Europeans couldn't wrap their minds around that. He gave it away after the revolution. In other words, his message is: I'm not Caesar. I'm not Cromwell. I'm not Napoleon. There hadn't been a Napoleon yet, but anyway, wasn't one. I had power and I gave it back.

And then he stepped down. He would have been president for life if he wanted to be. He did two terms. That's enough. Let somebody else do it. Who does that?

Lex： Yeah.

公民-士兵的原型：辛辛纳图斯

Gallagher： But he embodies the notion of what this is—what a citizen soldier does. He comes forward at a time of crisis. He does his duty. And when the crisis is over, he is Cincinnatus. He goes back to his farm when this is over with. Because the point is: he'd done what republic—small R republican virtue—dictated. And then he went back. And that image was invoked over and over and over again.

The small R republic has nothing to do with the Republican Party. Small R republican virtue of disinterested service to your republic. And Washington embodied that. He's crucial.

一群比他聪明的人，为何都服他？

What's always been fascinating to me, Lex, is you have this guy. He's surrounded by this freakishly talented group of people in this little nation. You have Madison and Hamilton and Jefferson and Franklin. All these people who are probably smarter than Washington. They've certainly read more Greek and Latin than Washington. And yet nobody's concerned about who the man is. It's Washington. He's the guy.

"We're smarter. He's..." It's like what Sherman said about Grant one time. Sherman's smarter than Grant, probably. Sherman's saying: "I know more about strategy than Grant. I know more about tactics. I know more about supply. I know more about everything than U.S. Grant does. But where he beats me and where he beats the world is he don't give a damn what the enemy is doing out of his sight, and that scares me like hell."

In other words, Grant could just let the background noise go away, focus on his thing, and do what he was going to do, and Sherman couldn't do that. Grant liberated Sherman to become a great general because he had Grant over him taking responsibility.

设立先例的自觉

It's really fascinating. And Washington, whatever faults he had, he could take responsibility and was aware that he was setting precedents as the first president of this new republic almost every time he did something. It's a precedent. What did Washington do? Well, he gave up his uniform, and then he gave up the presidency.

Lex： Yeah, just from studying history, understanding how difficult it is to give away power in the way that Washington did, I had to put him as the number one.

Gallagher： Yeah, because without him, the rest doesn't happen. I mean, that's my bottom line on it, and I really do believe that without him, the rest doesn't happen. I don't know what... if they hadn't had Washington to persuade people that a strong central—stronger central—government might be possible, because Washington's going to be president, who else would they agreed could be trusted? There's Washington, and then there's everybody else.

幸运的一个国家

Lex： And I think America is a truly positive force in human history. So, the fact that whatever ideas that were created at that time and that Washington was the foundation of that, is a great gift to humanity.

Gallagher： Lucky to have him. Lucky to have Lincoln. We've been lucky in our leaders, and we were lucky to have FDR in World War II. I mean, we've been lucky to have people at moments of real crisis.

但我们也需要"地下室"

Lex： But we need the basement, too. We need the full variety.

Gallagher： Well, we've got them. [laughter] And you never know when you might need a new sub-basement. That's so... it's just... it's complicated and an ongoing story.

Lex： And it is a beautiful theater, beautiful drama. And I, like you, have faith in the resilience of the people to deal with a full mess of it.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 华盛顿的超能力，是"减法"而非"加法"
大多数人分析伟大领袖时，习惯罗列他们做了什么——征服、建国、改革。但 Gallagher 在这里揭示的核心悖论是：华盛顿的政治天才恰恰在于**他两次主动"消失"**。放下军装，放下总统。他的历史地位不是靠"多做"建立的，而是靠**在权力巅峰选择做减法**建立的。
这是一个反直觉的系统性洞察：在一个奖赏"影响力最大化"的世界里，最高等级的影响力反而来自可信的自我限制。经济学里叫 credible commitment，博弈论里叫 tying one's hands，禅宗里叫"止"。华盛顿等于是把这三样东西同时演绎给了一个还没有先例可循的新国家看。
**跨领域的意外连接**：硅谷的"创始人-CEO 过渡困境"（Founder-to-CEO transition problem）本质上就是华盛顿问题的现代翻版。乔布斯、马斯克、扎克伯格没有一个人能做到华盛顿式的两届而退。18 世纪那个"骑马回农场"的弗吉尼亚种植园主，其实完成了一件当今世界市值最高的公司创始人们都做不到的事——**把身份认同与位置解耦**。

item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个荒诞的错位：标题与内容的"元级"启示

首先必须指出一个非常戏剧性的现象——你给出的标题是中文联储会议分析（"加息还是不加"），但转录原文却是英文的YouTube涨粉建议。这个错位本身，恰恰是这条内容最值得玩味的地方。它像是一面镜子，映照出当下内容生态最深层的一个真相：标题与内容的解耦已经成为一种系统性策略，而非偶然事故。 无论是财经博主用"美联储"当引流关键词，还是这条英文小片用"从零涨粉"当钩子，本质上都在做同一件事——把"包装层"和"信息层"独立优化。

跨领域连接：YouTube算法 ≡ 联储的双重使命

有趣的是，如果你把转录里说的两个指标——CTR（点击率）和 Retention（留存） ——放到联储的框架里看，会发现惊人的同构： - CTR ↔ 通胀预期：都是"第一眼反应"，决定人们是否被吸引进入这个系统。 - Retention ↔ 就业/增长：都是"进入之后能否留住"，决定这个系统能否持续运转。

YouTube算法在这两个指标之间做权衡（高CTR低留存会被惩罚，就像"标题党"），联储也在通胀和就业之间做权衡（过度刺激会通胀失控）。换句话说，YouTube的推荐算法本质上是一个"内容领域的央行"，它通过流量分配这一"货币政策"，来调节创作者行为的宏观均衡。小创作者盯着播放量（GDP总量），却看不到算法真正关心的是"效率比"（就像联储关心的不是名义GDP而是产出缺口）。

一个让人意外的观察：小创作者的"通胀陷阱"

大多数人以为"关注播放量"是错在"看错指标"——这只是表层。真正的深层问题是：播放量是一个"名义变量"，而CTR和Retention是"实际变量"。 就像一个国家盯着名义GDP庆祝，却忽略通胀正在掏空一切，小创作者盯着播放量涨了100，却没意识到这100可能来自一个虚高的推荐波，而算法在同时记录"这个人的实际质量还是很低"，并在下一次分发时对他征收"隐性税收"。

这就产生了一个反直觉的结论：越是追逐播放量的创作者，越会陷入"算法的滞胀"——投入更多，反馈递减。破局的方式不是更努力地发视频，而是像央行观察核心通胀一样，观察那些"去除了噪音的核心指标"：一个视频前30秒的留存曲线斜率，比它的总播放量重要一百倍。这也许就是为什么那些看起来"佛系"的创作者反而先跑出来——他们无意中做对了"实际变量优化"，而不是"名义变量崇拜"。

📝 转录文本

Opening Hook

I want to show you exactly how to grow on YouTube starting from zero views.

The Core Mistake

The biggest mistake I see small creators make is focusing on the wrong metrics. Instead of looking at views, you need to be looking at your click-through rate and retention.

The Underlying Logic

If people don't click, they don't watch. If they don't watch, YouTube won't promote you.

item.title: [Lex Clips] The final showdown of the Civil War - Grant vs Lee | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"时间革命"：格兰特发明的不是战术，而是"连续性"

大多数人把格兰特视为"屠夫"或"意志坚定的将军"，但转录中最容易被跳过的一个细节其实是革命性的：在 Wilderness 之战后，两支军队只行军了"一天"就开始了下一场战役。

在此之前的南北战争，甚至整个近代战争史，战役都是离散事件——打完一场，双方后撤、休整、补充、几周甚至几个月后再打。格兰特做的事情，本质上是把"战役"这个单位取消了，把战争变成了一个没有边界的连续函数。

这与其说是军事创新，不如说是一种认知框架的迁移——它更像是工业革命的思维：连续流水线取代了手工作坊的批处理。格兰特事实上把"战争"从"事件"变成了"过程"，这正是 20 世纪总体战的雏形。有意思的是，格兰特本人是"和平年代的失败者"（战前经商屡屡失败），恰恰是这种对"没有休止的日常消耗"的忍耐力，让他能承受连续作战对人类神经的碾压——这是李将军那种精英式、骑士式战争美学从根本上无法理解的东西。

二、一个惊人的悖论：让林肯连任的不是格兰特，而是谢尔曼——但"格兰特的失败"是必要条件

转录里有个几乎被顺口带过、但极其反直觉的判断："Grant against Lee would not reelect Lincoln"。

想想这多奇怪——历史叙事里，格兰特是"赢得战争的人"，但在 1864 年 8 月，恰恰是他"赢得战争的方式"（65,000 人的伤亡、看似原地踏步的围城）差点让林肯下台、让南方通过政治手段赢得战争。真正在选票上救了林肯的，是亚特兰大陷落 —— 一个看起来更"干净"的胜利。

这里有一个跨领域的深刻联系：这与创业公司的"烧钱换市场"结构几乎同构。格兰特扮演的是"消耗资源、把对手拖入死亡漩涡"的角色，而谢尔曼提供的是"可见的、可庆祝的里程碑"。没有格兰特把李钉死在彼得斯堡，谢尔曼根本无法自由穿越乔治亚州——但公众只会为后者鼓掌。这是所有系统性工作的宿命：做真正让胜利成为可能的人，永远无法获得胜利的荣耀。这一动力学在现代科技公司、科研突破、甚至个人职业生涯中反复上演。

三、被埋葬的"心理战原型"：谢尔曼的行军是人类史上第一次"品牌战争"

谢尔曼说的那句话值得反复咀嚼："我要向他们证明，我的军队想去哪里就去哪里，杰斐逊·戴维斯毫无办法。"

这不是军事目标，这是一句营销宣言。谢尔曼摧毁的不是南方的物质基础（谢里登在雪兰多山谷已经做过同样的事），他真正摧毁的是南方对"我们的政府能保护我们"这一叙事的信任。

跨领域联系来了：这与现代"品牌信任崩塌"的动力学完全一致——一家公司真正的死亡时刻，不是财务破产，而是客户在心理上开始默认"这家公司救不了我"。谢尔曼的直觉早于克劳塞维茨的正统军事理论一个世纪，指向了 20 世纪战略轰炸、恐怖主义、乃至今天信息战的核心逻辑：目标不是敌军，是敌方民众对自身国家有效性的信念。

四、最令人意外的观察：林肯之死如何"意外地"帮助了和解

这几乎是转录中最反直觉的一段——加拉赫暗示，处决四位刺杀阴谋者 + 处决安德森维尔战俘营指挥官这个"报复配额"，吸收了北方民众想要惩罚南方的心理能量，反而让整个国家降温。

这是一个非常黑暗但深刻的系统性洞察：任何一个刚经历创伤的群体，都需要一个"仪式性的血债偿还"来释放集体情绪。如果没有这个泄压阀，那种未消化的愤怒会变形成对整个战败方的持续报复——这正是凡尔赛条约之后德国的遭遇。

换句话说：林肯的死可能反而挽救了南方免于更严酷的重建。 这里的跨领域连接是精神分析中的"替罪羊机制"（勒内·基拉尔的模仿理论）——一个共同体只有通过对少数人的仪式性暴力，才能重建自身的和平。历史学家很少愿意说出这种冰冷的结构性真相。

五、格兰特与李"假装对方不是最强对手"这件事

加拉赫的观察极具穿透力：格兰特和李都在回忆录里贬低对方，这是荒谬的。他把这个现象与希特勒轻视美军相提并论——但更深一层的洞察是：顶尖的对抗者，一旦承认对方是"最强"，就等于承认了自己命运的一部分是被对方定义的。

这在心理学上叫"身份边界防御"——当你的自我价值和某个身份深度绑定（"我是最伟大的将军"），你必须在叙事上"缩小"任何真正挑战过你的人。这与现代科技界"创始人叙事"如出一辙：为什么乔布斯从不承认盖茨、马斯克从不真诚地承认贝索斯？因为承认对手，就是承认自己不是宇宙的中心。

李将军把麦克莱伦评为"最有智识的将军"——加拉赫敏锐地指出这不是赞美，是一句用绅士修辞包裹的刀子。这种"礼貌性贬低"是精英文化中最优雅也最致命的武器，值得每一个人在职场和学术圈中辨认。

📝 转录文本

一、格兰特的总体战略：目标不是里士满，而是李的军队

And then that uh — Where does that take us? That takes us in '64 with the Overland Campaign. That story plus Atlanta, Sherman's March. That sets up Grant is now planning for how the whole war is going to go. And he envisions five components.

The two most important are: he's going to move against Lee. And his plan is — lock up with Lee, inflict the greatest possible damage on Lee, prevent Lee from sending reinforcements anywhere else. And if all goes well, Richmond would fall. But he's not mainly interested in Richmond. He's interested in Lee's army — which is what Lincoln has been trying to get his generals to be interested in the whole time. Destroy Lee's army and of course Richmond falls.

So how was he thinking about the clash with Lee? Grant versus Lee.

Grant versus Lee is just confront him.

Mhm.

二、Overland 战役：连续 6 周的血腥消耗

And they're still near Fredericksburg where they — on the Rappahannock River frontier — engage with him. And what they ended up with was a period of 6 weeks of continuous combat that began with the Battle of the Wilderness on May the 5th and 6th.

The old pattern in the Civil War like was: you fight a battle, one side retreats, it might be weeks, might be months before you fight again. What happened here is Lee and Grant fought the Battle of the Wilderness. 12,000 Confederate casualties, 18,000 Union — 30,000 casualties at the Wilderness. They marched for 1 day. They started another battle, Spotsylvania Courthouse. 12,000 more Confederate casualties, 18,000 more Union casualties.

So now you've had 60,000 casualties in two battles with no interval. That continues through May. Cold Harbor. They end up near Richmond at Cold Harbor in early June. Grant launches frontal assaults there. They come to nothing. His men are — many of them are butchered.

The bottom line is that in the 6-week campaign, Grant suffers 65,000 casualties, which is as big as Lee's whole army had been. Lee suffers 35,000, which is a higher percentage of his army than Grant lost — or about the same percentage actually. But it is a kind of continuous campaign no one had seen before, and it shatters both armies. It eviscerates the officer corps in both armies. A lot of soldiers just break down. We would talk about PTSD now probably. They just hadn't been used to something like this.

And this kind of continuous warfare — we can attribute that to Grant.

Yes, this is — and this is where the Grant the Butcher image comes in.

But also, probably as hard as this to say, it's a — it's active military genius.

Right. Well, he's doing what he wanted to do. He's bleeding Lee's army and at the same time pushing it back toward Richmond. And what it ends up in is a siege at Petersburg, Virginia, which is just south of Richmond and controls the communications into Richmond. And it's a siege of actually Petersburg and Richmond, and that is the thing that Lee feared the most, and Grant had put him in exactly that position.

三、1864 年夏：北方士气崩塌与"盲备忘录"

But the perception behind the lines in the United States is endless casualties. Who's winning? We can't even tell who's winning. We have these casualties. And so Union morale drops to its lowest point of the entire war in July and August 1864.

Because while this is going on, Sherman is moving against Atlanta and he is taking his time, not fighting these big battles, but he's not capturing Atlanta either. The whole summer goes by, Atlanta hasn't fallen, Richmond hasn't fallen. There's an election coming up in the fall in the United States.

And Lincoln decides — the morale gets so bad — he calls his cabinet together in late August and makes them sign what's been called the blind memorandum. And what the memorandum said is: we're not going to be reelected. And we're going to have to win the war before the Democrats come in because we know they won't win the war. Lincoln did not think they would win — and that's in August.

And so I think the United States civilian morale, the lowest point of the war for the United States, is in July and August 1864. And if we'd been able to stick our microphones in people's faces and said, "Well, but what about Gettysburg? That was the turning point of the war." They would have said, "What are you talking about? That was a year ago. This is now, and we're not winning, and it's not worth it, and we're just about ready…"

四、麦克莱伦、民主党纲领与解放的存亡

McClellan incidentally was the Democratic nominee for president that year. So he's running against Lincoln.

So, first of all, if Lincoln didn't win — we know it would have been good for the Confederates if Lincoln didn't win, but just McClellan…

Still, it's interesting — McClellan was running kind of against the Democratic platform. What the Democratic platform called for was basically negotiations, an armistice and then negotiations. And many people believed if they ever stopped fighting, they're not going to start fighting again. And so some negotiated end of the war that might even yield a Confederacy.

McClellan, to his credit — and I hate to give him credit — at least said that he wasn't up for that. He said we need to win the war and then we'll have negotiations. But what's clear is — it would have been the end of emancipation. Because emancipation, what became the 13th Amendment, had passed through the Senate in April '64, but the House voted against it. That isn't going to happen till early '65.

How close was it that Lincoln won / lost?

Well, Lincoln won. Grant didn't reelect Lincoln — Grant against Lee would not reelect Lincoln. But other Grant's — other things that Grant, part of his overall plan as general in chief — Sherman captured Atlanta in early September. And that just changed everything.

That was the real turning point.

That was a huge military turning point. And then on the heels of that, Philip Sheridan won a series of crushing victories in the Shenandoah Valley, the last of which came just before the election. And it was Sherman, and to a lesser degree Sheridan, that reelected Lincoln — and not just Lincoln, but huge Republican majorities in both the House and the Senate in 1864.

五、谢尔曼向海洋进军：物理毁灭 + 心理击溃

And then the thing that broke the back of Confederacy is Sherman's March — 60,000 men across Georgia to the sea, burning the infrastructure.

Yes. As you said, "I'm going to go across and make Georgia howl." — is how he put it. He added a psychological twist.

What Grant envisioned he's doing — and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia — is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and Sherman did it in Georgia.

But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically." That's what he said. "I'm going to show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go, whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." He said, "When they decide that, they'll give up."

Didn't exactly work that way, but that's what he — so he marched first to Savannah, and then the final campaign for Sherman was up through the Carolinas. He went up through South Carolina and into North Carolina.

And Grant laid siege to Lee, and the siege lasted 9 months — the siege of Petersburg and Richmond. And finally, Grant broke Lee's lines on April 1st, 1865. Lee started a retreat. Grant just gave him no pause, and he ran him to ground at Appomattox after about a week, and Lee surrendered.

六、格兰特与李：陌生的对手、宽厚的胜利者

What know about the relationship between the two men? Grant and Lee?

Well, it's really interesting. I mean, they basically operated in totally different worlds. They were both in the war with Mexico, but they weren't with each other in Mexico. And they had some awkward kind of small talk at Appomattox before they got down to business. One said he remembered the other one; the other one said he didn't remember him at all.

[laughter]

But Grant was very generous. He gave 25,000 rations to Lee's army. And to the survived — Lee's began the retreat with about 60,000 men. Only fewer than 30,000 — his army disintegrated in a week. He only surrendered 28,000 at Appomattox. They were allowed to sign a parole and go home.

But at the peak of their Grant versus Lee, surely they were thinking about each other.

They were. And I've always found this interesting. They tended to be very generous toward other opponents. But Grant pretended that Lee wasn't the best opponent he ever faced. And Lee pretended that Grant wasn't the best opponent he ever faced. And it's ludicrous that they would have actually thought that. They clearly found out that that wasn't true.

七、心理的顽固：从希特勒到麦克莱伦

It's interesting when people do that. I sometimes wonder how is it possible — there's a million examples of this. For example, Hitler just completely dismissed America as a military force.

Oh, it's — yes, they're soft. They'll never do anything.

I have to say it's probably some silly psychological things. You make up your mind for some stupid reason —

And then you stick to it.

And you stick to it. And with a lot of great generals and leaders, you have to be stubborn in the face of facts sometimes because —

The wise, smart people around you will say don't do this.

Grant's a perfect example of that, Lex, at Vicksburg — where his problem was to get his army on the same side of the river as the Confederates, where he could come against Vicksburg. And the only way to do it was have the Union Navy run — and he said to do it. "No, don't do it," said the Navy. "No, don't. No, Sherman, no, don't." Everybody said no, and Grant said, "Do it." And it worked.

It has to do with — I guess you've criticized once or twice this guy named McClellan.

I did once or twice. [laughter]

You do have to take risk. You have to take risk in order to win battles.

And I'll finish — I can't resist getting one more shot. Lee is often quoted as saying that McClellan was the most talented general he ever faced.

Really? Mhm.

Yeah, but — that's — what he actually said. And the quote started with his nephew, Fitzhugh Lee, who wrote it in a book after the war. Lee called McClellan the most intellectual general he ever faced. And I think that is not a compliment. I think Lee is saying, "Yeah, he's an intellectual. He thinks about this. He thinks about — He never does anything. He thinks about things." So I think it's actually a slight, not a compliment. I really do. Because he couldn't have possibly thought he was the most talented one that he faced.

I think it's a polite wink and nod to criticize.

It's a wink and nod.

八、战争如何结束

All right. How does the war end?

So clearly, there's the turning point with Atlanta and Sherman's March. And the election of '64 is that drives the dagger in. There's no question but that the war will be pushed to the end because Lincoln and Grant are in charge, and they are not going to take their foot off the pedal. So it's a question of time.

It drags on still another 6 months. Lee surrenders on April 9th. They lay down their arms on April 12th. There are still tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers under arms in different places, but it's a measure of how important Lee and his army were that for everybody virtually on both sides, that's the end of the war. Lee surrendered, there's no reason to push this any farther, and other surrenders came pretty quickly.

Jefferson Davis is one of the few people who didn't figure that out. He thought something was still possible, but it wasn't. That was the end of the war. The final surrenders are over in June, and that's it. And everybody gets the same terms that Grant offered to Lee. His friend Sherman tried to do more, and they had to rein Sherman in and say, "You can't — you're a general, not a politician. You can't do this."

九、Appomattox 的宽厚：一位服从文官的将军

So can we talk about April 9th? This is a really important moment of what Grant did in terms of how he treated the opposing army.

As I said earlier, he treated him the way that he knew that Lincoln wanted them treated. And it may be that Grant thought exactly the same thing. But I think this is a measure of how Grant was a soldier who knew his place. He has civilian superiors. Other generals didn't act that way — I know I'm beating up on McClellan, he's one. Joseph Johnston on the Confederate side is one. They didn't really defer to their civilian superiors. U.S. Grant did.

He sent the rations. He didn't know that Confederates supplied their own horses. If you're a Confederate cavalryman, the government didn't buy a horse for you. You had to supply your horse. And if a horse got killed, you had to buy another one, or they'd make you an infantryman. When Grant found that out, he let them take their horses home with them. He said they'll need them for the planting and so forth.

He did everything in a generous way that you could reasonably think might happen in a situation like this. Still an unconditional surrender. You are surrendering. You're going home. You're not an army anymore. But nobody's going to prisoner of war camps. Nobody's doing those things. You lay your arms down, you lay your flags down, and you lay your ammunition down — but that's it.

十、羞辱与和平：从阿波马托克斯到凡尔赛

Yeah, but there's certain symbolic actions like this that can lay the groundwork for long-term peace.

Yes, he didn't demand that Lee give him his sword. He didn't do that. None of those kinds of things that you could have done.

Sorry to linger on it, but there's certain elements of humiliation that prevent long-term peace. I have to go back to Hitler and what Germany experienced at the end of World War I.

You mean Versailles, the terms from Versailles? No question about it.

Some of it is economic, some of it is geopolitics, but some of it is just on a basic human level — humiliation. And people are just not good with humiliation. They remember —

No, and they can turn that around into something you don't want it to be. To get back national pride. But Lincoln's bottom line was: the point is to put the nation back together, and the good way to start that is not by imprisoning tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers. That's not the way to do it. Send them home, make them accept the terms, but then send them home and leave them alone.

The president wanted — after Lincoln's death, Andrew Johnson wanted to go after Lee, and Grant said, "I'll resign if you do. His terms — we extended the terms. He's abiding by the terms. You can't change the rules here."

But it should be said this is not easy to do. You have just fought an extremely bloody battle. There's hatred.

There were lots of people who wanted Davis to swing and Lee to swing. Kill them. Execute the rebels. They're rebels and traitors who almost destroyed the nation. Why are you being so easy on them? Thaddeus Stevens was on board that train. Lots of radical Republicans were: you need to punish them for what — you haven't punished them enough. Yes, you took slavery away from them, but that's not enough. They should be punished more for what they did. Confiscate their lands. Take their wealth away from them.

十一、林肯遇刺：布斯与阴谋集团

So what happened next? In terms of reconciliation.

Well, Lincoln got assassinated just a few days after Lee's troops laid down their arms.

Can you talk to the assassination? He was shot five days after the surrender, right?

Yes, he was.

So who was Booth? Who was John Wilkes Booth? Why did he assassinate Lincoln? What impact did that have?

Well, he was the youngest of the most famous acting family in the United States. Junius Booth Brutus Booth and Edwin Booth, his father and older brother, were very famous actors. And he was a very successful actor, too. John Wilkes Booth was. He was good at jumping around the stage and he was very athletic.

An ardent pro-Confederate. That's the more important — not ardent enough to put on a uniform for the Confederacy, but ardent enough to argue for the Confederacy. He heard Lincoln make a statement about maybe black soldiers getting the vote. And he said that was it for him. Somebody needed to kill the tyrant. And this is after Lee had surrendered.

So he was on the Union side.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yes.

But Lincoln was a tyrant in his eyes.

Lincoln was a tyrant because of his treatment of the white South. And he had plotted earlier to kidnap Lincoln and hold him for ransom and that didn't work out. So then he got this little group of losers around him to help. I mean, real misfits.

Their plan was to kill Seward, Andrew Johnson. They were going to cut off the top leadership of the United States. Kill the president, kill the vice president, kill the secretary of state. That's what they wanted to do.

On the Johnson side, they chickened out.

That guy chickened out. A guy named Lewis Powell was sent to kill Seward. Seward had been in an accident and had his neck in a big brace. And he slashed at Seward. Huge scars on the side of his face, but the knife hit the brace and didn't kill Seward. So Seward was disfigured, his son was wounded. The guy who was supposed to kill Johnson chickened out — and Booth killed Lincoln.

And there was a manhunt for Booth. It took a while and he was shot in a barn rather than captured and put on trial. But four of the conspirators were put on trial, including one woman, a woman named Mary Surratt, who ran a boarding house where some of them stayed. And they were all hanged at Old Capitol Prison.

And the combination of that hanging — they were tried by military commission and hanged — but they also put on trial and hanged the commandant of Andersonville Prison, which was the most infamous of the Confederate prisoner of war camps. They hanged him as well. And it seemed that those hangings sort of took the edge, the sort of "we need some retribution" edge off attitudes in the North. I think those things helped offset Lincoln's assassination in a sort of odd way. Because the temperature went down after that.

十二、阴谋论的诱惑

You talk about — maybe a bit of an aside — that we Americans like to spin up conspiracy theories about assassinations of our presidents.

So that's certainly very true, maybe true more than most about Lincoln's assassination. There was a long literature — actually began with a chemist named Otto Eisenschiml many decades ago — that implicated Secretary of War Stanton and blamed the radicals who were unhappy with Lincoln for not being harsher on the former Confederates. And what they wanted to do was get him out of the way. They thought they could manipulate Andrew Johnson if they got Andrew Johnson in charge.

So they then would pose these questions. How come no one was guarding Lincoln that night? How come the only bridge over the Potomac that wasn't guarded is the one that Booth escaped across? How come Grant didn't go to the play with Lincoln? The Lincolns asked them. Well, they didn't because Mrs. Grant didn't like Mrs. Lincoln. There are answers to all the questions, but they put all these together, added two and two, and got —

five.

And said that it was a plot on the part of the radical wing of the Republican party to get rid of Lincoln because Lincoln didn't want to be harsh enough on the South.

Yeah, it's difficult to believe that dramatic — sometimes catastrophic — things happen for seemingly random reasons — as you said, one loser.

It's not satisfying. You want a more satisfying — and that is: a big conspiracy is better. There are all these forces at work to get rid of Lincoln, not just that the one guy assigned to guard Lincoln — there's no Secret Service then — went across the street to get a drink. And Booth had played in that theater many times. He knew exactly the layout. He'd come in earlier. He'd arranged — I mean, it's just — that's the way it worked out.

And I have to say it's kind of interesting. I have to be honest with my own mind that I love a good conspiracy. My brain does.

Almost everybody does.

What is it? It's maybe depressing or heartbreaking to know that so much destruction can be caused by random events. You want there to be a larger system at play that makes you feel like there's a meaning to this whole thing — as opposed to: the tides of history can turn on a stupid actor shooting one of the greatest, if not the greatest, president in the history.

That's correct. Killing him, jumping out of the presidential box, breaking his leg when he hit the stage, limping off, and getting away. Yep.

十三、缺席的林肯

Over 700,000 people dead, these epic battles, all of that — Lincoln survives all of it. And then there's —

When they had the grand review in Washington, when Sherman's army and the army of the Potomac marched over 2 days, this amazing display of the troops that had won the war — one of the most common comments was: Lincoln's not here. Of all people who should have been here, Lincoln should have been here, and he doesn't get to watch this. He's not in the presidential box watching this. And the soldiers talked about it, too.

It's heartbreaking, really. Especially — I would have loved to see his evolution as a leader, as a human being. And the words he may have found to direct us as a country in the reconstruction.

Yep. It would have been different. We can't tell how different, but it would have been different. And I think it would have worked more smoothly.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"时间革命"：格兰特发明的不是战术，而是"连续性"
大多数人把格兰特视为"屠夫"或"意志坚定的将军"，但转录中最容易被跳过的一个细节其实是革命性的：**在 Wilderness 之战后，两支军队只行军了"一天"就开始了下一场战役**。
在此之前的南北战争，甚至整个近代战争史，战役都是**离散事件**——打完一场，双方后撤、休整、补充、几周甚至几个月后再打。格兰特做的事情，本质上是把"战役"这个单位取消了，把战争变成了一个**没有边界的连续函数**。
这与其说是军事创新，不如说是一种**认知框架的迁移**——它更像是工业革命的思维：连续流水线取代了手工作坊的批处理。格兰特事实上把"战争"从"事件"变成了"过程"，这正是 20 世纪总体战的雏形。有意思的是，格兰特本人是"和平年代的失败者"（战前经商屡屡失败），恰恰是这种**对"没有休止的日常消耗"的忍耐力**，让他能承受连续作战对人类神经的碾压——这是李将军那种精英式、骑士式战争美学从根本上无法理解的东西。
## 二、一个惊人的悖论：让林肯连任的不是格兰特，而是谢尔曼——但"格兰特的失败"是必要条件

item.title: [Lex Clips] Historian debunks myth that black people fought for the Confederate Army | Gary Gallagher
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的"制度生态学"：为什么海军天然多种族，陆军却必须斗争

最容易被读者忽略的一句话是——"黑人一直在海军里，而且船员是混编的"。这不是一句无关紧要的历史备注，而是一个惊人的制度生态学观察。

军舰是一个封闭生态系统：空间稀缺、生死一体、劳动分工无法容纳种姓间距。陆军可以维持"营地分区"的社会等级，而船舱做不到。于是海军早在南北战争之前，就已经"偷偷跑赢了"整个美国社会的种族议程。

这个模式跨领域重复出现：南极科考站、国际空间站、潜艇部队——所有"封闭高风险生态"都是社会规范最早瓦解的地方。换句话说，要打破一种社会等级，最快的路径不是道德说服，而是把人放进一个物理上无法维持等级的空间。加拉赫其实是在暗示：平等，最先从"物理不可能不平等"的地方出现。

二、"黑人邦联军"神话的真正功能——它不是历史错误，而是身份工程

把这个神话当作"愚昧的历史误读"来嘲笑，是完全错过它的意义。请注意加拉赫措辞的克制——"我在努力管理我的语言"——他知道对方是一个功能性叙事，不是一个证据性错误。

这类神话的真正作用是：在保留"祖辈荣耀"的同时，把"奴隶制"从邦联的核心动机中剥离出去。逻辑很干净——如果连黑人都为南方作战，那么这场战争"就不可能真的是关于奴隶制"。

它的近亲遍布世界：日本对二战殖民地"志愿兵"的强调、法国对阿尔及利亚"共同体"的怀旧、苏联解体后俄罗斯对"多民族友谊"的重构。所有正在丢失道德高地的政治共同体，都会在事后追加一份"少数族裔背书"。这不是历史学问题，是追溯性道德合法化这门技艺。

三、镜像偏见与美国政治的"永动机结构"

真正让我震动的段落是加拉赫描述的——战前北方人如何看南方人（懒惰、暴力、只会用暴力解决问题），以及南方人如何看北方人（无情、拜金、没有家庭观念）。

请注意：这两组指控，几乎逐字对应今天美国左右两派对彼此的攻击。红州眼中蓝州"精致利己、拆散家庭、只信仰市场和精英"；蓝州眼中红州"暴力、反智、把政治当肉搏"。模板一字未改，只是换了服装。

这揭示了一个跨领域的深层规律：极化不是新的分歧，而是同一套心理基础设施在不同世代的重新装载。经济学中叫"路径依赖"，生物学中叫"遗传下来的行为模式"，认知科学中叫"文化脚本"（cultural scripts）。美国不是"又一次"分裂，而是从未离开过第一次的分裂结构——它只是学会了把这个结构穿在不同的议题外壳里。

四、一个额外的"啊哈时刻"：公民权是一份契约，而不是一份礼物

加拉赫无意间点出了政治哲学中一个极其锋利的观察——"手里拿着枪冒死上战场"和"投票权"之间不是道德关联，而是契约关联。

这是罗马辅助军团（auxilia）→ 法国外籍军团 → 廓尔喀 → 美国 DREAMers 参军路径的同一条路径。在人类历史上，最快、最难被撤销的一条通往公民权的道路，一直是"愿意为这个国家承担死亡"。

这也解释了为什么"黑人穿制服拿枪"对邦联那么震撼——他们本能地明白：这不是象征，这是一份不可撤销的契约签字。一旦签下，任何"不能投票"的说法都会自动瓦解。这是为什么邦联把武装黑人视为比解放更严重的挑衅——解放剥夺的是财产，武装授予的是主权。

最后一个隐藏观察：加拉赫说白人北方联邦士兵在南方投降后"想回家"，不愿意留下来强制推行黑人权利——这句话是整段访谈里最被低估的革命社会学定律：任何革命，只能推进到"中位数革命者的耐心极限"为止。这一条同时解释了法国大革命、俄国革命、中国革命、阿拉伯之春——革命的终点，从来不是革命目标，而是革命者的疲劳曲线。

📝 转录文本

神话破除：邦联军中根本没有大量黑人士兵

Lex： What about African Americans in the army?

Gallagher: African Americans made up—that about 200,000 black men served in what were called United States Colored Troops units, USCT.

Lex: It was on the Union side.

Gallagher: On the—yes. Okay, let's just dispense with the hallucination that there were a lot of black men in the Confederate Army. That is such total ridiculous nonsense. Utterly unsupported by any evidence that anyone would consider credible. This whole notion of—I mean it's just—it's preposterous. And I'm really managing my language right here. I'm not saying what I really think it is.

Lex: So I've seen estimates of as high as 100,000 black men in the Confederate Army.

Gallagher: Not true.

Lex: Really.

Gallagher: Really. No. No. Were there black men with the Confederate armies? Yes, there are enslaved black men who are doing all kinds of non-military things in the army—to free more white men to shoulder muskets and shoot at Yankees. That's what's going on in the Confederate Army. There are a lot of black men around Union armies before they became soldiers as well.

海军 vs 陆军：一个被忽略的结构性差异

But there are these 200,000 black men joined the military service during the war. They're in the Navy and in the army. They'd always been in the Navy. The US Navy. And they're not segregated in the Navy in the way that they can be in the army. They're just in—black—you have integrated crews on naval vessels. Although they're separated in some ways, but there've always been black sailors in the Navy.

The army, no. That was a big—it's a big thing to put black men in uniform. And for a Confederate, it's bad enough if you announce emancipation, but you then you start arming black men. That, to Confederates, is urging a widespread slave rebellion, basically.

Lex: Black regiments on the Union side was enraging the Confederate side.

Gallagher: Yes. And they have white officers for the—overwhelmingly. There are few black officers, but overwhelmingly the USCT units have white officers leading them.

Lex: But symbolically, that is really powerful thing, right?

Gallagher: It's hard for modern Americans to understand just how jarring that would be to a Confederate. That not only would you have enslaved people no longer enslaved, but you would have the men in uniforms carrying muskets.

黑人士兵的动机：终结奴隶制 + 建立公民权主张

Lex: So you, as a historian, you've looked at every layer of this, including diaries and—

Gallagher: Mhm.

Lex: What was motivating? What was going through the minds of African-Americans who were fighting for the Union side?

Gallagher: I think what you would expect is—I mean, they would talk about Union occasionally, but what that means to them—it's a Union without slavery. They have the most of all the people who can have a direct impact on what's going on versus slavery. There's nothing more direct than picking up a musket and firing at the people who are defending a slavery-based society. It doesn't get—

And at the same time, you are not only doing that, you're also establishing an unimpeachable claim to citizenship. The whole point of a citizen soldier is that you do your bit for the nation that's helping you, and the nation does these things for you. Well, okay, if I'm picking up and risking my life with a musket in my hand, are you going to tell me I can't vote after I do—I thought that's the whole point of this. When I'm protecting the right to vote by doing my citizen's role as a soldier.

And that was a big debate in Congress. That really changed the equation of that debate as well. How are you going to treat people after they've served in United States units? Can you tell them they can't vote? You're not going to give the vote to them?

Frederick Douglass 与"平等权利"的时代局限

Lex: How many people in the black regiments, but also, you know, folks like Frederick Douglass saw that black Americans and white Americans should have equal rights.

Gallagher: Well, Douglass saw that, of course. But even within their context, their notion of equal rights is that—doesn't mean that black women are going to vote. Just like for white people, it didn't mean white women would vote. But in terms of the context of the time, yes, equal rights should come out of this. Abolishing slavery is the first step of this. It's not the end game. The end game is equal rights for everybody.

Lex: Did many people see that?

Gallagher: No, a tiny percentage of people saw that.

北方也不愿承担的代价：士兵想回家

There's a notion that's very common that somehow the white north turned its back on black people after the war, and it should have tried harder during Reconstruction to force the white south to convey full equal rights to black people. The assumption there is simply flawed.

Most white people in the north didn't believe that. They believed: first save the Union, and yes, we'll need to kill slavery as well. Those are the two things on the list. Check, check, we've done those. Full equal rights for black people is not on their list. And they were not willing to do the things that would have taken to do that—including the white soldiers in uniforms who wanted out of the army after the Confederacy surrendered, and said, "Well, now we need the army to make the white south do the right thing vis-à-vis black people." They would have said, "What are you talking about? I signed on to do this. We did it. Send us home right now."

废奴是起点，不是终点

Lex: I think that's one of the lessons you learn from human history across the different places where slavery was abolished—is abolishing slavery is not the end of a journey. It's the beginning of the journey.

Gallagher: It's the beginning.

Lex: And then sometimes takes—quite often takes at least 100 years to go from that to something you would identify as equal rights. And then maybe even beyond that, there's a complicated story about—even outside of rights—just how society sees the different people.

Gallagher: Between passing—I mean, the Great Society passed most of the—you got the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, Fair Housing Act. You got all of this legislation that does a lot of the legal stuff, but it's what's in people's heads that takes longer and is a more frustrating process.

潜伏的分裂：随时可被利用的燃料

Lex: Remains, as has appeared in human history, potential fuel for the division to rise up again.

Gallagher: Of course. And then people can exploit that. It's waiting to be exploited, and people exploit it.

Lex: Is it something we do as humans? We like to otherize certain groups.

Gallagher: Good to have an enemy.

Lex: And the Civil War for our country is a story of this. So understanding the Civil War is in part extremely important for understanding the division—maybe the dormant division that's there.

镜像偏见：南北之间的相互刻板印象

Gallagher: Yes. And even before the war, there were notions about the other side that—for a lot of people in the free states looking south, they said: white southerners are—because of their—lazy, they're violent, they don't want to talk out a problem, they'll do what Preston Brooks did to Charles Sumner, they'll beat him over the head with a cane. And they're used to this because they have slavery, and they're used to brutalizing black people. That's just how they approach things.

And the white south would look north and say: they don't care anything about family, they're all just lusting after money, all they care about is material things, they don't have any sense of kinship or family. That's what Yankees are.

It doesn't even matter whether any of that is true, of course. Perceptions are more important than reality with human beings, and the perceptions on the eve of the Civil War were that the other side was different in a lot of ways.

They also had profoundly profound commonalities. They had a common language, a common religion, a common history. These founding documents—all of that would pull people together, but they found ways to see differences. And divided some of the churches. I mean, Protestant churches divided over slavery.

Lex: And many of these themes continue to today.

## 一、被遗忘的"制度生态学"：为什么海军天然多种族，陆军却必须斗争
最容易被读者忽略的一句话是——**"黑人一直在海军里，而且船员是混编的"**。这不是一句无关紧要的历史备注，而是一个惊人的**制度生态学**观察。
军舰是一个封闭生态系统：空间稀缺、生死一体、劳动分工无法容纳种姓间距。陆军可以维持"营地分区"的社会等级，而船舱做不到。于是海军早在南北战争之前，就已经"偷偷跑赢了"整个美国社会的种族议程。
这个模式跨领域重复出现：**南极科考站、国际空间站、潜艇部队**——所有"封闭高风险生态"都是社会规范最早瓦解的地方。换句话说，**要打破一种社会等级，最快的路径不是道德说服，而是把人放进一个物理上无法维持等级的空间**。加拉赫其实是在暗示：**平等，最先从"物理不可能不平等"的地方出现**。
## 二、"黑人邦联军"神话的真正功能——它不是历史错误，而是身份工程
把这个神话当作"愚昧的历史误读"来嘲笑，是完全错过它的意义。请注意加拉赫措辞的克制——"我在努力管理我的语言"——他知道对方是一个**功能性叙事**，不是一个**证据性错误**。

item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"反常识"：机器人产业的真正壁垒不是硬件，而是"信任基础设施"

四位嘉宾在不同段落里其实都在回答同一个问题——为什么中国制造的廉价机器人无法直接接管市场？ Anybotics 的 Funkhouser 说得最直白："中国机器人能后空翻、工程漂亮，但它们没在解决问题。" Boston Dynamics 的 McMaster 更是直接抛出"不安全"三个字。

这里有一个令人意外的观察：机器人产业正在经历一次"从制造业逻辑到金融业逻辑"的隐秘迁移。什么意思？——机器人已经不是"卖硬件"，而是"卖可托管的感知权"。当 Anybotics 强调 ISO 网络安全认证，当 McMaster 提到"泄漏回传中国"，他们真正在竞争的东西是"数据托管资质"——这跟瑞士银行、跟 AWS 的 SOC2、跟离岸信托的商业模式在结构上是同构的。

跨领域连接：谁最能类比今天的机器人公司？不是特斯拉，也不是 iRobot——而是冷战时期的 IBM 与 UNIVAC。当年美国政府之所以不允许苏联进入本国大型机市场，理由和 McMaster 今天说的一字不差："我们不能让对手赢得半导体，就更不能让他们赢机器人。"机器人正在悄悄接过"主权计算基础设施"这个位置。

二、1X 的 Bernt 无意间说出了一个"AI 时代的达尔文式豪赌"

大多数人只听到 Bernt 说"我们要让 Neo 尽量像人类"，但他真正说的是一件颠覆性的事：

"我们的 cross-embodiment 不是另一台机器人，我们的 cross-embodiment 是人类本身。"

这句话的含义比它听起来激进得多。所有做人形机器人的公司都在为"数据饥荒"焦虑——因为机器人训练数据比互联网文本少几个数量级。但 1X 的赌注是：如果机器人在生物力学上足够像人类，那么 YouTube 上每一段人类视频都自动变成了训练数据。

这是一个跨领域的深度类比：这就是生物学里的"趋同进化"——鲸鱼进化出鳍是为了利用海洋这个既存的物理媒介，1X 让 Neo 长得像人是为了利用人类视频这个既存的数据媒介。硬件形态不再是工程问题，而是"进入某个数据生态位"的门票。

让人意外的推论：这意味着人形机器人的"手指分辨率、皮肤摩擦系数、肌腱非线性"这些看似工程细节的参数，其实是数据战略参数。任何一处偏离人类过多，就等于把自己踢出了 YouTube 这个几十 ZB 的免费训练场。1X 不是在做机械工程，它在做数据地缘政治。

三、四家公司共同暴露了一个"系统性盲区"：机器人时代的经济学正在悄悄从"劳动力替代"转向"事件保险"

请注意这个惊人的一致性——

  • Anybotics 的 ROI 逻辑："避免停机，每小时损失数十万美元"
  • Boston Dynamics 的 ROI 逻辑："我们发现的气体泄漏，一天能省 300 万"
  • Agility 的 ROI 逻辑："40,000 小时寿命"
  • 1X 的 ROI 逻辑："让专家可以瞬移到任何地方"

表面上他们在卖机器人，实质上他们卖的是"负事件的期望值削减"。 这是保险精算的思维方式，不是制造业的思维方式。

这里最反直觉的洞见：当机器人以"$1/小时"进入市场，最先被颠覆的不是流水线工人，而是保险行业。为什么？因为过去工业保险的定价基础是"人为失误的概率分布"。但当机器人接管高危检测： - 石油钻井平台的事故概率结构性下降 - 变压器站的火灾频率被重估 - 高空维护的伤亡曲线消失

这会引发再保险公司底层数据模型的崩塌——就像自动驾驶让车险精算师失业一样，工业机器人正在悄悄拆解伦敦劳合社几百年建立起来的风险定价体系。

更深的连接：Bernt 提到"embodied AGI 会带来劳动力丰裕"，但真正到来的第一波冲击不是"人失业"，而是"风险精算失业"。这才是四位嘉宾没有一个人明说、但被整个访谈的结构性证据反复证明的隐藏真相：机器人时代的第一场革命，发生在会计科目里，而不是车间里。

尾声：一个让你重新看待整个视频的"啊哈时刻"

回头再看四个人的措辞，你会发现一件事——没有任何一位讨论"机器人的意识"、"机器人的伦理"、"机器人的权利"。 反而所有讨论都围绕主权、数据、事件、期望值这些完全属于"金融—国家—基础设施"的词汇。

这说明我们正在见证的不是"科幻电影里的机器人时代"，而是"机器人被吸纳进主权基础设施的一次静默国有化过程"。McMaster 那句"如果特朗普打电话来我们会做正确的选择"——不是玩笑，是这个时代真正的产业底色。

科幻小说家们错了半个世纪：机器人不会带来"银翼杀手式的哲学危机"，它带来的是"新的威斯特伐利亚体系"——每一台在你家客厅里的 Neo，最终都会被登记在某个国家的主权数据册上。

Hey everybody, it's your boy Jay Cal. I'm here in Paris, France at a conference called Machina. It's basically AI in the real world. Pardon my robot. Thanks for tuning in and uh let's get started. I'm going all in.

Apploven started with an $8 domain and no VC funding and became one of the largest ad platforms in the world. Now that same engine powers AppL ads for e-commerce. All right, everybody. Our interviews with the number one companies in robotics today continue here in Paris. Really excited to have Dr. Peter Funkhouser on the program. You're the co-founder and CEO of Anyotics. Uh you make the ENM mo. Get it? A lot of you have puns. Uh but you've been working in this uh space for close to 20 years. The company's been around for 10. First five years kind of a research lab. Last 5 years your what do you call these dog based robots?

Well, it's an inspection solution, right? It's about data collection and understanding in critical infrastructure.

But the form factor is a four-legged robot or a dog as you We like to call it a dog Obot, but why did that dog format become the standard? You're not the only person making it. There's many people making it now. Why did that one become the first one to hit, you know, relative scale and for a deployment?

Yeah, in nature, you know, a lot of animals have four legs, so there's a reason to that. So, for sure, you have a great mobility. You can climb stairs. You can go anywhere a person can go. So dexterity and balance, mobility, right? Balance, but also stability. Four legs if you wide footprint, a lot of footooth holes hold on to because we work in nasty environments, slippery floors, there's, you know, rainforming, this snow falling down, grass growing. So four legs is a real good format.

Well, now this is a silly question, but why don't we make cenotars for the human versions when people are making the Optimus, the Neo, the Atlas from Boston Dynamics, those standup robots. with two legs. The concern is they're always going to fall over. They constantly fall over in demos and if they fall over, they're going to break somebody's ankle. Why not put four legs on those?

You could absolutely. And it really depends on the use case. If you need to work, bring, you know, I don't know, in a coffee shop, bring it to there's narrower spaces, right? Yeah, that's right. For us, it's not about labor replacement, right? It's what can we do better? What can we do? Super human. Inspection is a great example. So that's why we can afford having really expensive sensors, really expensive GPUs on top of a robot.

Yeah, these have seriously powerful compute on them, right? And they have to have a significant amount of battery power then. So these things can do a mission of what? An hour or two?

Two hours an hour docking station to come back charge. But they do this over and over. Some of our customers run these missions 40 times a day. 14 14 five four because they're interested in a specific point when the electric arc furnace goes up. They want to know in that minute what's happening.

At what point can you offload the very um power hungry compute and put it in the cloud?

We also do that. There's always two parts. There's parts that need to run real time on the robot because you also cannot guarantee connectivity, obstacle avoidance, data quality, making sure you have the right thing. If you upload a blurry image to the cloud, it's too late. But in the cloud, of course, you do contextual analysis, historic downtime analysis etc.

Are people asking for these to be able to operate for 24 hours yet or 12 hours?

No, for sure. So the maximum is in the I 8 hour range. So it has enough time for charging. If you need to go beyond that, that's rare. There's diminishing returns to more frequently do it. But you have to manage. They do it manually today, maybe once or twice a day. And they get eight, 15, 20 times now, right? So it's already the frequency goes massively up. Without putting people into harm's way, plus the quality is so much higher.

well seems Like you could do the same team and build military applications.

How do you think about robots that are armed? Clearly, China has done demonstrations of these same type of, you know, four-legged robots with guns on them. And obviously with AI, these Terminator scenarios are here. Yeah, they're being built in China already. Yeah, we've seen drones on the battlefield in Ukraine. Norway is not far away from Russia. Yeah, I personally don't like it. I hate it. I think it's concerned, right? I mean, as an engineer, you should have pride, right, to build technology for good. Defense is one part. but another big one now is we haven't really announced this yet but uh I've dripped it in a bit which is we are going to allow a lot of people to build on Neo so we are also launching Neo as a platform

that will be part of it. But to me, NEO and 1X is about so much more than just consumer, right? And I sincerely believe that we have a platform now which is so uniquely capable and so well situated that allowing people to build on this will open up how to use Neo across all of our society not just in homes right but it will also benefit the consumer because this will mean there will be more things developed on Neo and part of that will be an app store targeted towards consumer which we're very excited about but also it will just be in general how do you create a bigger ecosystem that can just accelerate the autonomy and accelerate the path to actually having a fully autonomous agent at home that can do it.
